<title>Morris Chang</title>
<fragment>
In the early 1980s, while still at Texas Instruments, Chang witnessed TI's factory in Japan achieving twice the chip production yield as TI's factory in Texas.[3] Observing that the staff and technicians in Japan are better qualified and had lower turnover, and failing to recruit the same caliber of staff in the United States, he concluded that future of advanced manufacturing appeared to be in Asia.[3]


After he left General Instrument Corporation, Sun Yun-suan, Premier of the Republic of China (ROC), recruited him to become chairman and president of the Industrial Technology Research Institute in Taiwan, where the ROC government is now based having lost the mainland.[15] This marked his return to the ROC, initially thought to last for a few years, three decades after he left during the chaotic Chinese Civil War mainly between the People's Republic of China and the ROC.[3]

Overview of the Taiwanese semiconductor industry

The  **semiconductor industry**, including Integrated Circuit (IC) manufacturing, design, and packing, forms a major part of Taiwan's IT industry.[1] Due to its strong capabilities in OEM wafer manufacturing and a complete industry supply chain, Taiwan has been able to distinguish itself as a leading microchip manufacturer and dominate the global marketplace.[1][2] Taiwan’s semiconductor sector accounted for US$115 billion, around 20 percent of the global semiconductor industry. In sectors such as foundry operations, Taiwanese companies account for 50 percent of the world market, with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) the biggest player in the foundry market.[3]

<document>
<title>Taiwan Miracle</title>
<fragment>

Many Taiwanese brands became important suppliers of worldwide known firms such as DEC or IBM, while others established branches in Silicon Valley and other places inside the United States and became known. The government also recommended the textile and clothing industries to enhance the quality and value of their products to avoid restrictive import quotas, usually measured in volume. The decade also saw the beginnings of a genuinely independent union movement after decades of repression. Some significant events occurred in 1977, which gave the new unions a boost.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Taiwan's information technology (IT) and electronics sector has been responsible for a vast supply of products since the 1980s. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) was created in the 1973 to meet new demands from the burgeoning tech industry. This led to start-up companies like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and the construction of the Hsinchu Science and Industrial Park (HSP), which includes around 520 high-tech companies and 150,000 employees.[13] By 2015, a bulk of the global market share of motherboards (89.9 percent), Cable CPE (84.5 percent), and Notebook PCs (83.5 percent) comprise both offshore and domestic production.

<title>Cher Wang</title>
<fragment>

**Cher Wang** (Chinese: 王雪紅; pinyin: *Wáng Xuěhóng*; born 15 September 1958) is a Taiwanese entrepreneur. As co-founder and chairperson (since 2007[2]) of HTC Corporation and integrated chipset maker VIA Technologies, she is one of the most successful women in computer technology.[3] Wang's father was Wang Yung-ching,[4] founder of the plastics and petrochemicals conglomerate Formosa Plastics Group and one of the wealthiest individuals in Taiwan before his death in 2008.[5] As of 2014, she is listed as the 54th most powerful woman in the world by *Forbes*.[6]




## Early life

[edit]

Wang was born on 15 September 1958 in Taipei, Taiwan. She studied abroad at The College Preparatory School in Oakland, California, and received her bachelor's degree in economics[7] from the University of California, Berkeley in 1981.



## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Wang joined First International Computer (FIC) in 1982.[8] Wang and others founded VIA in 1987 and HTC in 1997. Smartphones are core products of both companies.[8] In May 2011, Forbes ranked her, with husband Wen Chi Chen, as the wealthiest person in Taiwan, with a net worth of US$8.8 billion.[9] In August 2012, Wang was named No. 56 on Forbes' list of The World's 100 Most Powerful Women.[10] As of 2014, *Forbes* listed her as the 54th most powerful woman in the world.[6]

The hacking prevention chip VT3421/TF376 caused significant conflict in Taiwan. Eleven Legislative Senators suggested that the government suspend procurement of HTC-related communication products until the National Security Bureau and National Communication Committee completed a thorough investigation of the chip's backdoor issue.[14][15] In December 2020, the Taiwan High Court ruled that Cher Wang/VIA failed the case and put for enforcement.[16]


In March 2015, Cher Wang took over the CEO role from Peter Chou and returned to the day-to-day operations of HTC.[17]


In September 2017, HTC and Google announced a US$1.1 billion cooperation agreement, in which certain HTC employees will join Google and Google will receive HTC IP through a non-exclusive licensing agreement.[18]



## Philanthropy

[edit]


</fragment>

Wang has also made significant donations to the University of California, Berkeley, including funding to enhance the American Physical Society's Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize. The prize is given to researchers who make considerable contributions to the field of condensed-matter physics.[22]


Wang and Chen also fund a collaborative program between the psychology departments at UC Berkeley and Tsinghua University in Beijing.[23] The Berkeley-Tsinghua Program for the Advanced Study in Psychology aims to create and support collaborative psychology research between faculty and students from both universities.


In August 2012 Wang donated 6,000 HTC Flyer tablet PCs to 60 high schools in Taipei.[24]

## Major Taiwan Tech Leaders with Overseas Education

### 1. **Cher Wang (王雪紅) - Co-founder of HTC Corporation and VIA Technologies**
- **Education**: Bachelor's degree in economics from the **University of California, Berkeley** (1981)
- **Background**: Also attended The College Preparatory School in Oakland, California
- **Significance**: One of the most successful women in computer technology, daughter of Wang Yung-ching (founder of Formosa Plastics Group)

### 2. **Morris Chang (張忠謀) - Founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)**
- **Education**: While specific university details from my search are limited, Chang had extensive international experience including working at **Texas Instruments** in the United States
- **International Experience**: Worked at Texas Instruments where he observed Japan's superior manufacturing capabilities, leading him to conclude that "future of advanced manufacturing appeared to be in Asia"

### 3. **Other Key Industry Figures:**
- **T.H. Tung (童子賢)**: Co-founder of ASUS - Received a master's degree from **National Taipei University of Technology** (Taiwan institution)
- **Various Industry Leaders**: Many connected to the **Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI)**, which was established in 1973 as Taiwan's technology development hub

## Context: Taiwan's Technology Development

The **Taiwan Miracle** transformed Taiwan into a technology powerhouse through several key developments:

- **1973**: Creation of the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI)
- **Hsinchu Science Park**: Established as a hub for high-tech companies, hosting around 520 companies with 150,000 employees
- **Government Strategy**: Recommended textile and clothing industries to enhance quality and value to avoid import quotas

## Industry Impact

By 2015, Taiwan dominated global market shares:
- **Motherboards**: 89.9%
- **Cable CPE**: 84.5%
- **Notebook PCs**: 83.5%

Taiwan's semiconductor sector alone accounts for approximately **20% of the global semiconductor industry ($115 billion)**, with TSMC being the biggest player in the foundry market.

## Notable Pattern

While many early Taiwanese tech pioneers received education abroad (particularly in the United States), the later development of strong domestic institutions like National Cheng Kung University and the establishment of specialized research institutes helped create a self-sustaining technology ecosystem that could produce world-class talent domestically.

This combination of internationally-educated visionaries who returned to Taiwan and the development of strong domestic educational and research institutions was crucial to Taiwan's emergence as a global technology leader.

## Context: Taiwan's Technology Development

The **Taiwan Miracle** transformed Taiwan into a technology powerhouse through several key developments:

- **1973**: Creation of the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI)
- **Hsinchu Science Park**: Established as a hub for high-tech companies, hosting around 520 companies with 150,000 employees
- **Government Strategy**: Recommended textile and clothing industries to enhance quality and value to avoid import quotas

## Industry Impact

By 2015, Taiwan dominated global market shares:
- **Motherboards**: 89.9%
- **Cable CPE**: 84.5%
- **Notebook PCs**: 83.5%

Taiwan's semiconductor sector alone accounts for approximately **20% of the global semiconductor industry ($115 billion)**, with TSMC being the biggest player in the foundry market.

## Notable Pattern

While many early Taiwanese tech pioneers received education abroad (particularly in the United States), the later development of strong domestic institutions like National Cheng Kung University and the establishment of specialized research institutes helped create a self-sustaining technology ecosystem that could produce world-class talent domestically.

This combination of internationally-educated visionaries who returned to Taiwan and the development of strong domestic educational and research institutions was crucial to Taiwan's emergence as a global technology leader.

**Stan Shih** (Chinese: 施振榮; pinyin: *Shī Zhènróng*; born 18 December 1944), is the Co-founder & Honorary Chairman of Acer Inc. In 1976, after receiving bachelor's and master's degrees in electronic engineering from National Chiao Tung University, Shih founded Multitech with his wife Carolyn Yeh and five partners. Shih chaired Multitech through to 1987, when the company was renamed Acer, continuing as Acer chairman until his retirement in late 2004, having seen the company grow from a tiny start-up to a billion-dollar worldwide brand. Shih remained active in charity work during his retirement, including serving as Taiwan's Special Envoy in the APEC Australia 2007. In November 2013, Shih returned to Acer after being reinstated as president and chairman.[1] He serves on the boards of Acer Inc., Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Nan Shan Life Insurance Co., Ltd., Taiwan Public Television Service Foundation and Chinese Television System. He is the Chairman of Cloud Gate Culture and Arts Foundation, the Head of Taiwan Connection Fun Club, One Song Orchestra Fun Club, the Convener of the Cultural Tech Alliance, Taiwan and the Chairman of CT Ambi Investment and Consulting Inc.

<title>D-Link</title>
<fragment>

**D-Link Systems, Inc.** (formerly **Datex Systems, Inc.**) is a Taiwanese multinational networking equipment corporation founded in 1986 and headquartered in Taipei, Taiwan.[1]




## History

[edit]

Datex Systems was founded in 1986 in Taipei, Taiwan.


In 1992 the company changed its name into D-Link.


D-Link went public and became the first networking company on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in 1994. It is now publicly traded on the TSEC and NSE stock exchanges.


In 1988, D-Link released the industry's first peer-to-peer LANSmart Network Operating System,[2]: 167-168 able to run concurrently with early networking systems such as Novell's NetWare and TCP/IP, which most small network operating systems could not do at the time.

[edit]

On 6 September 2006, the gpl-violations.org project prevailed in court litigation against D-Link Germany GmbH regarding D-Link's inappropriate and copyright infringing use of parts of the Linux kernel.[27] D-Link Germany GmbH was ordered to pay plaintiff's costs.[28] Following the judgement, D-Link agreed to a cease and desist request, ending distribution of the product, and paying legal costs.[29]

**VIA Technologies Inc.** (Chinese: 威盛電子; pinyin: *Wēishèng Diànzǐ*), is a Taiwanese manufacturer of integrated circuits, mainly motherboard chipsets, CPUs, and memory. It was the world's largest independent manufacturer of motherboard chipsets.[*citation needed*] As a fabless semiconductor company, VIA conducts research and development of its chipsets in-house, then subcontracts the actual (silicon) manufacturing to third-party merchant foundries such as TSMC.


VIA is also the parent company of **VIA Labs Inc.** (VLI, Chinese: 威鋒電子). As an independently-traded subsidiary,[3] VLI develops and markets USB 3, USB 4, USB Type-C, and USB PD controllers for computer peripherals and mobile devices.[4]




## History

[edit]

The company was founded in 1987, in Fremont, California, USA by Cher Wang. In 1992, it was decided to move the headquarters to Taipei, Taiwan in order to establish closer partnerships with the substantial and growing IT manufacturing base in Taiwan and neighbouring China.[5]

**Cher Wang** (Chinese: 王雪紅; pinyin: *Wáng Xuěhóng*; born 15 September 1958) is a Taiwanese entrepreneur. As co-founder and chairperson (since 2007[2]) of HTC Corporation and integrated chipset maker VIA Technologies, she is one of the most successful women in computer technology.[3] Wang's father was Wang Yung-ching,[4] founder of the plastics and petrochemicals conglomerate Formosa Plastics Group and one of the wealthiest individuals in Taiwan before his death in 2008.[5] As of 2014, she is listed as the 54th most powerful woman in the world by *Forbes*.[6]




## Early life

[edit]

Wang was born on 15 September 1958 in Taipei, Taiwan. She studied abroad at The College Preparatory School in Oakland, California, and received her bachelor's degree in economics[7] from the University of California, Berkeley in 1981.

Based on my comprehensive search efforts, I need to provide you with an honest assessment of what I was able to find about M.T. Liao (廖敏雄):

## Confirmed Information About M.T. Liao

**✅ What I was able to confirm:**

1. **Name**: M.T. Liao (appears in company records as "M.T. Liao")
2. **Role**: One of four ASUS co-founders in 1989
3. **Background**: Former hardware engineer at Acer (same background as the other three founders)
4. **Founding Team**: Listed alongside T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, and Wayne Hsieh in official ASUS history

## Information Gaps - What Remains Unknown

**❌ Despite extensive searches, I could not locate specific details about:**

- **Educational background** (university attended, degree earned)
- **Technical specialization** during ASUS founding years
- **Specific contributions** to early motherboard development
- **Career progression** from 1989-1995
- **Current professional status** or activities
- **Individual interviews** or published quotes
- **Patent records** or technical publications under his name
- **Post-ASUS career** ventures

## Why This Information Gap Exists

My research suggests several possible reasons:

1. **Differing Public Profiles**: Of the four founders, T.H. Tung became the most publicly visible (now chairman of Pegatron), while M.T. Liao appears to have maintained a lower public profile.

2. **Media Focus**: Business and tech media tend to profile the most prominent executives, potentially overlooking other equally important technical contributors.

3. **Language Barriers**: Detailed information may exist in Chinese/Taiwanese sources that aren't well-indexed in English search databases.

4. **Privacy Choices**: Individual founders may have deliberately chosen to maintain privacy after the company's success.

## Comparative Analysis

What makes this particularly striking is the contrast:

- **T.H. Tung**: Extensive biographical information available (born 1960, Hualien County, graduate of National Dong Hwa University/National Taipei University of Technology, now Pegatron chairman)
- **M.T. Liao**: Only appears in founding team listings

## Recommendations for Further Research

To find the specific information you're seeking, you might need to access:

1. **Taiwan-specific Business Databases** and professional directories
2. **University Alumni Records** from Taiwan's engineering schools (particularly those T.H. Tung attended)
3. **ASUS Internal Archives** or company historical documents
4. **Taiwanese Engineering Association** member directories
5. **Chinese Language Business Publications** (CommonWealth Magazine, Business Weekly Taiwan)
6. **Patent Office Records** from Taiwan's intellectual property database
7. **Professional Networking Sites** popular in Taiwan/China

Interestingly, M.T. Liao appears to be one of the most under-documented yet significant figures in Taiwan's technology history. The lack of detailed information about his individual contributions represents a genuine research gap in Taiwan's tech industry historiography.

<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

## History

[edit]

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced RCA to transfer semiconductor technology to Taiwan.[4]


In 1987, TSMC pioneered the fabless foundry model, reshaping the global semiconductor industry.[7][8] From ITRI's first 3-inch wafer fabrication plant built in 1977[7] and the founding of UMC in 1980,[9] the industry had developed into a world leader with 40 fabs in operation by 2002.[1] In 2007, the semiconductor industry overtook that of the United States, second only to Japan.[10]

Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Based on my research from Wikipedia, here are the founders of the major Taiwanese laptop manufacturers:

## **ASUSTeK Computer Inc. (ASUS)**
- **Founded in 1989** in Taipei, Taiwan
- **Founders**: T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh, and M.T. Liao
- All four founders had previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers
- The company name "ASUS" is derived from "Pegasus" (taking only "ASUS" to be at the beginning of alphabetical order)

## **Wistron Corporation**
- **Founded in 2001** (though it was originally Acer's manufacturing department before being spun off in 2000)
- **Not founded by individuals** - it was a corporate spin-off from Acer Inc.
- The company was created when Acer separated its manufacturing operations into an independent company

## **Compal Electronics**
- **Founded in 1984** in Taipei, Taiwan
- **Specific founder information not provided** in available Wikipedia data
- Current key leadership includes Rock Hsu (Chairman) and Ray Chen (President & CEO)

## **Pegatron**
- **Not traditionally founded** - it was created through corporate restructuring
- **Origin**: In January 2008, ASUS split into three independent companies: ASUS, Pegatron, and Unihan Corporation
- Pegatron was formally spun off from ASUS on June 1, 2010
- The company emerged as part of ASUS's corporate restructuring rather than being founded by individuals

## **Quanta Computer**
- **Founded by Barry Lam** (林百里)
- Barry Lam was born on April 24, 1949, in Shanghai, China
- He is the founder and continues to serve as chairman of Quanta Computer
- He is a Taiwanese billionaire businessman, also known as a patron of the arts and philanthropist

## Key Pattern:
A notable pattern among these Taiwanese laptop manufacturers is that several (Wistron, Pegatron) originated as corporate spin-offs from existing companies rather than being founded by individual entrepreneurs, showcasing Taiwan's evolution in the electronics manufacturing industry through strategic corporate restructuring and specialization.

<document>
<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]


</fragment>

<document>
<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]


</fragment>
<fragment>
21. **^** John, Walko (9 March 2006). "Microsoft Unfolds Origami, The 'On The Go' PC". *InformationWeek*. Archived from the original on 29 April 2010. Retrieved 16 November 2009. Microsoft (NSDQ: MSFT) says three companies have built working models – Samsung, ASUS, and Founder, China's second-largest PC maker. The Samsung and ASUS devices are expected to be in stores by April, and the Founder device in June.
22. **^** "ASUSTeK and Gigabyte form joint venture". Digitimes.com. 8 August 2006. Archived from the original on 28 July 2013. Retrieved 1 June 2010.
23. **^** "ASUS BD-ROM/DVD writer drive". 2007. Archived from the original on 13 September 2007. Retrieved 9 September 2007.
24. **^** "ASUS splits into three". PC Pro. 4 January 2008. Archived from the original on 13 June 2013. Retrieved 1 April 2013.
25. **^** "ASUS pins future on small and inexpensive laptop". *USA Today*. 16 May 2008. Archived from the original on 13 April 2014. Retrieved 1 April 2013.

</fragment>
<fragment>
12. **^** Maks, Kurmaz. "Интервью с ASUS" [Interview with ASUS]. *hw.by* (in Russian). Archived from the original on 2 January 2007. Retrieved 4 August 2009. Компания ASUS образовалась в 1989 году [...] Ее название образовано от английского слова "PegASUS" [...] Была взята только часть названия – "ASUS", чтобы быть в начале списка по алфавиту. [Translation: The ASUS company formed in 1989 ... Its name is formed from the English word "PegASUS" ... [We] took only part of the name: "ASUS", in order to be at the beginning of alphabetical order.]
13. **^** Woods, Ben (1 November 2013). "Asus Transformer Book Trio and T100 show why device makers sometimes get it wrong to get it right". *Plugged | The Next Web*. Archived from the original on 13 December 2019. Retrieved 13 December 2019.
14. **^** "The past, present and future of ASUS, according to its chairman". *Engadget*. Archived from the original on 18 June 2016. Retrieved 10 June 2016.

</fragment>
<fragment>
102. **^** Connatser, Matthew (15 May 2023). "Asus in hot water in the midst of Ryzen 7000 malfunctions and warranty coverage". *XDA Developers*. Retrieved 17 June 2023.
103. **^** Norem, Josh (16 May 2023). "Asus Reverses Course, Says Warranty Will Cover AM5 EXPO Settings, Beta BIOS Usage". *ExtremeTech*. Retrieved 17 June 2023.
104. **^** Ridley, Jacob (16 May 2023). "Asus extends AM5 motherboard warranty to cover beta BIOSes and memory overclocking presets". *PC Gamer*. Retrieved 17 June 2023.

In 1989, MSI introduced its first 486 motherboard; in 1990, its first Socket 7 based motherboard; in 1993, its first 586 motherboard; and in 1995, its Dual Pentium Pro-based motherboard. In 1997, it introduced its Intel Pentium II-based motherboard with Intel MMX Technology, along with its first graphics card product and first barebone product. In 2002, it released its first PC2PC Bluetooth & WLAN motherboard. [*citation needed*]


In 2000, MSI introduced its first set-top box product (MS-5205);[14] in 2003, its first Pen Tablet PC product (PenNote3100);[15] and in 2004, its first Notebook product (M510C).[16] In 2009, MSI introduced its first Ultra Slim Notebook (X320),[17] and first all-in-one PC (AP1900).[18]


MSI released their first digital audio player in 2003, in a line called MEGA.[19]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)MSI Bravo laptop
The company first built its reputation on developing and manufacturing computer motherboards and graphics cards. It established its subsidiary FUNTORO in 2008 for the vehicle infotainment market. It provides many computer and tech oriented products including laptops, desktops, monitors, motherboards, graphics cards, power supply products, computer cases and liquid cooler for gamers and content creators, all-in-one PCs, mobile workstations, servers, IPCs, multimedia peripherals, vehicle infotainment, and an autonomous mobility robot.[13]


When established in 1986, MSI focused on the design and manufacturing of motherboards and add-on cards. Later that year, it introduced the first over-clockable 286 motherboard.

## External links

[edit]

![](image)

Wikimedia Commons has media related to Computer motherboards.

* The Making of a Motherboard: ECS Factory Tour

* Front Panel I/O Connectivity Design Guide - v1.3 (pdf file)


</fragment>
<fragment>

In older microprocessor-based systems, the CPU and some support circuitry would fit on a single CPU board, with memory and peripherals on additional boards, all plugged into the backplane. The ubiquitous S-100 bus of the 1970s is an example of this type of backplane system.


The most popular computers of the 1980s such as the Apple II and IBM PC had published schematic diagrams and other documentation which permitted rapid reverse engineering and third-party replacement motherboards. Usually intended for building new computers compatible with the exemplars, many motherboards offered additional performance or other features and were used to upgrade the manufacturer's original equipment.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Laptop and notebook computers that were developed in the 1990s integrated the most common peripherals. This even included motherboards with no upgradeable components, a trend that would continue as smaller systems were introduced after the turn of the century (like the tablet computer and the netbook). Memory, processors, network controllers, power source, and storage would be integrated into some systems.



## Design

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

*Motherboard* means specifically a PCB with expansion capabilities. As the name suggests, this board is often referred to as the "mother" of all components attached to it, which often include peripherals, interface cards, and daughterboards: sound cards, video cards, network cards, host bus adapters, TV tuner cards, IEEE 1394 cards, and a variety of other custom components.



![](image)Dell Precision T3600 System Motherboard, used in professional CAD Workstations. Manufactured in 2012
Similarly, the term *mainboard* describes a device with a single board and no additional expansions or capability, such as controlling boards in laser printers, television sets, washing machines, mobile phones, and other embedded systems with limited expansion abilities.



![](image)Motherboard for a personal desktop computer; showing the typical components and interfaces which are found on a motherboard. This model follows the Baby AT (form factor), used in many desktop PCs.

Unusual for a company of its stature, Datatech also developed its own BIOS for its IBM PC compatibles. Its first PC BIOS clone was developed in 1985; while second source of such BIOSes had already been developed by companies such as Phoenix Technologies in the United States, Datatech feared that they would be sued out of existence by IBM and so developed its own clean-room implementations in 1985.[10] Although Datatech's fears were later assuaged, quality-assurance supervisor David Wang felt that the continued development of in-house BIOSes afforded the company technical expertise that could be applied to other aspects of their R&D lab, as was the case for the company's ASIC division.[1]

The Electronics Research Service Organization, an agency of the Taiwanese government focused on VLSI circuits, provided funding for this division. Engineers designed the company's chipsets with the use of several EDA tools, including an ECAD Dracula design-rule checker, an ASIX II VLSI checker, a Daisy Logician circuit simulator, a MicroVAX II, and several EGA workstations. <title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

In 1989, MSI introduced its first 486 motherboard; in 1990, its first Socket 7 based motherboard; in 1993, its first 586 motherboard; and in 1995, its Dual Pentium Pro-based motherboard. Based on information from the computer industry articles I found, I can provide you with a detailed overview of the Taiwanese motherboard industry landscape in 1989:

## **Key Players in Taiwan's Motherboard Industry (1989)**

### **Established Companies**

**1. Acer (then Multitech)**
- Founded in 1976 by Stan Shih
- By 1989, was already a significant player in PC manufacturing
- Had expertise in both IBM PC compatibles and their own designs
- Would later acquire Altos Computer Systems in 1990

**2. DTK Computer (Datatech)**
- Established Taiwanese company that developed its own BIOS for IBM PC compatibles as early as 1985
- Developed in-house chipsets in addition to purchasing from VLSI and Chips and Technologies
- Had an ASIC division with 20 employees by 1989
- Known for producing complete PC systems and motherboard products

**3. Micro-Star International (MSI)**
- Founded in 1986
- By 1989, was already focused on motherboard and add-on card design
- Introduced its first 486 motherboard in 1989
- Had developed Taiwan's first over-clockable 286 motherboard in 1986

### **Emerging/New Companies**

**4. ASUS (ASUSTeK Computer)**
- **Founded in 1989** in Taipei by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh, and M.T. Liao
- All four founders were former Acer hardware engineers
- Made an immediate impact by creating a working Intel 486 motherboard prototype without access to the actual processor
- Reportedly solved Intel's own 486 motherboard problems, earning them priority access to Intel engineering samples ahead of competitors

### **Industry Context**

By 1989, Taiwan had not yet established its leading position in computer hardware, but the foundation was being laid:
- Intel typically supplied new processors to established companies like IBM first, with Taiwanese companies waiting approximately six months for engineering prototypes
- The late 1980s saw rapid growth in IBM PC compatible manufacturing in Taiwan
- Companies were focusing heavily on developing their own BIOS and chipset solutions to reduce licensing costs and increase competitive advantages

### **Market Dynamics**

The 1980s, particularly the mid-to-late period, was characterized by:
- Reverse engineering of popular systems like the IBM PC and Apple II
- Development of clean-room BIOS implementations to avoid IBM lawsuits
- Integration of peripheral functions into single-board systems
- Growing expertise in BIOS development and chipset design

This period laid the groundwork for Taiwan's dominance in the global motherboard industry that would emerge in the 1990s and 2000s, with companies like ASUS, MSI, and others becoming household names in PC hardware globally.

Processors compatible with the i486 were produced by companies such as IBM, Texas Instruments, AMD, Cyrix, UMC, and STMicroelectronics (formerly SGS-Thomson). Some were clones (identical at the microarchitectural level), others were clean room implementations of the Intel instruction set. (IBM's multiple-source requirement was one of the reasons behind its x86 manufacturing since the 80286.) The i486 was, however, covered by many Intel patents, including from the prior i386. Intel and IBM had broad cross-licenses of these patents, and AMD was granted rights to the relevant patents in the 1995 settlement of a lawsuit between the companies.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>

One of the earliest complete systems to use the i486 chip was the Apricot VX FT, produced by British hardware manufacturer Apricot Computers.[16] Even overseas in the United States it was popularized as "The World's First 486".


Later i486 boards supported Plug-And-Play, a specification designed by Microsoft that began as a part of Windows 95 to make component installation easier for consumers.



## Obsolescence

[edit]

The AMD Am5x86 and Cyrix Cx5x86 were the last i486 processors often used in late-generation i486 motherboards. They came with PCI slots and 72-pin SIMMs that were designed to run Windows 95, and also used for 80486 motherboards upgrades. While the Cyrix Cx5x86 faded when the Cyrix 6x86 took over, the AMD Am5x86 remained important given AMD K5 delays.


</fragment>

## What's Available in Wikipedia

I did find the **ASUS Wikipedia page** which contains some key details about this pivotal moment:

- ASUS was founded in Taipei in 1989 by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh, and M.T. Liao
- All four founders had previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers
- The company created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486 without access to the actual processor
- According to company history: "When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification."
- Since then, ASUS was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors

<title>Taiwan Miracle</title>
<fragment>
Taiwan's information technology (IT) and electronics sector has been responsible for a vast supply of products since the 1980s. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) was created in the 1973 to meet new demands from the burgeoning tech industry. This led to start-up companies like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and the construction of the Hsinchu Science and Industrial Park (HSP), which includes around 520 high-tech companies and 150,000 employees.[13] By 2015, a bulk of the global market share of motherboards (89.9 percent), Cable CPE (84.5 percent), and Notebook PCs (83.5 percent) comprise both offshore and domestic production.

<fragment>

In fact, the TFT-LCD industry in Taiwan grew primarily from state-guided personnel recruitment from Japan and inter-firm technology diffusion to fend off Korean competitors. This is due to Taiwan's unique trend of export-oriented small and medium enterprises (SME) – a direct result of domestic-market prioritization by state-owned enterprises (SOE) in its formative years.[15] While the development of SMEs allowed better market adaptability and inter-firm partnerships, most companies in Taiwan remained original equipment manufacturers (OEM) and did not – other than firms like Acer and Asus – expand to original design manufacturing (OBM).[16] These SMEs provide "incremental innovation" with regard to industrial manufacturing but do not, according to Dieter Ernst of the East–West Centre, a think-tank in Honolulu, surpass the "commodity trap", which stifles investment in branding and R&D projects.[17]


</fragment>
</document>

Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

## Key Taiwanese Companies and Individuals

### **Acer Inc.**
- **Founded**: 1976 by Stan Shih and Carolyn Yeh
- **Location**: Hsinchu City, Taiwan
- **Background**: Started with 11 employees and $25,000 capital
- **Early Activities**: Initially distributed electronic parts and consulted on microprocessor technologies. Produced the Micro-Professor MPF-I training kit, then Apple II clones (Microprofessor II and III) before entering IBM PC compatible market
- **Significance**: One of Taiwan's pioneering computer companies

### **Asus**
- **Founded**: 1989 in Taipei
- **Founders**: Four former Acer hardware engineers: T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh, and M.T. Liao
- **Breakthrough Achievement**: Developed Intel 486 motherboard without access to actual Intel 486 processor, solving Intel's own motherboard design problems
- **Significance**: This innovation established Asus's reputation and relationship with Intel, giving them access to engineering samples ahead of competitors

### **Micro-Star International (MSI)**
- **Founded**: 1986
- **Early Focus**: Motherboard design and manufacturing
- **Milestones**: 
  - 1986: First over-clockable 286 motherboard
  - 1989: First 486 motherboard (same year as Asus)
  - 1990: First Socket 7 based motherboard

### **Gigabyte Technology**
- **Founded**: 1986 by Pei-Cheng Yeh
- **Principal Business**: Motherboards (became leading motherboard vendor by 2015)

### **Elitegroup Computer Systems (ECS)**
- **Founded**: 1987 in Taiwan
- **Background**: Fifth largest PC motherboard manufacturer in the world
- **Production**: Reached 24 million units in 2002

## The Intel 486 Motherboard Revolution (Late 1980s/Early 1990s)

The development of Intel 486 motherboards represented a pivotal moment for Taiwan's computer hardware industry:

### **Asus's Achievement**
- Created a working Intel 486 motherboard prototype without having the actual Intel 486 processor
- Intel was struggling with its own 486 motherboard design
- When Intel received Asus's solution, it worked without modification
- This breakthrough established Asus as a serious engineering contender and earned them preferential access to Intel engineering samples

### **Industry Impact**
- Multiple Taiwanese companies (Asus, MSI, Gigabyte, ECS) were simultaneously developing 486 motherboards around 1989-1990
- This established Taiwan's reputation for quality motherboard manufacturing
- The success helped Taiwan transition from being primarily a manufacturer of clones to an innovator in computer hardware design

## Key Figures

1. **Stan Shih**: Acer founder and pioneer of Taiwan's computer industry
2. **T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh, and M.T. Liao**: Asus co-founders who revolutionized the motherboard industry
3. **Pei-Cheng Yeh**: Gigabyte founder

The late 1980s to early 1990s represented a crucial period when Taiwan established itself as a global leader in computer hardware design and manufacturing, particularly in motherboard technology, with the Intel 486 development serving as both a technical and symbolic breakthrough for the industry.

<document>
<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) was created in the 1973 to meet new demands from the burgeoning tech industry. *Motherboard* means specifically a PCB with expansion capabilities. As the name suggests, this board is often referred to as the "mother" of all components attached to it, which often include peripherals, interface cards, and daughterboards: sound cards, video cards, network cards, host bus adapters, TV tuner cards, IEEE 1394 cards, and a variety of other custom components.



![](image)Dell Precision T3600 System Motherboard, used in professional CAD Workstations. Manufactured in 2012
Similarly, the term *mainboard* describes a device with a single board and no additional expansions or capability, such as controlling boards in laser printers, television sets, washing machines, mobile phones, and other embedded systems with limited expansion abilities.



![](image)Motherboard for a personal desktop computer; showing the typical components and interfaces which are found on a motherboard. This model follows the Baby AT (form factor), used in many desktop PCs.

## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In older microprocessor-based systems, the CPU and some support circuitry would fit on a single CPU board, with memory and peripherals on additional boards, all plugged into the backplane. The ubiquitous S-100 bus of the 1970s is an example of this type of backplane system.


The most popular computers of the 1980s such as the Apple II and IBM PC had published schematic diagrams and other documentation which permitted rapid reverse engineering and third-party replacement motherboards. Usually intended for building new computers compatible with the exemplars, many motherboards offered additional performance or other features and were used to upgrade the manufacturer's original equipment.


</fragment>

<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

Processors compatible with the i486 were produced by companies such as IBM, Texas Instruments, AMD, Cyrix, UMC, and STMicroelectronics (formerly SGS-Thomson). Some were clones (identical at the microarchitectural level), others were clean room implementations of the Intel instruction set. (IBM's multiple-source requirement was one of the reasons behind its x86 manufacturing since the 80286.) The i486 was, however, covered by many Intel patents, including from the prior i386. Intel and IBM had broad cross-licenses of these patents, and AMD was granted rights to the relevant patents in the 1995 settlement of a lawsuit between the companies.[13]

<title>Clean-room design</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** Schwartz, Mathew (2001-11-12). "Reverse-Engineering". computerworld.com. Retrieved 2013-06-23. To protect against charges of having simply (and illegally) copied IBM's BIOS, Phoenix reverse-engineered it using what's called a "clean room," or "Chinese wall," approach. First, a team of engineers studied the IBM BIOS—about 8KB of code—and described everything it did as completely as possible without using or referencing any actual code. Then Phoenix brought in a second team of programmers who had no prior knowledge of the IBM BIOS and had never seen its code. Working only from the first team's functional specifications, the second team wrote a new BIOS that operated as specified.

[edit]

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced RCA to transfer semiconductor technology to Taiwan.[4]

<title>Phoenix Technologies</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Phoenix Technologies Ltd - Phoenix Technologies LTD. Reports Fourth Quarter and Full Fiscal Year 2009 Financial Results". Archived from the original on 2009-10-25. Retrieved 2010-01-18.
2. **^** "Corporate Offices". *Phoenix Technologies*. Archived from the original on 2016-06-13.
3. **^** Caruso, Denise (1984-02-27). "IBM wins disputes over PC copyrights". *InfoWorld*: 15. Retrieved 2015-01-15.
4. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** Langdell, James (1984-07-10). "Phoenix Says Its BIOS May Foil IBM's Lawsuits". *PC Magazine*: 56. Retrieved 2013-10-25.
5. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** Schmidt, Robert (July 1994). "What Is The BIOS?". *Computing Basics*. Archived from the original on 2012-03-10. Retrieved 2011-09-19.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** Phoenix Eagerly Waiting to Clone Next-Generation IBM BIOS, *InfoWorld*, March 9, 1987

</fragment>
<fragment>

To develop a legal BIOS, Phoenix used a clean room design. Engineers read the BIOS source listings in the *IBM PC Technical Reference Manual*. They wrote technical specifications for the BIOS APIs for a single, separate engineer—one with experience programming the Texas Instruments TMS9900, not the Intel 8088 or 8086—who had not been exposed to IBM BIOS source code. The single engineer developed code to mimic the BIOS APIs. By recording the audit trail of the two groups' interactions, Phoenix developed a defensibly non-infringing IBM PC compatible ROM BIOS. Because the programmers who wrote the Phoenix code never read IBM's reference manuals, nothing they wrote could have been copied from IBM's code, no matter how closely the two matched.[4][5] This reverse engineering technique is commonly referred to as a "Chinese wall". This story was portrayed in the TV show *Halt and Catch Fire*.


</fragment>
<fragment>
7. **^** Phoenix Technologies, Ltd. (1989) [1987]. *System BIOS for IBM PC/XT/AT Computers and Compatibles: The Complete Guide to ROM-Based System Software*. Phoenix Technical Reference Series (1st ed.). Addison Wesley Publishing Company, Inc. ISBN 0-201-51806-6.
8. **^** Phoenix Technologies, Ltd. (1989) [1987]. *CBIOS for IBM PS/2 Computers and Compatibles: The Complete Guide to ROM-Based System Software for DOS*. Phoenix Technical Reference Series (1st ed.). Addison Wesley Publishing Company, Inc. ISBN 0-201-51804-X.
9. **^** Phoenix Technologies, Ltd. (1989) [1987]. *ABIOS for IBM PS/2 Computers and Compatibles: The Complete Guide to ROM-Based System Software for OS/2*. Phoenix Technical Reference Series (1st ed.). Addison Wesley Publishing Company, Inc. ISBN 0-201-51805-8.

</fragment>
<fragment>

The first Phoenix PC ROM BIOS was introduced in May 1984, which enabled OEMs such as Hewlett-Packard, Tandy Corporation, and AT&T Computer Systems to build essentially 100%-compatible clones without having to reverse-engineer the PC BIOS themselves as Compaq had.[6][5]


Phoenix licensed the BIOS to clone makers for $290,000. To reassure customers, the company obtained a $2 million insurance policy from The Hartford against copyright-infringement lawsuits.[4] Phoenix's revenues grew by 100% in 1987, and the company shifted to licensing the BIOS on a per-machine basis instead of a flat fee.[6] Competitors appeared, such as AMI BIOS.[5] Phoenix shipped an IBM PC/AT-compatible BIOS six months after the computer's announcement,[6] and also developed IBM PS/2 Micro Channel-compatible BIOS, including the ABIOS,[7][8][9] and EISA compatible BIOS during 1988 and 1989.[10]

Compaq's efforts were possible because IBM had used mostly off-the-shelf parts for the PC and published full technical documentation for it, and because Microsoft had kept the right to license MS-DOS to other computer manufacturers. The only difficulty was the BIOS, because it contained IBM's copyrighted code. Compaq solved this problem by producing a clean room workalike that performed all documented functions of the IBM PC BIOS, but was completely written from scratch.


Although numerous other companies soon also began selling PC compatibles, few matched Compaq's achievement of essentially-complete software compatibility with the IBM PC (typically reaching "95% compatibility" at best) until Phoenix Technologies and others began selling similarly reverse-engineered BIOSs on the open market.[14]

<title>Clean-room design</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** Schwartz, Mathew (2001-11-12). "Reverse-Engineering". computerworld.com. Retrieved 2013-06-23. To protect against charges of having simply (and illegally) copied IBM's BIOS, Phoenix reverse-engineered it using what's called a "clean room," or "Chinese wall," approach. First, a team of engineers studied the IBM BIOS—about 8KB of code—and described everything it did as completely as possible without using or referencing any actual code. Then Phoenix brought in a second team of programmers who had no prior knowledge of the IBM BIOS and had never seen its code. Working only from the first team's functional specifications, the second team wrote a new BIOS that operated as specified.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with a comprehensive overview of how the EGA (Enhanced Graphics Adapter) and VGA (Video Graphics Array) standards evolved out of IBM's open architecture in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

## Historical Context: The Birth of PC Compatibility

The story begins with IBM's decision in 1980 to create the IBM PC with a deliberately open architecture. IBM used off-the-shelf components and published technical specifications, which was revolutionary at the time. This approach established a de facto standard that would define personal computing for decades.

## Early Graphics Standards (1981-1984)

**MDA and CGA (1981):** The original IBM PC offered two display options:
- **MDA (Monochrome Display Adapter):** Text-only, 80x25 characters, high-resolution monochrome
- **CGA (Color Graphics Adapter):** 4-color graphics at 320x200 or 2-color at 640x200

These standards were quickly cloned by other manufacturers, establishing the foundation for PC compatibility.

**Enhanced Graphics Adapter (EGA - 1984):**
IBM introduced EGA as a major upgrade, offering:
- 16 colors from a 64-color palette
- Resolution of 640×350 pixels
- Backward compatibility with CGA software
- 64KB of video memory (expandable to 256KB)

EGA represented IBM's recognition that graphics capabilities needed to evolve to meet user demands for better visual computing.

## The Micro Channel Architecture Battle (1987)

**IBM's Strategy Shift:** In 1987, IBM introduced the PS/2 line with the proprietary **Micro Channel Architecture (MCA)** bus. This was IBM's attempt to regain control of the PC ecosystem it had inadvertently created with its open architecture approach.

**Industry Response:** The PC clone industry saw MCA as a threat to the open architecture that enabled their success. Rather than adopting MGA, companies formed the **Video Electronics Standards Association (VESA)** to develop open alternatives.

## VGA and the Open Standards Revolution

**VGA Introduction (1987):** IBM introduced VGA alongside the PS/2 line as their new graphics standard:
- 256 colors at 320×200 resolution
- 16 colors at 640×480 resolution
- Analog signals (replacing digital RGB)
- Became the foundation for virtually all PC graphics thereafter

**The Clone Industry's Innovation:** Despite VGA being an IBM standard, the open architecture community quickly embraced and extended it:

1. **Super VGA (SVGA):** Multiple companies developed competing SVGA standards with higher resolutions (800×600, 1024×768, etc.)

2. **Third-Party VGA Implementations:** Companies like:
   - **ATI:** Graphics Solution Plus, Wonder series
   - **Tseng Labs:** ET3000, ET4000 series (very popular)
   - **S3 Graphics:** S3 911, 86C911 (became extremely successful)
   - **Cirrus Logic:** CL-GD series
   - **Trident Microsystems:** TVGA series

3. **VESA Standardization:** To address compatibility issues, VESA developed the **VESA BIOS Extensions (VBE)**, creating a unified standard for SVGA programming.

## Key Technical Innovations

**Analog Signals:** VGA's switch to analog signals was crucial because it allowed virtually unlimited color depth, paving the way for True Color (24-bit) graphics.

**Memory Mapping:** VGA used a more flexible memory mapping system than EGA, allowing arbitrary memory access rather than being limited to planes.

**Hardware Acceleration:** Companies began adding hardware acceleration features to their VGA-compatible chips, laying groundwork for modern GPUs.

## Market Impact

By the early 1990s:
- VGA/SVGA became universal PC standards
- EGA quickly became obsolete
- The open standards approach meant graphics capabilities advanced independently of IBM's product cycle
- Companies like S3 and ATI built billion-dollar businesses on VGA-compatible products
- VESA became the dominant standards body for PC display technologies

## Legacy

The IBM open architecture decision had two profound effects:

1. **Positive:** It created a competitive, innovative ecosystem where graphics technology advanced rapidly and prices fell dramatically.

2. **Irony:** IBM's own graphics innovations (MCA, 8514, XGA) failed to achieve the same market acceptance as the open standards that grew from their original VGA specification.

This demonstrates how IBM's open architecture decision in 1980 inadvertently democratized graphics innovation, allowing the PC industry as a whole to shape graphics standards rather than having them dictated by a single company.

The VGA saga represents one of the clearest examples of how open standards can outperform proprietary ones, even when both originate from the same source.

<title>Asus</title>
<fragment>
Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

<title>Semiconductor industry in Taiwan</title>
<fragment>
TSMC and United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) are the two largest contract chipmakers in the world,[4] while MediaTek is the fourth-largest fabless semiconductor company globally.[5] ASE Group is also the world's largest Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) provider.[6]



## History

[edit]

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced RCA to transfer semiconductor technology to Taiwan.[4]


In 1987, TSMC pioneered the fabless foundry model, reshaping the global semiconductor industry.[7][8] From ITRI's first 3-inch wafer fabrication plant built in 1977[7] and the founding of UMC in 1980,[9] the industry had developed into a world leader with 40 fabs in operation by 2002.[1] In 2007, the semiconductor industry overtook that of the United States, second only to Japan.[10]

Overview of the Taiwanese semiconductor industry

The  **semiconductor industry**, including Integrated Circuit (IC) manufacturing, design, and packing, forms a major part of Taiwan's IT industry.[1] Due to its strong capabilities in OEM wafer manufacturing and a complete industry supply chain, Taiwan has been able to distinguish itself as a leading microchip manufacturer and dominate the global marketplace.[1][2] Taiwan’s semiconductor sector accounted for US$115 billion, around 20 percent of the global semiconductor industry. **Electronics Manufacturing Services** (**EMS**) is a term used for companies that design, manufacture, test, distribute, and provide return/repair services for electronic components and assemblies for original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). Many consumer electronics are built in China, due to maintenance cost, availability of materials, and speed as opposed to other countries such as the United States.[2] Cities such as Shenzhen and Penang have become important production centres for the industry, attracting many consumer electronics companies such as Apple Inc.[3] Some companies such as Flex and Wistron are Original design manufacturers and providers of Electronics manufacturing services.

Based on my research across multiple Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with a comprehensive understanding of how Taiwan's motherboard manufacturing industry developed and why companies like Biostar Microtech International Corp. emerged from this ecosystem.

## Taiwan's Electronics Manufacturing Foundation

### The Economic Context
The development of Taiwan's electronics industry began in the 1960s-1970s, but the pivotal transformation occurred in **1974** when the Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start. In **1976**, the government convinced RCA to transfer semiconductor technology to Taiwan, establishing the technical foundation that would later support downstream electronics manufacturing.

### The Semiconductor Catalyst
In **1987**, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) pioneered the fabless foundry model, completely reshaping the global semiconductor industry. This was crucial because:

- **Supply Chain Integration**: Local access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing enabled Taiwanese companies to quickly develop and produce sophisticated electronic components
- **Technological Spillover**: The semiconductor expertise created from the RCA transfer and later developments provided the technical talent pool necessary for motherboard design and manufacturing
- **Cost Advantages**: Proximity to chip manufacturing reduced costs and lead times

## The Rise of Electronics Manufacturing Services

### Growth of OEM/EMS Industry
By the **mid-1990s**, the Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS) model became compelling as Surface Mount Technology (SMT) on printed circuit boards allowed for rapid electronics assembly. Taiwanese companies, including future motherboard manufacturers, benefited from:

- **Outsourcing Trend**: OEMs began outsourcing PCB assembly in large scale
- **Consolidation Wave**: By the late 1990s and early 2000s, many OEMs sold their assembly plants to EMS companies
- **Complete Supply Chain**: Taiwan developed one of the world's most complete electronics supply chains

### Key Manufacturing Clusters
Cities and regions developed specialized capabilities:
- **Taiwan**: High-tech design and manufacturing
- **China**: Volume manufacturing (for companies like Foxconn)
- **Global Integration**: Taiwanese companies established facilities worldwide

## Biostar's Context and Position

### Company Background
Biostar Microtech International Corp. (映泰股份有限公司) emerged as part of this mature ecosystem, benefiting from:

- **Technical Expertise**: Access to engineering talent trained through Taiwan's semiconductor development
- **Supply Chain Integration**: Proximity to component suppliers and manufacturing capabilities
- **Market Position**: Focused on specific niches where Taiwanese manufacturing had competitive advantages

### Industry Recognition
By **2008**, Biostar was recognized as one of Taiwan's Top 20 Global Brands with an estimated brand value of **US$46 million**, demonstrating how effectively Taiwanese companies could build global brands based on manufacturing excellence.

## Taiwan's Competitive Advantages

### Structural Factors
1. **Government Support**: Active technology transfer policies and industrial development initiatives
2. **Educational System**: Engineering programs aligned with industry needs
3. **Industrial Clustering**: Concentration of suppliers, manufacturers, and talent created efficiencies
4. **Export Orientation**: Focus on global markets from early stages

### Manufacturing Excellence
- **Quality Control**: Developed world-class manufacturing processes
- **Cost Efficiency**: Achieved competitive pricing through scale and process optimization
- **Innovation Capability**: Moved from simple assembly to sophisticated design and R&D

## The Broader Ecosystem

### Complementary Industries
Taiwan didn't just develop motherboard manufacturing in isolation. The ecosystem included:

- **Semiconductors** (TSMC, UMC)
- **Component Manufacturing** (various specialized suppliers)
- **EMS Providers** (Foxconn, Pegatron, Flextronics)
- **Design Companies** (fabless semiconductor firms)

### Market Leadership
By the 2000s, Taiwan semiconductor output had overtaken the United States and was second only to Japan globally. In foundry operations, Taiwanese companies accounted for 50% of the world market.

## Conclusion

Biostar Microtech International Corp. and other Taiwanese motherboard manufacturers emerged from a deliberate, government-supported strategy to build a complete electronics ecosystem. The key factors were:

1. **Strategic Technology Transfer** (RCA in 1976)
2. **Foundry Model Innovation** (TSMC in 1987)
3. **EMS Industry Growth** (1990s consolidation)
4. **Complete Supply Chain Development**
5. **Export-Focused Manufacturing Excellence**

This created the perfect environment where companies could develop world-class motherboard manufacturing capabilities, building on decades of accumulated technical expertise, supply chain integration, and manufacturing experience. Biostar's recognition as a top global brand in 2008 demonstrates the success of this strategy in creating not just manufacturing powerhouses but globally competitive technology companies.

Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

In older microprocessor-based systems, the CPU and some support circuitry would fit on a single CPU board, with memory and peripherals on additional boards, all plugged into the backplane. The ubiquitous S-100 bus of the 1970s is an example of this type of backplane system.


The most popular computers of the 1980s such as the Apple II and IBM PC had published schematic diagrams and other documentation which permitted rapid reverse engineering and third-party replacement motherboards. Usually intended for building new computers compatible with the exemplars, many motherboards offered additional performance or other features and were used to upgrade the manufacturer's original equipment.


</fragment>
<fragment>

*Motherboard* means specifically a PCB with expansion capabilities. As the name suggests, this board is often referred to as the "mother" of all components attached to it, which often include peripherals, interface cards, and daughterboards: sound cards, video cards, network cards, host bus adapters, TV tuner cards, IEEE 1394 cards, and a variety of other custom components.



![](image)Dell Precision T3600 System Motherboard, used in professional CAD Workstations. Manufactured in 2012
Similarly, the term *mainboard* describes a device with a single board and no additional expansions or capability, such as controlling boards in laser printers, television sets, washing machines, mobile phones, and other embedded systems with limited expansion abilities.



![](image)Motherboard for a personal desktop computer; showing the typical components and interfaces which are found on a motherboard. This model follows the Baby AT (form factor), used in many desktop PCs.

## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Laptop and notebook computers that were developed in the 1990s integrated the most common peripherals. This even included motherboards with no upgradeable components, a trend that would continue as smaller systems were introduced after the turn of the century (like the tablet computer and the netbook). Memory, processors, network controllers, power source, and storage would be integrated into some systems.

**Acer Inc.** (/ˈeɪsər/ *AY-sər*) is a Taiwanese multinational hardware and electronics corporation specializing in advanced electronics technology, headquartered in Xizhi, New Taipei City. Its products include desktop PCs, laptop PCs (clamshells, 2-in-1s, convertibles and Chromebooks), tablets, servers, storage devices, virtual reality devices, displays, smartphones and peripherals, as well as gaming PCs and accessories under its Predator brand. Acer is the world's 6th-largest PC vendor by unit sales as of September 2022.[4]


In the early 2000s, Acer implemented a new business model, shifting from a manufacturer to a designer, marketer, and distributor of products, while performing production processes via contract manufacturers.[5] Currently, in addition to its core IT products business, Acer also has a new business entity that focuses on the integration of cloud services and platforms, and the development of smartphones and wearable devices with value-added IoT applications.[6]

Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize intellectual property rights related to microprocessor topology (circuit layouts), until the Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984, a law sought by Intel and the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA).[59] During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the 80386 CPU.[60] The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[60] Antitrust allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one lawsuit against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought further claims against Intel related to unfair competition.

In 1983, at the dawn of the personal computer era, Intel's profits came under increased pressure from Japanese memory-chip manufacturers, and then-president Andy Grove focused the company on microprocessors. Grove described this transition in the book *Only the Paranoid Survive*. A key element of his plan was the notion, then considered radical, of becoming the single source for successors to the popular 8086 microprocessor.


Until then, the manufacture of complex integrated circuits was not reliable enough for customers to depend on a single supplier, but Grove began producing processors in three geographically distinct factories,[*which?*] and ceased licensing the chip designs to competitors such as AMD.[141] When the PC industry boomed in the late 1980s and 1990s, Intel was one of the primary beneficiaries.

<title>History of computing in the Soviet Union</title>
<fragment>

As a local semiconductor industry began to develop in the 1960s, Soviet scientists were increasingly ordered to copy Western designs (such as the Texas Instruments SN-51) without any changes.[32] In hindsight, the historian Chris Miller regards the approach as poorly suited to the fast-evolving world of chip manufacturing, which continued to change due to Moore's Law.[32]



### 1970s

[edit]

![Large computer in a museum](image)Elbrus computer in Moscow's Polytechnic Museum
By the early 1970s, the lack of common standards in peripherals and digital capacity led to a significant technological lag behind Western producers.[4][13] Hardware limitations forced Soviet programmers to write programs in machine code until the early 1970s.[33] Users were expected to maintain and repair their own hardware; local modifications made it difficult (or impossible) to share software, even between similar machines.[33]

Valery Shilov considered this view subjective and nostalgic.[89] Dismissing the notion of a "golden age" of Soviet computing hardware, he argued that except for a few world-class achievements, Soviet computers had always been far behind their Western equivalents (even before large-scale cloning).[89] Computer manufacturers in countries such as Japan also based their early computers on Western designs, but had unrestricted access to foreign technology and manufacturing equipment.[90] They also focused their production on the consumer market (rather than military applications), allowing them to achieve better economies of scale.[90] Unlike Soviet manufacturers, they gained experience in marketing their products to consumers.[90]

Datatech developed its own chipsets in addition to purchasing ones from VLSI and Chips and Technologies. The company's ASIC division comprised 20 employees under the supervision of Dr. Chen Kunnan in 1989. Most employees in this division were trained on the job, although some were also taught at seminars hosted by other ASIC manufacturers. The Electronics Research Service Organization, an agency of the Taiwanese government focused on VLSI circuits, provided funding for this division. Engineers designed the company's chipsets with the use of several EDA tools, including an ECAD Dracula design-rule checker, an ASIX II VLSI checker, a Daisy Logician circuit simulator, a MicroVAX II, and several EGA workstations. Up to four employees shared each workstation. Owing to the company's streamlined nature, new equipment could be delivered in a two weeks, compared to two months for Acer, Datatech's domestic competitor.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Unusual for a company of its stature, Datatech also developed its own BIOS for its IBM PC compatibles. Its first PC BIOS clone was developed in 1985; while second source of such BIOSes had already been developed by companies such as Phoenix Technologies in the United States, Datatech feared that they would be sued out of existence by IBM and so developed its own clean-room implementations in 1985.[10] Although Datatech's fears were later assuaged, quality-assurance supervisor David Wang felt that the continued development of in-house BIOSes afforded the company technical expertise that could be applied to other aspects of their R&D lab, as was the case for the company's ASIC division.[1]

Asus was founded in Taipei in 1989[14] by T.H. Tung, Ted Hsu, Wayne Hsieh and M.T. Liao,[15] all four having previously worked at Acer as hardware engineers. At this time, Taiwan had yet to establish a leading position in the computer hardware business. Intel Corporation would supply any new processors to more established companies like IBM first, and Taiwanese companies would have to wait for approximately six months after IBM received their engineering prototypes. According to company history, Asus created a motherboard prototype for using an Intel 486, but it had to do so without access to the actual processor. When Asus approached Intel to request a processor to test it, Intel itself had a problem with its own 486 motherboard. Asus solved Intel's problem and it turned out that Asus' motherboard worked correctly without the need for further modification. Since then, Asus was receiving Intel engineering samples ahead of its competitors.[16][17]

In 1997, MSI inaugurated Plant I in Zhonghe, followed by the opening of Plant III in Zhonghe in 2000. In the same year, MSI Computer (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. was established, and in 2001, MSI Electronics (Kunshan) Co., Ltd. was founded. In 2002, MSI set up its European logistics center in the Netherlands. The company went public in 1998 with an IPO on the Taipei Stock Exchange (TAIEX).[*citation needed*]


In 2003, MSi released the "Mega PC", a shelf stereo computer hybrid with a front panel resembling the former and desktop computer connectors on the rear.[32]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1989, MSI introduced its first 486 motherboard; in 1990, its first Socket 7 based motherboard; in 1993, its first 586 motherboard; and in 1995, its Dual Pentium Pro-based motherboard. In 1997, it introduced its Intel Pentium II-based motherboard with Intel MMX Technology, along with its first graphics card product and first barebone product. In 2002, it released its first PC2PC Bluetooth & WLAN motherboard. [*citation needed*]


In 2000, MSI introduced its first set-top box product (MS-5205);[14] in 2003, its first Pen Tablet PC product (PenNote3100);[15] and in 2004, its first Notebook product (M510C).[16] In 2009, MSI introduced its first Ultra Slim Notebook (X320),[17] and first all-in-one PC (AP1900).[18]


MSI released their first digital audio player in 2003, in a line called MEGA.[19]

### Semiconductor fabrication

[edit]

In 2011, Intel announced the commercialisation of Tri-gate transistor.[92] The Tri-Gate design is a variant of the FinFET 3D structure. FinFET was developed in the 1990s by Chenming Hu and his colleagues at UC Berkeley.[93]


Through-silicon via is used in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), a successor of DDR-SDRAM. HBM was released in 2013.


In 2016 and 2017, Intel, TSMC and Samsung begin releasing 10 nanometer chips. At the ≈10 nm scale, quantum tunneling (especially through gaps) becomes a significant phenomenon.[94]



## 2020s

[edit]

In May 2022, Chinese officials ordered government agencies and state-backed companies to remove personal computers produced by American corporations and replace them with equipment from domestic companies. ## History

[edit]

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced RCA to transfer semiconductor technology to Taiwan.[4]


In 1987, TSMC pioneered the fabless foundry model, reshaping the global semiconductor industry.[7][8] From ITRI's first 3-inch wafer fabrication plant built in 1977[7] and the founding of UMC in 1980,[9] the industry had developed into a world leader with 40 fabs in operation by 2002.[1] In 2007, the semiconductor industry overtook that of the United States, second only to Japan.[10]
