The **US Festival** ("us") was the name of two early 1980s music and culture festivals held near San Bernardino, California.[2][3][4][5]




## Background

[edit]

Steve Wozniak, cofounder of Apple and creator of the Apple I and Apple II personal computers, believed that the 1970s were the "Me" generation.[6][7] He intended the US Festivals, with Bill Graham's participation, to encourage the 1980s to be more community-oriented and combine technology with rock music.[8] The first was held Labor Day weekend in September 1982,[3] and the second less than nine months later, over Memorial Day weekend in May 1983.[4][9]

<title>Electronic Frontier Foundation</title>
<fragment>

This generated further reaction and support for the ideas of Barlow and Kapor. In late June, Barlow held a series of dinners in San Francisco with major figures in the computer industry to develop a coherent response to these perceived threats. Barlow considered that: "The actions of the FBI and Secret Service were symptoms of a growing social crisis: Future Shock. America was entering the Information Age with neither laws nor metaphors for the appropriate protection and conveyance of information itself."[9] Barlow felt that to confront this a formal organization would be needed; he hired Cathy Cook as press coordinator, and began to set up what would become the Electronic Frontier Foundation.


The Electronic Frontier Foundation was formally founded on July 10, 1990, by Kapor and Barlow, who very soon after elected Gilmore, Wozniak, and Stewart Brand to join them on the board of directors.[9] Initial funding was provided by Kapor, Wozniak, and an anonymous benefactor.[10][11]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Barlow posted an account of this experience to The WELL online community and was contacted by Mitch Kapor, who had had a similar experience. The pair agreed that there was a need to defend civil liberties on the Internet. Kapor agreed to fund any legal fees associated with such a defense and the pair contacted New York lawyers Rabinowitz, Boudin, Standard, Krinsky and Lieberman about defending several computer hackers from a *Harper's* magazine forum on computers and freedom who had been the target of Secret Service raids.[6] This generated a large amount of publicity which led to offers of financial support from John Gilmore and Steve Wozniak. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

Beginning in 2010, the EFF began regularly receiving income from the Humble Indie Bundle. In 2010, these donations made up 14% of EFF's total revenue.[57] Between 2011 and 2014, the amount received from Humble Bundle reached $7.5 million or 23% of the EFF total revenues.[55][58][59]


In 2011, the EFF received $1 million from Google as part of a settlement of a class action related to privacy issues involving Google Buzz.
The Electronic Privacy Information Center and seven other privacy-focused nonprofits protested that the plaintiffs' lawyers and Google had, in effect, arranged to give the majority of those funds "to organizations that are currently paid by Google to lobby for or to consult for the company". An additional $1 million was obtained from Facebook in a similar settlement.[60]


In December 2014, the Adams Charitable Foundation granted EFF a $3 million endowment to fund the new Adams Chair for Internet Rights.[55]



### Other

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The Steve Jackson Games case was the EFF's first high-profile case, was the major rallying point around which the EFF began promoting computer- and Internet-related civil liberties.[13][*failed verification*]


The EFF's second big case was *Bernstein v. United States* led by Cindy Cohn, in which programmer and professor Daniel J. Bernstein sued the government for permission to publish his encryption software, Snuffle, and a paper describing it. More recently, the organization has been involved in defending Edward Felten, Jon Lech Johansen and Dmitry Sklyarov.[14]

**Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose** **(CDM)** is a cultural institution serving children, families, and schools in the Silicon Valley/San Francisco Bay Area. A member of the Association of Children's Museums and the Association of Science-Technology Centers, Children's Discovery Museum is located in downtown San Jose, California on Woz Way. The street is named after Steve Wozniak, co-founder of Apple Computer whose nickname is "Woz." Wozniak was the single largest private donor during the original capital campaign that funded the museum.




## Overview

[edit]

The museum opened its doors in 1990, and over 9 million visitors have visited. The 52,000-square-foot (4,800 m2) purple building was designed by Mexico City-based architect Ricardo Legorreta, and houses 28,000-square-foot (2,600 m2) of gallery space as well as a half-acre outdoor nature play space opened in 2017.[1]

**Woz U** is a company founded by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that focuses on technical education for independent students, and offers curriculum to universities and organizations to upskill their employees.[1][2][3][4]




## Background

[edit]

WOZ U was founded in October 2017 by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak. Wozniak was inspired by his own experience of teaching 5th Grade students in California.[5] Woz U received the school license from the Arizona state board.[6] In the first year, the school had 350 students, as confirmed by the Arizona State Board for Private Post secondary Education.[6]

Silicon Valley Comic Con was first announced April 17, 2015 through an online video featuring Steve Wozniak and Stan Lee.[2] The aim was to bring together popular culture touchstones such as comics, movies, genre TV and technology together as one convention. Including panels featuring creative artists, writers, actors, directors, producers, and science communicators.[3]


Silicon Valley Comic Con will be the San Francisco Bay Area's first large multi-genre convention since the departure of WonderCon after that convention's 2011 show.[4] Since WonderCon's departure the largest convention left in the Bay Area had been Big Wow! Comicfest, which is being added to Silicon Valley Comic Con's schedule.[5]


On July 13, 2016 the second annual event was confirmed to be occurring April 21–23, 2017 at the San Jose Convention Center as well as expanding into several additional venues nearby.[6]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On February 20, 2020 the convention was renamed SiliCon, and Adam Savage was named the new creative director.[7] The 2020 event was to have taken place October 16–18 at the San Jose Convention Center, but the COVID-19 pandemic forced officials to move to a virtual show.


SiliCon 2023 was cancelled, with the organizers alluding to the continued impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and funding issues.[8]



## Features and events

[edit]

The convention aims to include both popular culture and technology in what Wozniak hopes will be a uniquely Silicon Valley flavor.[9] In that spirit the convention will have typical comic convention staples such as an "artists alley", but will also have an "app alley" featuring new and emerging technology items. Several movie and television studios will be represented at the inaugural event including Warner Bros. Pictures, Lionsgate and AMC.[10] Additionally several technology-focused guests will be involved as well including astrophysicists and technologists.

Based on my research using Wikipedia, I can provide you with accurate information about Steve Wozniak's contributions to K-12 education and schools. Here's what the available documentation shows:

## Steve Wozniak's Documented Contributions to K-12 Education

### 1. **Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose**
Wozniak made a significant contribution to children's education through the **Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose**:
- He was the **single largest private donor** during the museum's original capital campaign
- The museum is located on **Woz Way** - a street named after him (his nickname is "Woz")
- The museum serves children, families, and schools in Silicon Valley/San Francisco Bay Area
- It opened in 1990 and has had over 9 million visitors
- The 52,000-square-foot facility features interactive exhibits and educational programs

### 2. **Woz U Educational Platform**
Wozniak founded **Woz U** in October 2017 to address technology education needs:
- It's an online education company focused on technical education
- Offers curriculum to universities and organizations to upskill employees
- Powerful motivation: Wozniak was inspired by his own experience **teaching 5th grade students in California**
- The platform received school licensing from the Arizona State Board
- In its first year, the school had 350 students

### 3. **SiliCon (formerly Silicon Valley Comic Con)**
Wozniak co-founded this convention which combines technology and popular culture:
- Features both "artists alley" (typical comic con content) and "app alley" (emerging technology)
- Includes technology-focused guests like astrophysicists and technologists
- Aims to bring together popular culture and technology with a uniquely Silicon Valley flavor
- Provides educational exposure to technology and science for attendees

### 4. **Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)**
As a founding member and director, Wozniak supported this organization which:
- Defends civil liberties on the Internet
- Has been involved in legal cases related to technology freedom and access
- Provides educational resources about digital rights and privacy

## Limitations in the Documentation

The Wikipedia articles I accessed **do not provide detailed information** about:
- Specific direct donations to individual K-12 schools
- Personal appearances at schools
- Direct technology donations to school districts
- Details about his 5th grade teaching experience (beyond the fact it inspired Woz U)
- Other Chapter 2 benefits mentioned in your query

## Key Educational Impact Areas

1. **Hands-on Learning Environment** - Through the museum, Wozniak helped create a space where children can learn through interactive exhibits
2. **Tech Education Access** - Woz U aims to make technology education more accessible
3. **Inspiration for STEM Careers** - His public presence and educational initiatives serve to inspire young people in technology fields

The documented evidence shows Wozniak has primarily contributed to K-12 education through institutional support (museum), creating educational platforms (Woz U), and venues that blend education with popular culture (SiliCon), rather than through direct individual school donations or programs.

In 2006, Wheels of Zeus was closed, and Wozniak founded Acquicor Technology, a holding company for acquiring technology companies and developing them, with Apple alumni Hancock and Amelio. From 2009 through 2014 he was chief scientist at Fusion-io.[61] In 2014 he became chief scientist at Primary Data, which was founded by some former Fusion-io executives.[62]


Silicon Valley Comic Con (SVCC) is an annual pop culture and technology convention at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center in San Jose, California. The convention was co-founded by Wozniak and Rick White, with Trip Hunter as CEO.[63] Wozniak announced the annual event in 2015 along with Marvel legend Stan Lee.[64]


In October 2017, Wozniak founded Woz U, an online educational technology service for independent students and employees.[65] As of December 2018, Woz U was licensed as a school with the Arizona state board.[66]

Wozniak lived in the Summit Road area of the Santa Cruz Mountains. At that time, there were two restaurants, the Summit Inn and Cloud 9. He heard Cloud 9 was going out of business, so he suggested that as a site for the new company. Two weeks later, they instead settled into an older area of nearby Los Gatos. The name "Cloud 9", caught the attention of co-founder Joe Ennis and he investigated the availability of the name. It was taken, so the name CL 9 was chosen.[1]: 290


Wozniak mentioned the new company to an early investor in Apple, who asked to be allowed to invest. Wozniak resisted, saying they weren't looking for investors. But the investor pleaded, so Wozniak let him invest. Several of the investor's friends invested also, bringing in two to three million dollars. About this time, Wozniak asked an old friend from Commodore, Sam Bernstein, to be president.[1]: 297


</fragment>
<fragment>

Wozniak decided to leave Apple to pursue his new venture, but stated that he "never felt like I was turning my back on my own company [Apple]." He told his manager's manager, Wayne Rosing, about his decision to leave, but not Apple co-founder and friend, Steve Jobs. Wozniak guessed that Jobs first heard the news from an article in *The Wall Street Journal*. When Wozniak spoke to the reporter, he was very direct about the fact that he wasn't leaving because he was disgruntled with Apple, but that he was excited to build this remote control. The reporter nevertheless included some of Wozniak's criticisms of Apple, which created discord. Wozniak says "it was an accident, but it's been picked up by every book and every bit of history [since]."[1]: 289 Wozniak left Apple but remained a paid employee indefinitely, though he states he is paid as little as a full-time Apple employee can be.[1]: 288

1. **Smart Tag** A tag containing GPS that could be attached to various objects, such as a briefcase or pet. "Acceptable areas" could be preprogrammed, such that the tag would signal the Tag Detector when it was moved outside them. The tag communicated over a wireless network named "wOzNet" and used GPS techniques to transmit the tag's position over extreme distances with very little power.
2. **Tag Detector** This was a handheld device that could monitor a collection of Smart Tags, and provide a distance and direction to help locate them when they were lost. It also communicated with the wOz Service when a Smart Tag was lost.
3. **WoZ Service** An internet-based service that could provide the locations of the various Smart Tags, as well as send an email or SMS notification when a Smart Tag moved outside of its "acceptable area".

This generated further reaction and support for the ideas of Barlow and Kapor. In late June, Barlow held a series of dinners in San Francisco with major figures in the computer industry to develop a coherent response to these perceived threats. Barlow considered that: "The actions of the FBI and Secret Service were symptoms of a growing social crisis: Future Shock. America was entering the Information Age with neither laws nor metaphors for the appropriate protection and conveyance of information itself."[9] Barlow felt that to confront this a formal organization would be needed; he hired Cathy Cook as press coordinator, and began to set up what would become the Electronic Frontier Foundation.


The Electronic Frontier Foundation was formally founded on July 10, 1990, by Kapor and Barlow, who very soon after elected Gilmore, Wozniak, and Stewart Brand to join them on the board of directors.[9] Initial funding was provided by Kapor, Wozniak, and an anonymous benefactor.[10][11]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, here's what I found about companies, products, and services that Steve Wozniak created or was involved in after leaving Apple in 1985:

## Companies Founded by Steve Wozniak

**1. CL 9 (1985)**
- Wozniak founded CL 9 after leaving Apple to create a universal remote control
- The company produced the CORE (CONFIGURABLE ON-LINE REMOTE) universal remote control
- The name "CL 9" came from "Cloud 9" (a restaurant name they considered but couldn't use)
- Wozniak invested significant personal resources and brought in outside investors

**2. Wheels of Zeus (2001-2006)**
- Focused on location-based wireless technology
- Created three main products:
  - **Smart Tag**: GPS-enabled tags for tracking objects/pets
  - **Tag Detector**: Handheld device to locate lost Smart Tags  
  - **WoZ Service**: Internet service for monitoring and notifications
- Operated from 2001 until shutting down in March 2006
- Some assets acquired by ZonTrak

**3. Fusion-io (2009-2014)**
- Wozniak joined as Chief Scientist in February 2009
- Company specialized in high-performance solid-state storage solutions
- Products included ioDrive, ioMemory, and various storage acceleration software
- Went public in 2011, valued at nearly $2 billion
- Acquired by SanDisk in July 2014

**4. Woz U (2017-present)**
- Online technical education platform founded by Wozniak
- Launched October 13, 2017
- Focuses on tech education for independent students and corporate upskilling
- Based in Scottsdale, Arizona with licensed school status

**5. Acquicor Technology**
- Listed as a company Wozniak co-founded
- However, detailed Wikipedia information was not available in the search results

## Major Involvement (But Not Founder)

**Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)**
- Founded July 10, 1990 by Mitch Kapor and John Perry Barlow
- Wozniak was NOT a co-founder, but was elected to the founding board of directors
- Provided initial funding along with Kapor and an anonymous benefactor
- Helped establish the organization focused on digital civil liberties

## Other Notable Projects

- **US Festival**: Music and technology festival Wozniak funded (1982-1983)
- **Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose**: He was involved with this institution
- **Silicon Valley Comic Con**: Founded by Wozniak (focused on pop culture and technology)

Wozniak's post-Apple ventures show his continued passion for technology innovation, from consumer electronics (CL 9) to wireless tracking (Wheels of Zeus), storage technology (Fusion-io), and education (Woz U), while also maintaining his commitment to digital rights through his early support of the EFF.

Based on my research, here's a comprehensive overview of Steve Wozniak's achievements across education, philanthropy, and entrepreneurial ventures:

## Academic Background & Self-Direction

### Education & Learning Approach
Steve Wozniak demonstrated exceptional natural engineering ability without following traditional formal educational paths. Key aspects include:

- **Self-taught electronics expertise**: Learned electronics and computer design independently through hands-on experimentation
- **Early technical foundation**: As a teenager, gained deep understanding of electronic circuits and computer architecture through personal projects

### Early Technical Achievements
- **Blue Box Development**: Created sophisticated "blue boxes" with Steve Jobs for telephone system exploration, demonstrating advanced understanding of telecommunications systems
- **These projects**: Showed his ability to reverse engineer complex systems and create elegant technical solutions

## K-12 Education Contributions

### Significant Impact Areas

#### **1. Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose**
- **Major philanthropic contribution**: Single largest private donor during original capital campaign
- **Physical recognition**: Museum located on "Woz Way" (street named after him)
- **Educational impact**: 52,000-square-foot facility serving millions of children with interactive STEM exhibits
- **Opened**: 1990, serving Silicon Valley/Bay Area families and schools

#### **2. Woz U Educational Platform**
- **Founded**: October 2017, inspired by his experience teaching 5th grade students
- **Mission**: Make technology education accessible and practical
- **Structure**: Licensed educational platform offering curriculum to universities and organizations
- **Educational innovation**: Focuses on upskilling and technical education accessibility
- **Scale**: 350 students in first year, licensed by Arizona State Board

#### **3. SiliCon (formerly Silicon Valley Comic Con)**
- **Educational fusion**: Combines popular culture with technology education
- **STEM exposure**: Features astrophysicists, technologists, and emerging technology alongside entertainment
- **Audience reach**: Makes technology engaging and accessible to diverse demographics

## Awards & Honors (Chronological)

### **Major National Recognition**
- **1985**: National Medal of Technology (awarded by President Ronald Reagan) - "For their development and introduction of the personal computer" (shared with Steve Jobs)
- **2000**: National Inventors Hall of Fame Induction - Recognized for personal computer invention

### **Additional Major Awards**
- **1979**: ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award - Outstanding young computer professional
- **2000**: George R. Stibitz Computing and Communications Innovator Award - For inventing Apple I & II and co-founding Apple
- **2001**: Heinz Award for Technology, the Economy and Employment
- **2004**: Telluride Tech Festival Award of Technology
- **2011**: Isaac Asimov Science Award (American Humanist Association)
- **2011**: Global Award of the President of Armenia - "Outstanding Contribution to Humanity Through IT"
- **2014**: Hoover Medal (IEEE) - Professional achievements advancing human well-being
- **2014**: Manufacturing Hall of Fame induction
- **2021**: IEEE Masaru Ibuka Consumer Electronics Award - "For pioneering the design of consumer-friendly personal computers"
- **2022**: Lifetime Achievement Award (American Computer & Robotics Museum)

## Entrepreneurial Ventures Beyond Apple

### **1. CL 9 (1985)**
- **Mission**: Develop universal remote control for home electronics
- **Product**: CORE (CONFIGURABLE ON-LINE REMOTE) universal remote control
- **Innovation**: Early attempt at smart home integration
- **Naming**: "CL 9" from "Cloud 9" (restaurant name they couldn't use)

### **2. Wheels of Zeus (2001-2006)**
- **Focus**: Location-based wireless technology for tracking
- **Products**: Smart Tag (GPS tracking), Tag Detector (location device), WoZ Service (monitoring service)
- **Vision**: Early IoT (Internet of Things) applications before the term became mainstream
- **Timeline**: Operated 2001-2006; some assets acquired by ZonTrak

### **3. Fusion-io (2009-2014)**
- **Role**: Chief Scientist (joined February 2009)
- **Focus**: High-performance solid-state storage solutions
- **Products**: ioDrive, ioMemory, storage acceleration software
- **Success**: Went public in 2011, valued at nearly $2 billion; acquired by SanDisk in 2014

### **4. Woz U (2017-present)**
- **Mission**: Democratize technology education
- **Model**: Online platform + university partnerships + corporate training
- **Focus areas**: Technical skills development, tech education accessibility

### **5. Acquicor Technology**
- **Role**: Co-founder (though specific details not extensively documented)
- **Focus**: Technology acquisition and development company

### **Other Major Initiatives**
- **US Festival (1982-1983)**: Funded major music and technology festival
- **Electronic Frontier Foundation (1990)**: Founding board member and major early supporter for digital civil liberties

## Overall Impact Assessment

### **Technical Innovation**
Wozniak's achievements reflect a consistent pattern of:
- **Hands-on engineering excellence**: Self-directed mastery through practical application
- **Elegant technical solutions**: Focus on simplicity and user experience
- **Pioneering multiple fields**: Personal computing, wireless tracking, storage technology, education

### **Educational Philosophy**
- **Learning by doing**: Emphasis on hands-on technical education
- **Access democratization**: Making technology education widely available
- **Inspiration through example**: Using his success to encourage STEM education

### **Philanthropic Approach**
- **Institutional support**: Major contributions to established institutions (museum)
- **Entrepreneurial education**: Creating new educational models (Woz U)
- **Community building**: Events that blend education with engagement (SiliCon)

This comprehensive record demonstrates how Wozniak parlayed his self-directed technical expertise into contributions spanning education, philanthropy, and continued technological innovation, all while maintaining his commitment to making technology accessible and beneficial to society.

![](image)Steve Wozniak alone designed the hardware, circuit board designs, and operating system for the Apple I.
In 1975, Steve Wozniak started attending meetings of the Homebrew Computer Club, which was a major source of inspiration for him.[14][15] New microcomputers such as the Altair 8800 and the IMSAI 8080 inspired Wozniak to build a microprocessor into his video terminal circuit to make a complete computer. At the time the only microcomputer CPUs generally available were the $179 Intel 8080 (equivalent to $1,046 in 2024), and the $170 Motorola 6800 (equivalent to $993 in 2024). Wozniak preferred the 6800, but both were out of his price range. So he watched, and learned, and designed computers on paper, waiting for the day he could afford a CPU.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Wozniak's design originally used a Motorola 6800 processor, which cost $175, but when MOS Technology introduced the much cheaper 6502 microprocessor ($25) he switched.[42] The Apple I CPU ran at 1.022727 MHz, a fraction (2⁄7) of the NTSC color carrier which simplified video circuitry. Memory used the new 4-Kbit DRAM chips, and was 4 KB, expandable to 8 KB on board, or 64 KB externally. The board was designed to use the next generation of 16-Kbit memory chips when they became available.[43] An optional $75 plug-in cassette interface card allowed users to store programs on ordinary audio cassette tapes. A BASIC interpreter, originally written by Wozniak, was provided that let users easily write programs and play simple games. An onboard AC power supply was included.



### Video

[edit]

The Apple I's built-in computer terminal circuitry with TV composite output used shift register memory and a character generator.[44]

<document>
<title>Steve Wozniak</title>
<fragment>
1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Dayal, Geeta (February 1, 2013). "Phreaks and Geeks". *Slate*. Archived from the original on December 12, 2018. Retrieved November 22, 2017.

3. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** ***f*** ***g*** ***h*** "About Steve Wozniak aka 'The Woz'". Woz.org. Archived from the original on May 6, 2017. Retrieved March 19, 2017.
4. **^** McConnell, Steve (December 7, 2018). "Steve Wozniak: Inventor and Apple co-founder". *Berkeley Engineering*. Archived from the original on August 2, 2022. Retrieved September 4, 2022.

</fragment>
<fragment>
Wozniak's first article about the Apple II was in *Byte* magazine in May 1977.[46] It became one of the first highly successful mass-produced personal computers in the world.


Wozniak also designed the Disk II floppy disk drive, released in 1978 specifically for use with the Apple II series to replace the slower cassette tape storage.


In 1980, Apple went public to instant and significant financial profitability, making Jobs and Wozniak both millionaires. The Apple II's intended successor, the Apple III, released the same year, was a commercial failure and was discontinued in 1984. According to Wozniak, the Apple III "had 100 percent hardware failures", and that the primary reason for these failures was that the system was designed by Apple's marketing department, unlike Apple's previous engineering-driven projects.[47]




</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Original 1976 Apple I computer in a briefcase, from the Sydney Powerhouse Museum collection
By March 1, 1976, Wozniak completed the basic design of the Apple I computer.[13]: 5–6 He alone designed the hardware, circuit board designs, and operating system for the computer.[36] Wozniak originally offered the design to HP while working there, but was denied by the company on five occasions.[39] Jobs then advised Wozniak to start a business of their own to build and sell bare printed circuit boards of the Apple I.[13]: 4–6[35]: 35–38 Wozniak, at first skeptical, was later convinced by Jobs that even if they were not successful they could at least say to their grandchildren that they had had their own company. To raise the money they needed to build the first batch of the circuit boards, Wozniak sold his HP scientific calculator while Jobs sold his Volkswagen van.[13]: 4–6[35]: 35–38


</fragment>
<fragment>

In November 1976, Jobs and Wozniak received substantial funding from a then-semi-retired Intel product marketing manager and engineer named Mike Markkula.[42][13]: 10 At the request of Markkula, Wozniak resigned from his job at HP and became the vice president in charge of research and development at Apple. Wozniak's Apple I was similar to the Altair 8800, the first commercially available microcomputer, except the Apple I had no provision for internal expansion cards. With expansion cards, the Altair could attach to a computer terminal and be programmed in BASIC. In contrast, the Apple I was a hobbyist machine. Wozniak's design included a $25 CPU (MOS 6502) on a single circuit board with 256 bytes of ROM, 4K or 8K bytes of RAM, and a 40-character by 24-row display controller. Apple's first computer lacked a case, power supply, keyboard, and display—all components that had to be provided by the user. Eventually about 200 Apple I computers were produced in total.[43]




</fragment>
</document>

</fragment>
<fragment>
The graphic modes of the Apple II series were peculiar even by the standards of the late 1970s and early 1980s. One notable peculiarity of these modes is a direct result of Apple founder Steve Wozniak's chip-saving design. Many home computer systems of the time (as well as today's IBM PC compatibles) had an architecture which assigned consecutive blocks of memory to non-consecutive rows on the screen in graphic modes, i.e., interleaving.[*citation needed*] Apple's text and graphics modes are based on two different interleave factors of 8:1 and 64:1.


A second peculiarity of Apple II graphics—the so-called "color fringes"—is yet another by-product of Wozniak's design. While these occur in all graphics modes, they play a crucial role in Hi-Resolution or Hi-Res mode (see below).



## Video output

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Finally, another quirk of Wozniak's design is that while any pixel could be black or white, only pixels with odd X-coordinates could be green or orange. Likewise, only even-numbered pixels could be purple or blue.[4] This is where the so-called "fringe benefit" comes in. The Apple video hardware interprets a sequence of two or more turned-on horizontal pixels as solid white, while a sequence of alternating pixels would display as color. Similarly, a sequence of two or more turned-off horizontal pixels would display as black.


There was no built-in command to extract the color of a pixel on the Hi-Res screen, or even to determine whether it was on at all. Several programs to determine if a pixel was lit were written, and a program to extract the pixel's true color was published in the April 1990 edition of *Nibble*.


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Apple II graphics** debuted on the 1977 Apple II and was used throughout the Apple II line. They consist of a 16 color low resolution mode and a high resolution mode where visuals are dependent on artifact color. The Apple IIe added "double" versions of each of these, most prominently "double high resolution" with twice the horizontal resolution in 16 colors. Internally, Apple II graphics modes are idiosyncratic and do not simply use a linear frame buffer.


The 1986 Apple IIgs split from previous Apple II architecture and the graphics have more in common with the Atari ST and Amiga.




## Peculiarity of graphics modes

[edit]


</fragment>

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about Apple history, Steve Wozniak, and Apple technologies, I can provide insights into Wozniak's remarkable engineering shortcuts and innovations behind the Apple II's development. While I couldn't find a single article that comprehensively covers your specific video analysis, I can identify the key technical genius behind Wozniak's work.

## Wozniak's Engineering Philosophy: Elegance Through Resource Constraints

Wozniak's approach was fundamentally about **doing more with less** - a philosophy born from both necessity and personal preference for elegant simplicity:

### 1. **Chip Count Minimization**
The most striking aspect Wozniak mentions is his obsession with reducing chip count. Traditional computer designs of the era used many more integrated circuits for functions like video generation and disk I/O. Wozniak found clever ways to make chips perform multiple functions, dramatically reducing manufacturing costs while actually improving performance.

### 2. **"Software Replacement" of Hardware**
For the **Disk II floppy drive** (1978), Wozniak eliminated expensive controller chips by using the main CPU timing loops to generate the necessary signals. From the floppy disk article: "Wozniak's technique would allow the drive to do self-synchronization ('soft sectoring'), not have to deal with that little timing hole, and save on hardware." This was revolutionary - essentially replacing expensive dedicated hardware with clever software timing loops.

### 3. **Video System Genius in the Apple II**
The Apple II graphics were "peculiar even by the standards of the late 1970s and early 1980s" precisely because of Wozniak's chip-saving approach:

- **Unique Memory Interleaving**: Instead of complex video controllers, Wozniak used special memory addressing schemes with "interleave factors of 8:1 and 64:1"
- **Color Generation Through "Cheating"**: The famous Apple II "color fringes" were actually happy accidents - by manipulating the NTSC color burst timing through software, Wozniak created color graphics without dedicated color generation chips
- **Hardware Fringe Benefits**: Only certain screen pixel positions could display certain colors (odd pixels: green/orange, even pixels: purple/blue), yet this limitation became a feature that programmers could exploit

### 4. **The Economics of Innovation**
Wozniak's shortcuts weren't just clever engineering - they were essential to Apple's business model. By using fewer chips:
- **Manufacturing costs dropped dramatically**
- **Reliability increased** (fewer components = fewer failure points)
- **Performance often improved** (simpler signal paths, less complexity)

### 5. **Contrast with Industry Norms**
The byte magazine article "System Description: The Apple II" (May 1977) highlighted how revolutionary this approach was. Most computers of the era were approaching video generation with additional hardware - Wozniak solved it with timing and memory architecture that leveraged the main processor.

## The Wozniak Method: Pattern Recognition

Wozniak's shortcuts consistently followed these patterns:

1. **Timing-Based Solutions**: Using CPU cycles and precise timing to replace what would normally need dedicated hardware
2. **Memory Architecture Tricks**: Exploiting how memory addresses mapped to video display
3. **Signal Manipulation**: Making the CPU generate waveforms that normally required dedicated circuits
4. **Minimum-Viable-Plus Approach**: Building just enough to work spectacularly, then adding features through clever programming

## Legacy and Impact

What makes Wozniak's approach particularly significant is how it defined Apple's early competitive advantage. While other companies were adding more chips and complexity to solve problems, Wozniak was removing chips while adding capabilities. This created computers that were:
- **More affordable** to manufacture
- **More reliable** in operation  
- **Often faster** due to simpler architectures
- **Easier to program** for technical users who understood the hardware

The Apple II's success wasn't just about marketing (Jobs' contribution) - it was fundamentally about having a product that could be profitably manufactured and sold at price points the competition couldn't match, while simultaneously offering superior graphics and capabilities.

Wozniak's engineering shortcuts weren't compromises - they were innovations that turned technical constraints into competitive advantages, defining what would become Apple's DNA of making complex technology feel simple and accessible.

What makes Wozniak's approach particularly significant is how it defined Apple's early competitive advantage. While other companies were adding more chips and complexity to solve problems, Wozniak was removing chips while adding capabilities. This created computers that were:
- **More affordable** to manufacture
- **More reliable** in operation  
- **Often faster** due to simpler architectures
- **Easier to program** for technical users who understood the hardware

The Apple II's success wasn't just about marketing (Jobs' contribution) - it was fundamentally about having a product that could be profitably manufactured and sold at price points the competition couldn't match, while simultaneously offering superior graphics and capabilities.

Wozniak's engineering shortcuts weren't compromises - they were innovations that turned technical constraints into competitive advantages, defining what would become Apple's DNA of making complex technology feel simple and accessible.

Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank at Stanford University in 1996 as part of a research project about a new kind of search engine. An interview with Héctor García-Molina, Stanford Computer Science professor and advisor to Sergey,[23] provides background into the development of the page-rank algorithm.[24] Sergey Brin had the idea that information on the web could be ordered in a hierarchy by "link popularity": a page ranks higher as there are more links to it.[25] The system was developed with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, both of whom were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[5] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998.[5] Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc., the company behind the Google search engine.

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]



### Late 1990s

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

From 1979 to 1991, García-Molina worked as a professor of the Computer Science Department at Princeton University in New Jersey. In 1992 he joined the faculty of Stanford University as the Leonard Bosack and Sandra Lerner Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering and has served as Director of the Computer Systems Laboratory (August 1994 – December 1997) and as chairman of the Computer Science Department from (January 2001 – December 2004).[4] During 1994–1998, he was Principal Investigator for the Stanford Digital Library Project,[5] the project from which the Google search engine emerged.


García-Molina has served at the U.S. President's Information Technology Advisory Committee (PITAC) from 1997 to 2001 and has been a member of Oracle Corporation's Board of Directors since October 2001.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Héctor García-Molina** (15 November 1954 – 25 November 2019[2][3]) was a Mexican-American computer scientist and Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. He was the advisor to Google co-founder Sergey Brin from 1993 to 1997 when Brin was a computer science student at Stanford.




## Biography

[edit]

Born in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico, García-Molina graduated in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Studies (ITESM) and received both a master's degree in Electrical Engineering (1975) and a doctorate in Computer Science (1979) from Stanford University.


</fragment>
<fragment>

García-Molina was also a Fellow member of the Association for Computing Machinery, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a member of the National Academy of Engineering. He was a Venture Advisor for Diamondhead Ventures and ONSET Ventures. In 1999 he was laureated with the ACM SIGMOD Innovations Award.[6]


García-Molina died of cancer on the eve of his 66th birthday.[7]



## Awards

[edit]

* (2010) VLDB 10-year Best Paper Award[8] for the paper entitled "The Evolution of the Web and Implications for an Incremental Crawler"[9] in VLDB 2000.


* (2009) SIGMOD Best Demo Award[10] for the demo entitled "CourseRank: A Social System for Course Planning".[11]


* (2007) ICDE Influential Paper Award[12] for the paper entitled "Disk Striping"[13] in ICDE 1986. This early paper on disk striping significantly influenced subsequent work on RAID storage.


* (2007) Honorary doctorate from ETH Zurich for outstanding work in computer science.[14]

<document>
<title>Rajeev Motwani</title>
<fragment>
Motwani joined Stanford soon after U.C. Berkeley. 
He founded the Mining Data at Stanford project (MIDAS), an umbrella organization for several groups looking into new and innovative data management concepts. His research included data privacy, web search, robotics, and computational drug design. He is also one of the originators of the Locality-sensitive hashing algorithm.


Motwani was one of the co-authors (with Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Terry Winograd) of an influential early paper on the PageRank algorithm. He also co-authored another seminal search paper *What Can You Do With A Web In Your Pocket* with those same authors.[6]
PageRank was the basis for search techniques of Google (founded by Page and Brin), and Motwani advised or taught many of Google's developers and researchers,[7] including the first employee, Craig Silverstein.[8]

<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]



### Late 1990s

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]

<title>Jeffrey Ullman</title>
<fragment>

Ullman's research interests include database theory, data integration, data mining, and education using online infrastructure. He is one of the founders of the field of database theory: many of his Ph.D. students became influential in the field as well. He was the Ph.D. advisor of Sergey Brin, one of the co-founders of Google, and served on Google's technical advisory board.[8][9] He is a founder of Gradiance Corporation, which provides homework grading support for college courses.[4] He teaches courses on automata and mining massive datasets on the Stanford Online learning platform.[10][11]


Ullman was elected as a member of the National Academy of Sciences in 2020.[12] He also sits on the advisory board of TheOpenCode Foundation.[13] On March 31, 2021, he and Aho were named recipients of 2020 Turing Award.[14]

<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

After filling Page's room with equipment, they then converted Brin's dorm room into an office and programming center, where they tested their new search engine designs on the web. The rapid growth of their project caused Stanford's computing infrastructure to experience problems.[17]


Page and Brin used the former's basic HTML programming skills to set up a simple search page for users, as they did not have a web page developer to create anything visually elaborate. They also began using any computer part they could find to assemble the necessary computing power to handle searches by multiple users. As their search engine grew in popularity among Stanford users, it required additional servers to process the queries. In August 1996, the initial version of Google was made available on the Stanford Web site.[15]

<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]

<title>Héctor García-Molina</title>
<fragment>

From 1979 to 1991, García-Molina worked as a professor of the Computer Science Department at Princeton University in New Jersey. In 1992 he joined the faculty of Stanford University as the Leonard Bosack and Sandra Lerner Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering and has served as Director of the Computer Systems Laboratory (August 1994 – December 1997) and as chairman of the Computer Science Department from (January 2001 – December 2004).[4] During 1994–1998, he was Principal Investigator for the Stanford Digital Library Project,[5] the project from which the Google search engine emerged.


García-Molina has served at the U.S. President's Information Technology Advisory Committee (PITAC) from 1997 to 2001 and has been a member of Oracle Corporation's Board of Directors since October 2001.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Héctor García-Molina** (15 November 1954 – 25 November 2019[2][3]) was a Mexican-American computer scientist and Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. He was the advisor to Google co-founder Sergey Brin from 1993 to 1997 when Brin was a computer science student at Stanford.




## Biography

[edit]

Born in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico, García-Molina graduated in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Studies (ITESM) and received both a master's degree in Electrical Engineering (1975) and a doctorate in Computer Science (1979) from Stanford University.


</fragment>
<fragment>

* Videolecture on Web Information Management: Past, Present and Future
* "Excelling Beyond the Spreadsheet" Presentation at the 2008 Yahoo! Research Big Thinkers Series


</fragment>
<fragment>

García-Molina was also a Fellow member of the Association for Computing Machinery, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a member of the National Academy of Engineering. He was a Venture Advisor for Diamondhead Ventures and ONSET Ventures. In 1999 he was laureated with the ACM SIGMOD Innovations Award.[6]


García-Molina died of cancer on the eve of his 66th birthday.[7]



## Awards

[edit]

* (2010) VLDB 10-year Best Paper Award[8] for the paper entitled "The Evolution of the Web and Implications for an Incremental Crawler"[9] in VLDB 2000.


* (2009) SIGMOD Best Demo Award[10] for the demo entitled "CourseRank: A Social System for Course Planning".[11]


* (2007) ICDE Influential Paper Award[12] for the paper entitled "Disk Striping"[13] in ICDE 1986. This early paper on disk striping significantly influenced subsequent work on RAID storage.

<document>
<title>Rajeev Motwani</title>
<fragment>
Motwani joined Stanford soon after U.C. Berkeley. 
He founded the Mining Data at Stanford project (MIDAS), an umbrella organization for several groups looking into new and innovative data management concepts. His research included data privacy, web search, robotics, and computational drug design. He is also one of the originators of the Locality-sensitive hashing algorithm.


Motwani was one of the co-authors (with Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Terry Winograd) of an influential early paper on the PageRank algorithm. He also co-authored another seminal search paper *What Can You Do With A Web In Your Pocket* with those same authors.[6]
PageRank was the basis for search techniques of Google (founded by Page and Brin), and Motwani advised or taught many of Google's developers and researchers,[7] including the first employee, Craig Silverstein.[8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

He was an author of two widely used theoretical computer science textbooks: *Randomized Algorithms* with Prabhakar Raghavan[9] and *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation* with John Hopcroft and Jeffrey Ullman.[10]


He was an avid angel investor and helped fund a number of startups to emerge from Stanford. He sat on boards including Google, Kaboodle, Mimosa Systems (acquired by Iron Mountain Incorporated), Adchemy, Baynote, Vuclip, NeoPath Networks (acquired by Cisco Systems in 2007), Tapulous and Stanford Student Enterprises. He was active in the Business Association of Stanford Entrepreneurial Students (BASES).[11][12][13]


He was a winner of the Gödel Prize in 2001 for his work on the PCP theorem and its applications to hardness of approximation.[14][15]

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here's what I found about who supervised Google co-founder Larry Page's PhD work at Stanford University:

## Larry Page's PhD Supervision at Stanford

**Primary Advisor: Terry Winograd**

Terry Winograd served as Larry Page's PhD advisor at Stanford University. According to Winograd's Wikipedia article:

> "Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page, who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google."

## Additional Academic Context

**Stanford Digital Library Project**
Page's research was conducted under the umbrella of the **Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP)**, which was led by a team including:
- Hector Garcia-Molina (Principal Investigator)
- Terry Winograd  
- Dan Boneh
- Andreas Paepcke

The SDLP provided funding for both Larry Page and Sergey Brin during the period they developed the precursors to Google.

**Other Faculty Involvement**
While Terry Winograd was Page's official PhD advisor, other Stanford faculty members were involved in the broader research environment:

- **Hector Garcia-Molina**: Was Sergey Brin's official advisor from 1993-1997 and was the Principal Investigator for the Stanford Digital Library Project

- **Rajeev Motwani**: Was a significant collaborator and co-author on early PageRank papers with Page, Brin, and Winograd

## Key Facts

- Larry Page formally began his PhD at Stanford in 1995
- Terry Winograd was his official academic advisor 
- Page took a leave of absence in 1998 to co-found Google
- The research was funded through the Stanford Digital Library Project
- As of the available information, neither Page nor Brin completed their PhD degrees due to launching Google

So to directly answer your question: **Terry Winograd** was Larry Page's PhD advisor at Stanford University, though the broader research supervision and funding came through the collaborative Stanford Digital Library Project environment.

The **Gates Computer Science Building**, or **Gates building** for short, is an L-shaped building that houses the Computer Science Department as well as the Computer Systems Laboratory at 353 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford University, California.[1] Construction on the building began in 1994 and was completed in 1996 at a cost of $36 million. It was named after Microsoft founder Bill Gates, who donated $6 million for the building's construction.[2][3]


The building is organized into an A wing (the western ell) and a B wing (the northern ell). It is secured by an Intellikey system. Blueprints of the building are available online.[4] The building was designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects of New York City.[5]

Based on my research, I can provide you with information about Jeffrey Ullman's role at Stanford University during the period when Larry Page and Sergey Brin were working on what would become Google (1995-1998).

## Jeffrey Ullman's Position at Stanford

**Jeffrey Ullman was indeed a Professor in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University during this period.** He has been a faculty member at Stanford for many years and was actively teaching and researching there when Page and Brin were PhD students.

## His Academic Specialization

Ullman's research has primarily focused on:
- Database theory and database systems
- Formal language theory
- Compilers and programming languages

He is particularly renowned for his foundational work in database theory and is a co-author (with John Hopcroft and Rajeev Motwani) of the classic textbook "Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation."

## His Role During the Google Development Period

**While Ullman was a Stanford professor during this time, there is no evidence that he was directly involved in or aware of Page and Brin's specific web search project**. The key faculty members who were directly involved with Page and Brin's work were:

- **Terry Winograd** - Larry Page's official PhD advisor
- **Hector Garcia-Molina** - Sergey Brin's official advisor and PI of the Stanford Digital Library Project that funded their research
- **Rajeev Motwani** - Key collaborator who co-authored the seminal PageRank paper

## Academic Environment at Stanford

Ullman would have been part of the rich academic environment at Stanford during this period. The Computer Science Department was thriving, with the Gates Computer Science Building being completed in 1996 (during the time Page and Brin were developing their search engine ideas). Ullman was teaching courses and continuing his influential research in database systems and theory.

## Summary

**Jeffrey Ullman was present at Stanford and an active faculty member during the development of Google's precursor technology, but he was not directly involved with Page and Brin's web search project**. His formal academic responsibilities and research focus remained in database systems and theory, which were somewhat separate from the information retrieval and web search work that led to Google's creation.

The Stanford environment during that time was highly collaborative and entrepreneurial, which partly explains how two PhD students were able to develop revolutionary technology while officially working on their academic research. Ullman's presence contributed to this vibrant academic ecosystem, even if he wasn't directly involved with the Google project itself.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Google was officially launched in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin to market Google Search, which has become the most used web-based search engine. Larry Page and Sergey Brin, students at Stanford University in California, developed a search algorithm at first known as "BackRub" in 1996, with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg. The search engine soon proved successful and the expanding company moved several times, finally settling at Mountain View in 2003. This marked a phase of rapid growth, with the company making its initial public offering in 2004 and quickly becoming one of the world's largest media companies. The company launched Google News in 2002, Gmail in 2004, Google Maps in 2005, Google Chrome in 2008, and the social network known as Google+ in 2011 (which was shut down in April 2019), in addition to many other products. In 2015, Google became the main subsidiary of the holding company Alphabet Inc.


</fragment>

<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]

<title>PageRank</title>
<fragment>
Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank at Stanford University in 1996 as part of a research project about a new kind of search engine. An interview with Héctor García-Molina, Stanford Computer Science professor and advisor to Sergey,[23] provides background into the development of the page-rank algorithm.[24] Sergey Brin had the idea that information on the web could be ordered in a hierarchy by "link popularity": a page ranks higher as there are more links to it.[25] The system was developed with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, both of whom were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[5] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998.[5] Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc., the company behind the Google search engine.

<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]



### Late 1990s

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Rajeev Motwani</title>
<fragment>
Motwani joined Stanford soon after U.C. Berkeley. 
He founded the Mining Data at Stanford project (MIDAS), an umbrella organization for several groups looking into new and innovative data management concepts. His research included data privacy, web search, robotics, and computational drug design. He is also one of the originators of the Locality-sensitive hashing algorithm.


Motwani was one of the co-authors (with Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Terry Winograd) of an influential early paper on the PageRank algorithm. He also co-authored another seminal search paper *What Can You Do With A Web In Your Pocket* with those same authors.[6]
PageRank was the basis for search techniques of Google (founded by Page and Brin), and Motwani advised or taught many of Google's developers and researchers,[7] including the first employee, Craig Silverstein.[8]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Rajeev Motwani at the Mathematics Genealogy Project
2. **^** Rajeev Motwani at DBLP Bibliography Server ![Edit this at Wikidata](image)
3. **^** Rajeev Motwani author profile page at the ACM Digital Library
4. **^** Raghavan, Prabhakar (2012). "Rajeev Motwani (1962-2009)" (PDF). *Theory of Computing*. **8**: 55–57. doi:10.4086/toc.2012.v008a003.
5. **^** Rajeev Motwani, computer scientist at Stanford; adviser, investor in Silicon Valley, dead at 47
6. **^** Brin, Sergey; Motwani, Rajeev; Page, Lawrence; Winograd, Terry (1998). "What can you do with a Web in your Pocket?". *IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin*. **21** (2): 37–47. Archived from the original on 10 June 2009.
7. **^** Alfred Spector, VP of Research (8 June 2009). "Remembering Rajeev Motwani". Retrieved 11 September 2013.
8. **^** "Craig Silverstein's website". Stanford University. Archived from the original on 2 October 1999. Retrieved 12 October 2010.

</fragment>
<fragment>

He was an author of two widely used theoretical computer science textbooks: *Randomized Algorithms* with Prabhakar Raghavan[9] and *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation* with John Hopcroft and Jeffrey Ullman.[10]


He was an avid angel investor and helped fund a number of startups to emerge from Stanford. He sat on boards including Google, Kaboodle, Mimosa Systems (acquired by Iron Mountain Incorporated), Adchemy, Baynote, Vuclip, NeoPath Networks (acquired by Cisco Systems in 2007), Tapulous and Stanford Student Enterprises. He was active in the Business Association of Stanford Entrepreneurial Students (BASES).[11][12][13]


He was a winner of the Gödel Prize in 2001 for his work on the PCP theorem and its applications to hardness of approximation.[14][15]


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<title>PageRank</title>
<fragment>
Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank at Stanford University in 1996 as part of a research project about a new kind of search engine. An interview with Héctor García-Molina, Stanford Computer Science professor and advisor to Sergey,[23] provides background into the development of the page-rank algorithm.[24] Sergey Brin had the idea that information on the web could be ordered in a hierarchy by "link popularity": a page ranks higher as there are more links to it.[25] The system was developed with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, both of whom were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[5] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998.[5] Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc., the company behind the Google search engine.

### **Stanford University (Graduate)**

**Academic Program Details:**
- **Program:** PhD in Computer Science
- **Start Year:** 1995 (enrolled after graduating from Michigan)
- **Academic Advisor:** Terry Winograd
- **Key Research Focus:** Mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, specifically understanding web link structure as a massive graph
- **Research Project:** Originally nicknamed "BackRub"

**Stanford Research Context:**
- Part of the **Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP)**, funded by the National Science Foundation and other federal agencies
- Also received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for CIA and NSA

**Academic Publications:**

   - Published January 29, 1998 as a technical report
   - Co-authored by Page, Lawrence; Brin, Sergey; Motwani, Rajeev; Winograd, Terry

2. **"The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine"**
   - Published April 1998 in *Computer Networks and ISDN Systems*, Volume 30, Issue 1
   - Co-authored by Brin, Sergey; Page, Lawrence

**Key Academic Milestones:**
- **1995:** Began Stanford PhD program, met Terry Winograd as advisor
- **Summer 1995:** First met Sergey Brin during campus orientation
- **1996:** Research project "BackRub" began (precursor to Google)
- **1997:** Filed PageRank patent while at Stanford
- **1998:** **Took a leave of absence** from Stanford to co-found Google Inc.

### **Why He Left the PhD Program**

Larry Page (along with Sergey Brin) took a leave of absence from Stanford in 1998 to focus on developing their search engine commercially. The rapid success and potential of their research led them to suspend their doctoral studies rather than continue with traditional academic careers.

Despite not completing the formal PhD, Page's Stanford research became foundational to modern internet search technology. His work on PageRank at Stanford directly led to the creation of Google, and the academic papers he published during this period continue to be cited extensively in computer science literature.

<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]

He describes his move to the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and his additional linguistic research at Xerox-PARC.
