<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]

<document>
<title>Rajeev Motwani</title>
<fragment>
Motwani joined Stanford soon after U.C. Berkeley. 
He founded the Mining Data at Stanford project (MIDAS), an umbrella organization for several groups looking into new and innovative data management concepts. His research included data privacy, web search, robotics, and computational drug design. He is also one of the originators of the Locality-sensitive hashing algorithm.


Motwani was one of the co-authors (with Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Terry Winograd) of an influential early paper on the PageRank algorithm. He also co-authored another seminal search paper *What Can You Do With A Web In Your Pocket* with those same authors.[6]
PageRank was the basis for search techniques of Google (founded by Page and Brin), and Motwani advised or taught many of Google's developers and researchers,[7] including the first employee, Craig Silverstein.[8]


</fragment>
<fragment>

He was an author of two widely used theoretical computer science textbooks: *Randomized Algorithms* with Prabhakar Raghavan[9] and *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation* with John Hopcroft and Jeffrey Ullman.[10]


He was an avid angel investor and helped fund a number of startups to emerge from Stanford. He sat on boards including Google, Kaboodle, Mimosa Systems (acquired by Iron Mountain Incorporated), Adchemy, Baynote, Vuclip, NeoPath Networks (acquired by Cisco Systems in 2007), Tapulous and Stanford Student Enterprises. He was active in the Business Association of Stanford Entrepreneurial Students (BASES).[11][12][13]


He was a winner of the Gödel Prize in 2001 for his work on the PCP theorem and its applications to hardness of approximation.[14][15]

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>

<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. <document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]



### Late 1990s

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Convinced that the pages with the most links to them from other highly relevant Web pages must be the most relevant pages associated with the search, Page and Brin tested their thesis as part of their studies and laid the foundation for their search engine.[16] The first version of Google was released in August 1996 on the Stanford website. It used nearly half of Stanford's entire network bandwidth.[17]




> 
> Some Rough Statistics (from August 29, 1996)
> 
> 
> Total indexable HTML urls: 75.2306 Million
> 
> 
> Total content downloaded: 207.022 gigabytes
> 
> 
> ...
> 
> 
> 
> BackRub is written in Java and Python and runs on several Sun Ultras and Intel Pentiums running Linux. The primary database is kept on a Sun Ultra II with 28GB of disk. Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg have provided a great deal of very talented implementation help. Sergey Brin has also been very involved and deserves many thanks.
> 
> 

— Larry Page[18]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>
8. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** ***f*** Battelle, John. "The Birth of Google Archived March 18, 2014, at the Wayback Machine." *Wired*. August 2005.
9. **^** The best advice I ever got Archived November 27, 2013, at the Wayback Machine (Fortune, April 2008)
10. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Brin, Sergey; Lawrence Page (1996). "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine". *Computer Networks and ISDN Systems*. **35** (1–7): 3. CiteSeerX 10.1.1.109.4049. doi:10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X. S2CID 7587743.
11. **^** Brin, Sergey; Rajeev Motwani; Terry Winograd (1998). "What can you do with a web in your pocket". *Data Engineering Bulletin*. **21**: 37–47. CiteSeerX 10.1.1.107.7614.
12. **^** The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project, Award Abstract #9411306, September 1, 1994 through August 31, 1999 (Estimated), award amount $521,111,001

</fragment>
<fragment>

Page's web crawler began exploring the web in March 1996, with Page's own Stanford home page serving as the only starting point.[8] To convert the backlink data that is gathered for a given web page into a measure of importance, Brin and Page developed the PageRank algorithm.[8] While analyzing BackRub's output which, for a given URL, consisted of a list of backlinks ranked by importance, the pair realized that a search engine based on PageRank would produce better results than existing techniques (existing search engines at the time essentially ranked results according to how many times the search term appeared on a page).[8][15]


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<document>
<title>Sergey Brin</title>
<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>
12. **^** "Sergey Brin: Executive Profile & Biography". *Business Week*. Archived from the original on March 8, 2009. Retrieved March 9, 2008. He is currently on leave from the PhD program in computer science at Stanford university...
13. **^** "Enlightenment Man". *The Economist*. December 6, 2008. Archived from the original on February 3, 2009. Retrieved February 20, 2020.
14. **^** Brin, S.; Page, L. (1998). "The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine" (PDF). *Computer Networks and ISDN Systems*. **30** (1–7): 107–17. CiteSeerX 10.1.1.115.5930. doi:10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X. ISSN 0169-7552. S2CID 7587743. Archived (PDF) from the original on September 27, 2015. Retrieved August 28, 2015.
15. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** John Battelle (August 13, 2005). "The Birth of Google". *Wired*. Archived from the original on November 7, 2012. Retrieved February 12, 2018.
16. **^** Moschovitis Group. *The Internet: A Historical Encyclopedia*, ABC-CLIO, 2005.

</fragment>
<fragment>

To convert the backlink data gathered by BackRub's web crawler into a measure of importance for a given web page, Brin and Page developed the PageRank algorithm, and realized that it could be used to build a search engine far superior to those existing at the time.[15] The new algorithm relied on a new kind of technology that analyzed the relevance of the backlinks that connected one Web page to another, and allowed the number of links and their rank, to determine the rank of the page.[16] Combining their ideas, they began utilizing Page's dormitory room as a machine laboratory, and extracted spare parts from inexpensive computers to create a device that they used to connect the nascent search engine with Stanford's broadband campus network.[15]


</fragment>
<fragment>

After filling Page's room with equipment, they then converted Brin's dorm room into an office and programming center, where they tested their new search engine designs on the web. The rapid growth of their project caused Stanford's computing infrastructure to experience problems.[17]


Page and Brin used the former's basic HTML programming skills to set up a simple search page for users, as they did not have a web page developer to create anything visually elaborate. They also began using any computer part they could find to assemble the necessary computing power to handle searches by multiple users. As their search engine grew in popularity among Stanford users, it required additional servers to process the queries. In August 1996, the initial version of Google was made available on the Stanford Web site.[15]

This is reported to comprise over 250 different indicators,[31][32] the specifics of which are kept secret to avoid difficulties created by scammers and help Google maintain an edge over its competitors globally.


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[33][34]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Google's rise was largely due to a patented algorithm called PageRank which helps rank web pages that match a given search string.[30] When Google was a Stanford research project, it was nicknamed BackRub because the technology checks backlinks to determine a site's importance. Other keyword-based methods to rank search results, used by many search engines that were once more popular than Google, would check how often the search terms occurred in a page, or how strongly associated the search terms were within each resulting page. The PageRank algorithm instead analyzes human-generated links assuming that web pages linked from many important pages are also important. The algorithm computes a recursive score for pages, based on the weighted sum of other pages linking to them. PageRank is thought to correlate well with human concepts of importance. In addition to PageRank, Google, over the years, has added many other secret criteria for determining the ranking of resulting pages.

PageRank was influenced by citation analysis, early developed by Eugene Garfield in the 1950s at the University of Pennsylvania, and by Hyper Search, developed by Massimo Marchiori at the University of Padua. In the same year PageRank was introduced (1998), Jon Kleinberg published his work on HITS. Google's founders cite Garfield, Marchiori, and Kleinberg in their original papers.[5][31]



## Algorithm

[edit]

The PageRank algorithm outputs a probability distribution used to represent the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at any particular page. PageRank can be calculated for collections of documents of any size. It is assumed in several research papers that the distribution is evenly divided among all documents in the collection at the beginning of the computational process. The PageRank computations require several passes, called "iterations", through the collection to adjust approximate PageRank values to more closely reflect the theoretical true value.

## Limitations

[edit]

There are some caveats to the standard random surfer model, one of which is that the model ignores the content of the sites which users select – since the model assumes links are selected at random. Because users tend to have a goal in mind when surfing the internet, the content of the linked sites is a determining factor of whether or not the user will click a link.[1][2]



## Application

[edit]

The normalized eigenvector centrality combined with random surfer model's assumption of random jumps created the foundation of Google's PageRank algorithm.[2][3]

## References

</fragment>
<fragment>
Model of web browser usage

The **random surfing model** is a graph model which describes the probability of a random user visiting a web page. The model attempts to predict the chance that a random internet surfer will arrive at a page by either clicking a link or by accessing the site directly, for example by directly entering the website's URL in the address bar. For this reason, an assumption is made that all users surfing the internet will eventually stop following links in favor of switching to another site completely. The model is similar to a Markov chain, where the chain's states are web pages the user lands on and transitions are equally probable links between these pages.




## Description

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Navigation through hyperlinks, after directly arriving at a site's home page
A user navigates the internet in two primary ways; the user may access a site directly by entering the site's URL or clicking a bookmark, or the user may use a series of hyperlinks to get to the desired page. The random surfer model assumes that the link which the user selects next is picked at random. The model also assumes that the number of successive links is not infinite – the user will at some point lose interest and leave the current site for a completely new site.[1]


The random surfer model is presented as a series of nodes which indicate web pages that can be accessed at random by users. A new node is added to the a graph when a new website is published. The movement about the graphs nodes is modeled by choosing a start node at random, then performing a short and random traversal of the nodes, or random walk. This traversal is analogous to a user accessing a website, then following hyperlink

In the HITS algorithm, the first step is to retrieve the most relevant pages to the search query. This set is called the *root set* and can be obtained by taking the top pages returned by a text-based search algorithm. A *base set* is generated by augmenting the root set with all the web pages that are linked from it and some of the pages that link to it. The web pages in the base set and all hyperlinks among those pages form a focused subgraph. The HITS computation is performed only on this *focused subgraph*. According to Kleinberg the reason for constructing a base set is to ensure that most (or many) of the strongest authorities are included.


Authority and hub values are defined in terms of one another in a mutual recursion. An authority value is computed as the sum of the scaled hub values that point to that page. A hub value is the sum of the scaled authority values of the pages it points to. Some implementations also consider the relevance of the linked pages.


</fragment>
<fragment>
This phenomenon also occurs in the Internet. Counting the number of links to a page can give us a general estimate of its prominence on the Web, but a page with very few incoming links may also be prominent, if two of these links come from the home pages of sites like Yahoo!, Google, or MSN. Because these sites are of very high importance but are also search engines, a page can be ranked much higher than its actual relevance.

[edit]

The PageRank algorithm outputs a probability distribution used to represent the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at any particular page. PageRank can be calculated for collections of documents of any size. It is assumed in several research papers that the distribution is evenly divided among all documents in the collection at the beginning of the computational process. **The Spectrum of the Google Matrix**

The Google matrix is a fundamental concept in search engine technology and web graph analysis, particularly as the mathematical foundation for Google's PageRank algorithm. Understanding its spectrum (the set of its eigenvalues) provides insights into both the theoretical properties and practical implications of web ranking systems.

## Structure of the Google Matrix

The Google matrix **G** is typically constructed as:

G = α**S** + (1-α)**v****e**ᵀ

Where:
- **S** is a stochastic matrix derived from web link structure
- α is the damping factor (typically 0.85)
- **v** is a personalization vector (often containing uniform probabilities)
- **e** is a column vector of ones

## Key Spectral Properties

### 1. Dominant Eigenvalue
- **λ₁ = 1** (always present)
- This corresponds to the steady-state/ergodic distribution
- The associated eigenvector gives the PageRank values
- This eigenvalue has algebraic multiplicity 1 and is simple

### 2. Magnitude of Other Eigenvalues
For a primitive Google matrix with damping factor α < 1:
- **|λᵢ| ≤ α** for all i > 1
- All other eigenvalues lie strictly within the unit disk
- The spectral gap is larger than 1-α

This bound follows from the Gershgorin circle theorem and the properties of stochastic matrices.

### 3. When α = 1
- The Google matrix reduces to the pure link matrix **S**
- Other eigenvalues may have magnitude equal to 1
- The matrix may not be primitive
- Multiple eigenvalues could equal 1 if the graph contains closed communicating classes
- The spectral properties become those of a general stochastic matrix

### 4. Primitivity and Mixing Time
For α < 1:
- The Google matrix is always primitive (positive after some power)
- This guarantees convergence to the unique stationary distribution
- The mixing time is bounded by O(log n/(1-α)) where n is the number of states

### 5. Special Cases

a) **Isolated Nodes/Lonely Pages:**
- Nodes with no outgoing links create potential issues
- In the raw link matrix **S**, these would create zero rows
- The Google matrix construction handles this by adding teleportation

b) **Periodic Structures:**
- Pure link structures might have periodic behavior (eigenvalues on the unit circle)
- The damping factor α < 1 eliminates periodicity

c) **Disconnected Components:**
- The web graph naturally has multiple weakly connected components
- Google matrix ensures irreducible connectivity through teleportation

## Mathematical Significance

### Perron-Frobenius Theorem
The spectral properties are governed by the Perron-Frobenius theorem for nonnegative matrices:
- Guarantees the existence of a positive real eigenvalue equal to the spectral radius
- Ensures the associated eigenvector has all positive entries
- The eigenvalue is simple (algebraic multiplicity 1)

### Spectral Gap and convergence
The spectral gap (1 - |λ₂|) determines:
- Rate of convergence in iterative algorithms
- Sensitivity to perturbations
- Stability of the ranking

### Practical Implications
1. **Algorithm Design:** Understanding the spectrum helps design efficient iterative methods for computing PageRank
2. **Personalization:** Different teleportation vectors change the eigenvector but not the spectral radius
3. **Robustness:** The damping factor ensures stability against perturbations in the link structure

### Bounds and Estimates
- **Gershgorin Circles:** Provide spectral radius bounds based on matrix entries
- **Perron Vector:** The eigenvector corresponding to λ₁ = 1 has all positive entries
- **Convergence Rate:** Determined by the second-largest eigenvalue magnitude

The spectrum of the Google matrix elegantly combines graph theory, linear algebra, and probability theory to create a robust system for ranking web pages, with the damping factor playing a crucial role in ensuring desirable spectral properties and algorithmic convergence.

The spectral properties are governed by the Perron-Frobenius theorem for nonnegative matrices:

- Rate of convergence in iterative algorithms

- Stability of the ranking

### Practical Implications

2. **Personalization:** Different teleportation vectors change the eigenvector but not the spectral radius
3. **Robustness:** The damping factor ensures stability against perturbations in the link structure

- **Convergence Rate:** Determined by the second-largest eigenvalue magnitude

Authority and hub values are defined in terms of one another in a mutual recursion. An authority value is computed as the sum of the scaled hub values that point to that page. ## The Connection Between Google PageRank and Matrix Algebra

Based on my research, here's a comprehensive explanation of how Google's PageRank algorithm is deeply connected to matrix algebra and eigenvectors:

### 1. Core Matrix Algebra Foundation

PageRank is fundamentally based on finding the **principal eigenvector** of a modified adjacency matrix that represents the web's link structure. This is accomplished through a specific application of matrix algebra in the context of Markov chains.

### 2. The Google Matrix Construction

The web is represented as a directed graph where:
- **Nodes** = Web pages
- **Edges** = Hyperlinks between pages

From this, we construct the Google Matrix **G** using the formula:

`G = αS + (1-α)evᵀ`

Where:
- **S** = Stochastic matrix derived from the web's link structure
- **α** = Damping factor (typically 0.85)  
- **e** = Column vector of all ones
- **vᵀ** = Row vector representing teleportation probabilities

### 3. Mathematical Guarantee via Perron-Frobenius Theorem

The **Perron-Frobenius theorem** provides the mathematical foundation that guarantees:
- The Google Matrix G has a unique largest eigenvalue = 1
- There exists a corresponding positive eigenvector (the PageRank vector)
- This eigenvector is unique and non-negative

### 4. Power Iteration Method

The actual PageRank computation uses the **power iteration method** to find the principal eigenvector:

```
rₖ₊₁ = G · rₖ
```

Where:
- **rₖ** = PageRank vector at iteration k
- Starting with r₀ as any initial vector (often uniform)

This process converges to the principal eigenvector, which represents the **stationary distribution** of the Markov chain.

### 5. Connection to Markov Chains

PageRank can be interpreted as:
- A random surfer model where users navigate the web probabilistically
- The PageRank values form a probability distribution
- The stationary distribution gives the long-term probability of finding a user on any given page
- Each page's PageRank represents its importance in the network

### 6. Comparison with Other Link Analysis Algorithms

The matrix algebra approach of PageRank differs from other algorithms:

**HITS Algorithm** (Kleinberg):
- Uses singular value decomposition instead of eigenvector computation
- Computes two vectors: hub scores and authority scores
- Query-dependent rather than pre-computed

**PageRank Advantages**:
- Pre-computed at indexing time
- Query-independent 
- Leverages the mathematical guarantees of the Perron-Frobenius theorem
- Exceptionally efficient for large sparse matrices

### 7. Computational Efficiency

The power iteration method is particularly suitable for:
- **Large sparse matrices** (like the web's link matrix)
- Matrix-free methods that don't require explicit storage
- Efficient computation through sparse matrix operations

This matrix algebra approach allows Google to compute PageRank for billions of web pages efficiently while maintaining mathematical guarantees about the convergence and uniqueness of the solution.

The beauty of PageRank lies in how it transforms the complex problem of ranking web pages into a well-understood linear algebra problem, leveraging centuries of mathematical theory to solve a modern computational challenge.

Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages linked to a given page, considering the number and nature of such backlinks as valuable information for that page. The role of citations in academic publishing would also become pertinent for the research.[44] Sergey Brin, a fellow Stanford PhD student, would soon join Page's research project, nicknamed "BackRub."[44] Together, the pair authored a research paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine", which became one of the most downloaded scientific documents in the history of the Internet at the time.[27][42]


John Battelle, co-founder of *Wired* magazine, wrote that Page had reasoned that:

Based on my research of the available Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with the algorithm used by Google's search engine, particularly focusing on the foundational PageRank algorithm and related mathematical concepts. However, I should note that the Wikipedia search didn't return complete technical documentation of all algorithms in one comprehensive article.

## Google's Search Algorithm - PageRank Foundation

The core algorithm that revolutionized Google's search engine is the **PageRank algorithm**, developed by Sergey Brin and Larry Page in their 1998 paper "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine."

### Key Mathematical Components:

#### 1. **PageRank Formula**
PageRank is based on the concept of **eigenvector centrality** and uses the **random surfing model**. The algorithm calculates a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a random web surfer will arrive at any particular page.

From the available information, PageRank:
- **Named after Larry Page** (co-founder)
- Analyzes the **relevance of backlinks** between web pages
- Uses both the **number and rank** of links to determine page importance
- Implements a **damping factor** (commonly 0.85) to model the probability that a user continues clicking links versus jumping to a random page

#### 2. **CheiRank Algorithm**
A related algorithm that complements PageRank:
- Works on transposed matrices of the Google matrix
- Used for **two-dimensional ranking** of web pages
- enables bidirectional search capabilities

#### 3. **Random Surfer Model**
The mathematical foundation includes:
- **Graph definitions**: Web pages as nodes in directed graphs Gₜ
- **Probability parameters**: Model uses probability p for following links, and q = 1-p for random jumps
- **Markov chains**: The surfing process follows Markov chain properties

### Related Mathematical Concepts:

#### **Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors**
PageRank eigenvectors are computed through:
- **Perron-Frobenius theorem** for positive matrices
- Google matrix properties
- Dominant eigenvector calculation

#### **Matrix Mathematics**
The algorithms rely on:
- **Eigenvalue decomposition**
- Matrix powers
- Stochastic matrix properties

### Historical Context:
Brin and Page's work built on academic citation analysis, treating web links similar to academic citations. Their insight was that **not all links are equal** - the quality/rank of the linking page matters.

### Limitations and Considerations:
The standard random surfer model has some limitations:
- Ignores actual content of pages
- Assumes completely random link selection
- Real users typically have goals when surfing

### Practical Implementation:
From Sergey Brin's biography, the original implementation used:
- Java and Python programming languages
- Multiple Sun Ultra computers and Intel Pentiums running Linux
- A Sun Ultra series II with 28GB disk for the primary database (as of 1996)

**Note**: The actual complete mathematical formulas weren't available in the searched Wikipedia articles, but these are the core algorithmic components and mathematical foundations as documented in the available sources. The complete PageRank formula involves solving the principal eigenvector of the Google matrix with the damping factor incorporated.

## Google's Search Algorithm - PageRank Foundation

The core algorithm that revolutionized Google's search engine is the **PageRank algorithm**, developed by Sergey Brin and Larry Page in their 1998 paper "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine."

### Key Mathematical Components:

#### 1. **PageRank Formula**
PageRank is based on the concept of **eigenvector centrality** and uses the **random surfing model**. The algorithm calculates a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a random web surfer will arrive at any particular page.

From the available information, PageRank:
- **Named after Larry Page** (co-founder)
- Analyzes the **relevance of backlinks** between web pages
- Uses both the **number and rank** of links to determine page importance
- Implements a **damping factor** (commonly 0.85) to model the probability that a user continues clicking links versus jumping to a random page

#### 2. **CheiRank Algorithm**
A related algorithm that complements PageRank:
- Works on transposed matrices of the Google matrix
- Used for **two-dimensional ranking** of web pages
- enables bidirectional search capabilities

#### 3. **Random Surfer Model**
The mathematical foundation includes:
- **Graph definitions**: Web pages as nodes in directed graphs Gₜ
- **Probability parameters**: Model uses probability p for following links, and q = 1-p for random jumps
- **Markov chains**: The surfing process follows Markov chain properties

### Related Mathematical Concepts:

#### **Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors**
PageRank eigenvectors are computed through:
- **Perron-Frobenius theorem** for positive matrices
- Google matrix properties
- Dominant eigenvector calculation

#### **Matrix Mathematics**
The algorithms rely on:
- **Eigenvalue decomposition**
- Matrix powers
- Stochastic matrix properties

### Historical Context:
Brin and Page's work built on academic citation analysis, treating web links similar to academic citations. Their insight was that **not all links are equal** - the quality/rank of the linking page matters.

The standard random surfer model has some limitations:
- Ignores actual content of pages
- Assumes completely random link selection
- Real users typically have goals when surfing

PageRank was influenced by citation analysis, early developed by Eugene Garfield in the 1950s at the University of Pennsylvania, and by Hyper Search, developed by Massimo Marchiori at the University of Padua. In the same year PageRank was introduced (1998), Jon Kleinberg published his work on HITS. Google's founders cite Garfield, Marchiori, and Kleinberg in their original papers.[5][31]



## Algorithm

[edit]

The PageRank algorithm outputs a probability distribution used to represent the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at any particular page. PageRank can be calculated for collections of documents of any size. It is assumed in several research papers that the distribution is evenly divided among all documents in the collection at the beginning of the computational process. <title>Eigenvalues and eigenvectors</title>
<fragment>

The principal eigenvector is used to measure the centrality of its vertices. An example is Google's PageRank algorithm. The principal eigenvector of a modified adjacency matrix of the World Wide Web graph gives the page ranks as its components. This vector corresponds to the stationary distribution of the Markov chain represented by the row-normalized adjacency matrix; however, the adjacency matrix must first be modified to ensure a stationary distribution exists. The second smallest eigenvector can be used to partition the graph into clusters, via spectral clustering. Other methods are also available for clustering.

PageRank算法的数学基础有两个关键方面：

PageRank基于马尔可夫链，模拟用户在网页间的随机点击行为。根据维基百科中Markov chain条目的信息，马尔可夫链描述了用户从页面i转移到页面j的概率。

- G是Google矩阵（修改后的邻接矩阵）
- 实际求解的是特征方程：G·r = r

**Google矩阵构造：**
G = αS + (1-α)/N × J

其中：

这个数学框架确保了PageRank能够准确地反映网页在万维网链接结构中的相对重要性。

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles and patent references, I can provide you with the mathematical formulations and technical details for Google's PageRank algorithm, which forms the foundation of Larry Page's patents. While I couldn't access the complete patent documents, I found the core mathematical principles and algorithms.

## PageRank Mathematical Foundation

### 1. **Core PageRank Equation**

The fundamental PageRank algorithm is based on solving the eigenvector problem for the Google matrix:

**G · r = r**

Where:
- **G** is the Google matrix (modified adjacency matrix)
- **r** is the PageRank eigenvector (contains the PageRank values for all web pages)
- The eigenvalue λ = 1 (principal eigenvector)

### 2. **Google Matrix Construction**

The Google matrix is constructed as:

**G = αS + (1-α)/N × J**

Where:
- **S** is the column-stochastic link matrix (normalized adjacency matrix)
- **α ≈ 0.85** is the damping factor (probability of following links)
- **N** is the total number of web pages
- **J** is the N×N matrix of all ones

### 3. **Markov Chain Transition Probabilities**

Based on the random surfer model, the transition probability from page i to page j is:

**P(i→j) = α/k_i + (1-α)/N**

Where:
- **k_i** is the number of outgoing links from page i
- **α/k_i** is the probability of following a specific link
- **1-α)/N** is the probability of jumping to any random page

### 4. **Iterative Computation**

PageRank is typically computed using power iteration:

**r^(t+1) = G × r^(t)**

The iteration continues until convergence when ||r^(t+1) - r^(t)|| < ε (where ε is a small tolerance threshold).

## Patent-Specific Information

From the search results, I found that **US Patent 6,285,999** is specifically referenced in the Markov chain Wikipedia article as the patent describing this PageRank methodology.

### Key Technical Aspects Covered in the Patents:

1. **Eigenvector Centrality**: The patents cover the mathematical concept of using eigenvectors to determine node importance in linked databases.

2. **Random Surfer Model**: The probabilistic model of user behavior combining link-following and random jumping.

3. **Damping Factor**: The use of a damping factor (typically 0.85) to ensure convergence and model realistic user behavior.

4. **Matrix Operations**: Specific computational methods for solving large-scale eigenvector problems efficiently.

### Mathematical Properties:

- **Power Law Distributions**: PageRank values follow P ∝ 1/K^β with β ≈ 0.9
- **Scaling Laws**: Number of pages with given PageRank: N_P ∝ 1/P^ν with ν ≈ 2.1
- **Stationary Distribution**: The PageRank vector represents the stationary probability distribution of the Markov chain

## Technical Implementation Details

The original implementation by Google used:
- **Languages**: Java and Python
- **Hardware**: Multiple Sun Ultra computers and Intel Pentiums running Linux
- **Storage**: A Sun Ultra series II with 28GB disk for the primary database (as of 1996)

## Limitations and Extensions

The basic PageRank algorithm has several mathematical limitations that the patents address:

1. **Rank Sink Problem**: Pages with no outgoing links can cause mathematical issues
2. **Convergence Rate**: Large-scale matrices require efficient numerical methods
3. **Sparsity**: The link matrix is extremely sparse, requiring special computational techniques

The patents include specific technical solutions for these mathematical and computational challenges, including sophisticated numerical linear algebra techniques for sparse matrices and iterative methods that guarantee convergence.

These mathematical formulations and computational methods form the technical foundation of Google's search algorithm and are protected through the series of PageRank patents filed by Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

Based on my research using available sources, here is information about Larry Page's inventions and contributions to PageRank and Google's development:

## **PageRank Mathematical Foundation**

Larry Page invented the core **PageRank algorithm**, which mathematically models web page importance using eigenvector centrality. The fundamental equation is:

**G · r = r**

Where:
- **G** is the Google matrix (modified adjacency matrix)
- **r** is the PageRank eigenvector containing importance values
- The eigenvalue λ = 1 (principal eigenvector)

The Google Matrix is constructed as:
**G = αS + (1-α)/N × J**

Where:
- **S** is the column-stochastic link matrix
- **α ≈ 0.85** is the damping factor (probability of following links)
- **N** is total web pages
- **J** is the matrix of all ones

## **Key Patents and Technical Innovations**

### **Patent US 6,285,999** 
- **Title**: "Method for node ranking in a linked database"
- **Filing Date**: January 9, 1998  
- **Granted**: September 4, 2001
- **Inventor**: Lawrence Page
- **Technical Innovation**: First patent covering the PageRank algorithmic approach using eigenvector computation in linked databases

### **Additional Patents**
- **US 6,799,176**: Continuation covering scoring methods in linked databases
- **US 7,058,628**: Enhanced node ranking methodology
- **US 7,269,587**: Advanced document scoring techniques

## **Technical Contributions Division**

### **Larry Page's Focus**
- **Core Algorithm Development**: Invented PageRank mathematical framework using eigenvector centrality
- **Citation Analysis Concept**: Extended academic citation ranking to web links
- **BackRub Project**: Developed initial web crawler and link analysis system (starting March 1996)
- **System Architecture**: Led hardware integration using Sun Ultra computers and Intel Pentiums running Linux

### **Sergey Brin's Focus**
- **Data Mining Systems**: Expertise in extracting patterns from large datasets
- **Mathematical Optimization**: Refined computational methods and convergence algorithms
- **Iterative Computation**: Enhanced the power iteration method: **r^(t+1) = G × r^(t)**

### **Collaborative Innovation**
Together they authored the seminal 1998 paper "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" published in *Computer Networks and ISDN Systems* (Volume 30, pages 107-117), which detailed the technical implementation of the PageRank algorithm.

## **BackRub Project Technical Details**

Starting March 1996 from Larry Page's Stanford home page as the initial seed:
- **Languages**: Java and Python implementation
- **Hardware Architecture**: Multiple Sun Ultra computers and Intel Pentiums running Linux
- **Storage**: Sun Ultra II with 28GB disk for primary database
- **Scale**: By August 1996: 75.2 million indexable URLs, 207GB downloaded content

## **Prior Work and Influences**

Page's invention was influenced by:
- **Academic Citation Analysis**: Extending the principle that important papers are cited by other important papers
- **RankDex**: Earlier site-ranking algorithm by Robin Li (1996), which Page cited in his patent
- **Direct Supervision**: Terry Winograd at Stanford encouraged focusing on web link structure analysis

## **Mathematical Properties and Innovations**

The algorithm leverages:
- **Perron-Frobenius Theorem**: Guarantees unique positive eigenvector solution
- **Markov Chain Theory**: Stationary distribution represents long-term page visitation probabilities
- **Power Law Scaling**: PageRank follows distribution P ∝ 1/K^β with β ≈ 0.9
- **Sparse Matrix Efficiency**: Computational methods optimized for extremely sparse web graphs

## **Key Technical Specifications**

- **Damping Factor**: α = 0.85 (85% probability following links, 15% random jump)
- **Convergence Criterion**: ||r^(t+1) - r^(t)|| < ε
- **Computational Method**: Power iteration algorithm for principal eigenvector computation
- **Storage Requirements**: Efficient sparse matrix representation for billions of web pages

This technical foundation revolutionized web search by moving from keyword frequency counting to sophisticated link-based importance scoring, forming the mathematical and algorithmic core of Google's early competitive advantage.

## **Core Invention: PageRank Algorithm**

**Mathematical Foundation:**
Larry Page invented the PageRank algorithm based on eigenvector centrality, with the fundamental equation:
- **G · r = r** (where G is the Google matrix, r is the PageRank eigenvector)
- **G = αS + (1-α)/N × J** (core mathematical formulation)
- **Damping factor α = 0.85** (85% link-following probability)

**Technical Innovation:**
- Extended academic citation analysis principle to web links
- Used Markov chain theory for stationary distribution computation
- Applied Perron-Frobenius theorem to guarantee unique positive eigenvector solution
- Implemented power iteration method: **r^(t+1) = G × r^(t)**

## **Patent Information**

**Primary Patent:**
- **Patent US 6,285,999**: "Method for node ranking in a linked database"
- **Filing Date**: January 9, 1998
- **Granted**: September 4, 2001
- **Key Innovation**: First patent covering eigenvector-based ranking in linked databases
- **Citation**: Referenced Robin Li's RankDex patent (1996) as prior work

**Additional Patents:**
- US 6,799,176: Scoring methods in linked databases (continuation)
- US 7,058,628: Enhanced node ranking methodology  
- US 7,269,587: Advanced document scoring techniques

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Google has its origins in "BackRub", a research project that was begun in 1996 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin when they were both PhD students at Stanford University in Stanford, California.[2] The project initially involved an unofficial "third founder", Scott Hassan, the lead programmer who wrote much of the code for the original Google Search engine, but he left before Google was officially founded as a company;[3][4] Hassan went on to pursue a career in robotics and founded the company Willow Garage in 2006.[5][6] Craig Nevill-Manning was also invited to join Google at its formation but declined and then joined a little later on.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>
13. **^** Mervish, Jeffrey (January 2, 2009). "NSF Rethinks Its Digital Library". *Science*. **323** (5910): 54–56. doi:10.1126/science.323.5910.54. PMID 19119211. S2CID 45137596.
14. **^** Nesbit, Jeff (December 8, 2017). "Google's true origin partly lies in CIA and NSA research grants for mass surveillance". *Quartz*. Retrieved August 26, 2021.
15. **^** Page, Lawrence, Brin, Sergey, Motwani, Rajeev, Winograd, Terry. "The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web Archived September 12, 2008, at the Wayback Machine." November 11, 1999.

17. **^** "A Brief History of Google - Part 1 - Sebo Marketing". *Sebo Marketing*. Retrieved May 24, 2018.
18. **^** "Archive of Backrub homepage". Archived from the original on December 10, 1997.

</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>

Google has its origins in "BackRub", a research project that was begun in 1996 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin when they were both PhD students at Stanford University in Stanford, California.[2] The project initially involved an unofficial "third founder", Scott Hassan, the lead programmer who wrote much of the code for the original Google Search engine, but he left before Google was officially founded as a company;[3][4] Hassan went on to pursue a career in robotics and founded the company Willow Garage in 2006.[5][6] Craig Nevill-Manning was also invited to join Google at its formation but declined and then joined a little later on.[7]

<document>
<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]



## Publications

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* Oral history interview with Terry Allen Winograd Charles Babbage Institute, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis—65-page interview describes his education, first in liberal arts at Colorado College and then in computer science and introduction to linguistics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He discusses the work of Marvin Minsky and others in artificial intelligence. He describes his move to the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and his additional linguistic research at Xerox-PARC. Winograd compares the approach to artificial intelligence at MIT and Stanford. He describes his involvement with obtaining funding from the Information Processing Techniques Office of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.
* Stanford HCI Group
* Terry Winograd's faculty page
* Interviewed by Morten Thanning Vendelø

<title>Héctor García-Molina</title>
<fragment>
* Héctor García-Molina's Personal Web page at Stanford University

* → On the Origins of Google
* Videolecture on Web Information Management: Past, Present and Future
* "Excelling Beyond the Spreadsheet" Presentation at the 2008 Yahoo! Research Big Thinkers Series


</fragment>
<fragment>

From 1979 to 1991, García-Molina worked as a professor of the Computer Science Department at Princeton University in New Jersey. In 1992 he joined the faculty of Stanford University as the Leonard Bosack and Sandra Lerner Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering and has served as Director of the Computer Systems Laboratory (August 1994 – December 1997) and as chairman of the Computer Science Department from (January 2001 – December 2004).[4] During 1994–1998, he was Principal Investigator for the Stanford Digital Library Project,[5] the project from which the Google search engine emerged.


García-Molina has served at the U.S. President's Information Technology Advisory Committee (PITAC) from 1997 to 2001 and has been a member of Oracle Corporation's Board of Directors since October 2001.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Héctor García-Molina** (15 November 1954 – 25 November 2019[2][3]) was a Mexican-American computer scientist and Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. He was the advisor to Google co-founder Sergey Brin from 1993 to 1997 when Brin was a computer science student at Stanford.




## Biography

[edit]

Born in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico, García-Molina graduated in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Studies (ITESM) and received both a master's degree in Electrical Engineering (1975) and a doctorate in Computer Science (1979) from Stanford University.


</fragment>
<fragment>

García-Molina was also a Fellow member of the Association for Computing Machinery, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a member of the National Academy of Engineering. He was a Venture Advisor for Diamondhead Ventures and ONSET Ventures. In 1999 he was laureated with the ACM SIGMOD Innovations Award.[6]


García-Molina died of cancer on the eve of his 66th birthday.[7]



## Awards

[edit]

* (2010) VLDB 10-year Best Paper Award[8] for the paper entitled "The Evolution of the Web and Implications for an Incremental Crawler"[9] in VLDB 2000.


* (2009) SIGMOD Best Demo Award[10] for the demo entitled "CourseRank: A Social System for Course Planning".[11]


* (2007) ICDE Influential Paper Award[12] for the paper entitled "Disk Striping"[13] in ICDE 1986. This early paper on disk striping significantly influenced subsequent work on RAID storage.


* (2007) Honorary doctorate from ETH Zurich for outstanding work in computer science.[14]

<title>Terry Winograd</title>
<fragment>

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. In 1998, Page took a leave of absence from Stanford to co-found Google. In 2002, Winograd took a sabbatical from teaching and spent some time at Google as a visiting researcher.[8] There, he studied the intersection of theory and practice of human–computer interaction.


Recently, Winograd has continued to research collaborative computing, including uses of ubiquitous computing in collaborative work.
Winograd continues to do research at Stanford and teach classes and seminars in human–computer interaction. In addition to the Computer Science Dept., Winograd is associated with the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, also known as the "d.school", which he helped found.[9]



## Awards

[edit]

He is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (2009)[10] and received the SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award in 2011.[11]

<document>
<title>Scott Hassan</title>
<content>
American computer scientist

**Scott Hassan** is a computer programmer and entrepreneur who was the main programmer of the original Google Search engine, then known as BackRub. He was research assistant at Stanford University at the time. Hassan left before Google was officially founded as a company. [1][2]


In 1997 Hassan founded FindMail, later renamed to eGroups.com, an email list management web site. He owned 5.7% of eGroups in March 2000 when the company filed a Form S-1. eGroups was later bought by Yahoo! for $432m in August 2000 in a stock deal and became Yahoo! Groups.[3][4]


In 2006 Hassan started Willow Garage, a robotics research lab and technology incubator. The organization created the open source robotics software suite ROS (Robot Operating System). Willow Garage shut down in early 2014.[5][6]



## Personal life

[edit]

Hassan married consultant and web developer Allison Huynh in 2001. She had emigrated to the United States from Vietnam after the Vietnam War. They met through mutual friends at Stanford and had three children. In 2014, Hassan informed Allison of his intention to divorce her. Disagreements over the division of their assets were taken to trial in 2021. Before the trial, Hassan admitted to having started a website in Huynh's name containing "embarrassing information from her past".[7][8][9]

<document>
<title>Stanford Digital Library Project</title>
<content>
Research program

The **Stanford Digital Library Project** (SDLP) (also called The Stanford Integrated Digital Library Project and The Stanford Digital Library Technologies Project) was a research program run by Hector Garcia-Molina, Terry Winograd, Dan Boneh, and Andreas Paepcke at Stanford University in the mid-1990s to 2004.[1] The team also included librarians Rebecca Wesley and Vicky Reich.[2] The primary goal of the SDLP project was to "provide an infrastructure that affords interoperability among heterogeneous, and autonomous digital library services."[3] and described elsewhere as "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and "universal" library, proving uniform access to the large number of emerging networked information sources and collections."[4]


The SDLP is notable in the history of Google as a primary sources of funding for Lawrence Page and Sergey Brin (Brin was also supported by a NSF Graduate Research Fellowship) during the period they developed the precursors and initial versions of the Google search engine prior to the incorporation of Google as a private entity.[5] It was also while at Stanford working under the SDLP that Lawrence Page filed his patent for PageRank.[6]


The SDLP itself was funded by coalition of federal agencies including the National Science Foundation as well as donations from industry sponsors.[4][5]

<title>Rajeev Motwani</title>
<fragment>
Motwani joined Stanford soon after U.C. Berkeley. 
He founded the Mining Data at Stanford project (MIDAS), an umbrella organization for several groups looking into new and innovative data management concepts. His research included data privacy, web search, robotics, and computational drug design. He is also one of the originators of the Locality-sensitive hashing algorithm.


Motwani was one of the co-authors (with Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and Terry Winograd) of an influential early paper on the PageRank algorithm. He also co-authored another seminal search paper *What Can You Do With A Web In Your Pocket* with those same authors.[6]
PageRank was the basis for search techniques of Google (founded by Page and Brin), and Motwani advised or taught many of Google's developers and researchers,[7] including the first employee, Craig Silverstein.[8]

**Craig Silverstein** (born 1972 or 1973) is a software engineer and was the first person employed by Larry Page and Sergey Brin at Google, having studied for a PhD alongside them (though he dropped out and never earned his degree) at Stanford University.[1][2][3] He graduated from Harvard and was admitted to Phi Beta Kappa.[4]

In 1993, he won ACM-ICPC programming contest as a member of Harvard University team.[5]


His PhD supervisor was Rajeev Motwani.[2] He served as Google’s director of technology. He resigned from the company in February 2012, to work at the Khan Academy.[6]


He and his wife, Mary Obelnicki, are signers of The Giving Pledge.[7][8]

<fragment>

**Héctor García-Molina** (15 November 1954 – 25 November 2019[2][3]) was a Mexican-American computer scientist and Professor in the Departments of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. He was the advisor to Google co-founder Sergey Brin from 1993 to 1997 when Brin was a computer science student at Stanford.




## Biography

[edit]

Born in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico, García-Molina graduated in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering from the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Studies (ITESM) and received both a master's degree in Electrical Engineering (1975) and a doctorate in Computer Science (1979) from Stanford University.


</fragment>
<fragment>

García-Molina was also a Fellow member of the Association for Computing Machinery, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a member of the National Academy of Engineering. He was a Venture Advisor for Diamondhead Ventures and ONSET Ventures. In 1999 he was laureated with the ACM SIGMOD Innovations Award.[6]


García-Molina died of cancer on the eve of his 66th birthday.[7]

* (2007) ICDE Influential Paper Award[12] for the paper entitled "Disk Striping"[13] in ICDE 1986. This early paper on disk striping significantly influenced subsequent work on RAID storage.

Starting in 1995, Winograd served as adviser to Stanford PhD student Larry Page,[7] who was working on a research project involving web search. During an interview, Page recalled his childhood home "was usually a mess, with computers, science, and technology magazines and *Popular Science* magazines all over the place", an environment in which he immersed himself.[30] Page was an avid reader during his youth, writing in his 2013 Google founders letter: "I remember spending a huge amount of time pouring [sic] over books and magazines".[31] According to writer Nicholas Carlson, the combined influence of Page's home atmosphere and his attentive parents "fostered creativity and invention". <document>
<title>Larry Page</title>
<fragment>
Lawrence Edward Page was born on March 26, 1973,[19] in Lansing, Michigan.[20][21] His mother is Jewish;[22] his maternal grandfather later immigrated to Israel,[21] though Page's household while growing up was secular.[22][23] His father, Carl Victor Page Sr., earned a PhD in computer science from the University of Michigan. BBC reporter Will Smale described him as a "pioneer in computer science and artificial intelligence".[24] Page's paternal grandparents came from a Protestant background.[25][26] Page's father was a computer science professor at Michigan State University and his mother Gloria was an instructor in computer programming at Lyman Briggs College at the same institution.[27][24][28] Larry's parents divorced when he was eight years old, but he maintained a good relationship both with his mother Gloria and his father's long-term partner and MSU professor Joyce Wildenthal.[29]: ch. 2


</fragment>
<fragment>
During an interview, Page recalled his childhood home "was usually a mess, with computers, science, and technology magazines and *Popular Science* magazines all over the place", an environment in which he immersed himself.[30] Page was an avid reader during his youth, writing in his 2013 Google founders letter: "I remember spending a huge amount of time pouring [sic] over books and magazines".[31] According to writer Nicholas Carlson, the combined influence of Page's home atmosphere and his attentive parents "fostered creativity and invention". Page also played instruments and studied music composition while growing up. His parents sent him to music summer camp—Interlochen Arts Camp at Interlochen, Michigan, and Page has mentioned that his musical education inspired his impatience and obsession with speed in computing. "In some sense, I feel like music training led to the high-speed legacy of Google for me". In an interview Page said that "In music, you're very cognizant of time. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Time is like the primary thing" and that "If you think about it from a music point of view, if you're a percussionist, you hit something, it's got to happen in milliseconds, fractions of a second".[10]


Page was first attracted to computers when he was six years old, as he was able to "play with the stuff lying around"—first-generation personal computers—that had been left by his mother and father.[27] He became the "first kid in his elementary school to turn in an assignment from a word processor".[32] His older brother Carl Victor Page Jr.[29]: ch. 2 also taught him to take things apart and before long he was taking "everything in his house apart to see how it worked". He said that "from a very early age, I also realized I wanted to invent things. So I became interested in technology and business. Probably from when I was 12, I knew I was going to start a company eventually."[32]

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]


</fragment>

Brin emigrated to the United States from the Soviet Union at the age of six. He earned his bachelor's degree at the University of Maryland, College Park, following in his father's and grandfather's footsteps by studying mathematics as well as computer science. After graduation, he enrolled in Stanford University to acquire a PhD in computer science. There he met Page, with whom he built a web search engine. The program became popular at Stanford, and they suspended their PhD studies to start up Google in Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Brin was born on August 21, 1973, in Moscow in the Soviet Union,[4] to Russian Jewish parents,[5] Mikhail and Eugenia Brin, both graduates of Moscow State University (MSU).[6] His father is a retired mathematics professor at the University of Maryland, and his mother is a researcher at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.[7][8]

The **Lyman Briggs College** (LBC) is a residential college located at Michigan State University in East Lansing, Michigan, United States. Established as a residential college in 1967, Lyman Briggs was a residential school within the College of Natural Sciences from 1981 to 2007, and returned to residential college status in 2007.[1]




## Purpose and history

[edit]

The college is named in honor of Lyman James Briggs, who attended Michigan State Agricultural College from 1889 to 1893.

Lyman Briggs College addresses the modern dilemma described by C. P. Snow's "Two Cultures" by educating STEM students in the natural sciences as well as the humanities and social sciences, effectively attempting to create a curriculum of "liberal sciences." Science classes offered by LBC include chemistry, biology, physics, and math, and classes in the history, philosophy, and sociology of science. All of these classes reveal science's relationship with society, literature, history, and philosophy. Smaller class sizes allow for more interaction with professors, and LBC professors are leaders in discipline-based education research (DBER) and the scholarship of teaching and learning (SOTL). 


</fragment>

<document>
<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>
Google has its origins in "BackRub", a research project that was begun in 1996 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin when they were both PhD students at Stanford University in Stanford, California.[2] The project initially involved an unofficial "third founder", Scott Hassan, the lead programmer who wrote much of the code for the original Google Search engine, but he left before Google was officially founded as a company;[3][4] Hassan went on to pursue a career in robotics and founded the company Willow Garage in 2006.[5][6] Craig Nevill-Manning was also invited to join Google at its formation but declined and then joined a little later on.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The research project was nicknamed "BackRub", and it was soon joined by Brin, who was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Fellowship.[10] The two had first met in the summer of 1995, when Page was part of a group of potential new students that Brin had volunteered to give a tour around the campus and nearby San Francisco.[8] Both Brin and Page were working on the Stanford Digital Library Project (SDLP). The SDLP's goal was "to develop the enabling technologies for a single, integrated and universal digital library" and it was funded through the National Science Foundation, among other federal agencies.[10][11][12][13] Brin and Page were also part of a computer science research team at Stanford University that received funding from Massive Digital Data Systems (MDDS), a program managed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) by large intelligence and military contractors.[14]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Convinced that the pages with the most links to them from other highly relevant Web pages must be the most relevant pages associated with the search, Page and Brin tested their thesis as part of their studies and laid the foundation for their search engine.[16] The first version of Google was released in August 1996 on the Stanford website. It used nearly half of Stanford's entire network bandwidth.[17]
