<title>Andrew Ng</title>
<fragment>

He started working as an assistant professor at Stanford University in 2002 and as an associate professor in 2009.[13]


He currently lives in Los Altos Hills, California. In 2014, he married Carol E. Reiley.[14] They have two children: a daughter born in 2019[15] and a son born in 2021.[16] The *MIT Technology Review* named Ng and Reiley an "AI power couple".[17][18]



## Career

[edit]

### Academia and teaching

[edit]

Ng is a professor at Stanford University departments of Computer Science and electrical engineering. He served as the director of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL), where he taught students and undertook research related to data mining, big data, and machine learning. His machine learning course CS229 at Stanford is the most popular course offered on campus with over 1,000 students enrolling some years.[19][20] As of 2020, three of most popular courses on Coursera are Ng's: Machine Learning (#1), AI for Everyone, (#5), Neural Networks and Deep Learning (#6).[21]


</fragment>
<fragment>

His early work includes the Stanford Autonomous Helicopter project, which developed one of the most capable autonomous helicopters in the world.[35][36] He was the leading scientist and principal investigator on the STAIR (Stanford Artificial Intelligence Robot) project,[37] which resulted in Robot Operating System (ROS), a widely used open source software robotics platform. His vision to build an AI robot and put a robot in every home inspired Scott Hassan to back him and create Willow Garage.[38] He is also one of the founding team members for the Stanford WordNet project, which uses machine learning to expand the Princeton WordNet database created by Christiane Fellbaum.[11][39]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Ng is an adjunct professor at Stanford University (formerly associate professor and Director of its Stanford AI Lab or SAIL). Ng has also worked in the field of online education, cofounding Coursera and DeepLearning.AI.[5] He has spearheaded many efforts to "democratize deep learning" teaching over 2.5 million students through his online courses.[6][3] He is one of the world's most famous and influential computer scientists being named one of *Time* magazine's 100 Most Influential People in 2012, and *Fast Company*'s Most Creative People in 2014. In 2018, he launched and currently heads the AI Fund, initially a $175-million investment fund for backing artificial intelligence startups. He has founded Landing AI, which provides AI-powered SaaS products.[7]




## Biography

[edit]

Ng was born in the United Kingdom in 1976. His parents Ronald P. Ng and Tisa Ho[8][9][10] are both immigrants from Hong Kong. He has at least one brother.[9] Growing up, he spent time in Hong Kong and Singapore.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 2014, he joined Baidu as chief scientist, and carried out research related to big data and AI.[24] There he set up several research teams for things like facial recognition and Melody, an AI chatbot for healthcare.[4] He also developed for the company the AI platform called DuerOS and other technologies that positioned Baidu ahead of Google in the discourse and development of AI.[25] In March 2017, he announced his resignation from Baidu.[3][26]


He soon afterward launched Deeplearning.ai, an online series of deep learning courses.[27] Then Ng launched Landing AI, which provides AI-powered SaaS products.[28]


In January 2018, Ng unveiled the AI Fund, raising $175 million to invest in new startups.[29] In November 2021, Landing AI secured a $57 million round of series A funding led by McRock Capital, to help manufacturers adopt computer vision.[30]



## Research

<title>Fei-Fei Li</title>
<fragment>
From 2005 to 2006, Li was an assistant professor in the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and from 2007 to 2009, she was an assistant professor in the Computer Science Department at Princeton University. She joined Stanford in 2009 as an assistant professor, and was promoted to associate professor with tenure in 2012, and then full professor in 2018.[19] At Stanford, Li served as the director of Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab (SAIL) from 2013 to 2018. She became the founding co-director of Stanford's University-level initiative - the Human-Centered AI Institute, along with co-director Dr. John Etchemendy, former provost of Stanford University.[20]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Prior to establishing AI4ALL in 2017, Li and her former student Olga Russakovsky,[37] currently an assistant professor in Princeton University, co-founded and co-directed the precursor program at Stanford called SAILORS (Stanford AI Lab OutReach Summers).[38][39] SAILORS was an annual summer camp at Stanford dedicated to 9th grade high school girls in AI education and research, established in 2015 till it changed its name to AI4ALL @Stanford in 2017.[39] In 2018, AI4ALL has successfully launched five more summer programs in addition to Stanford, including Princeton University,[40] Carnegie Mellon University,[41] Boston University,[42] U. of California Berkeley,[43] and Canada's Simon Fraser University.[44]




</fragment>
<fragment>

In the fall of 2018, Li left Google and returned to Stanford University to continue her professorship.[29]


Li is also known for her nonprofit work as the co-founder and chairperson of nonprofit organization AI4ALL, whose mission is to educate the next generation of AI technologists, thinkers and leaders by promoting diversity and inclusion through human-centered AI principles.[30][31][32][33][34] The program was created in collaboration with Melinda Gates and Jensen Huang.[35][36]

Based on my research, here is the comprehensive academic and technical information about Larry Page:

## **Educational Background**

### **University of Michigan (1991-1995)**
- **Degree:** Bachelor of Science in Engineering (BSE) in Computer Engineering
- **Graduation Year:** 1995
- **Ac Achievement:** Graduated with honors
- **Context:** Father Carl Victor Page Sr. earned PhD in Computer Science from same institution

### **Stanford University (1995-1998)**
- **Initial Program:** PhD in Computer Science (enrolled Fall 1995)
- **Degree Completed:** Master of Science (MS) in Computer Science (1998)
- **Academic Advisor:** Terry Winograd
- **Research Collaborator:** Rajeev Motwani
- **Research Context:** Stanford Digital Library Project (NSF funded)
- **Status:** Took leave of absence in 1998 to found Google

## **Technical Contributions & Inventions**

### **PageRank Algorithm**
**Mathematical Foundation:**
- **Core Equation:** G · r = r (Google matrix eigenvector formulation)
- **Implementation:** G = αS + (1-α)/N × J
- **Key Parameters:** Damping factor α = 0.85
- **Method:** Power iteration algorithm: r^(t+1) = G × r^(t)
- **Theory:** Based on Perron-Frobenius theorem and Markov chain stationary distribution

**Technical Innovation:**
- Extended academic citation analysis to web links
- Applied eigenvector centrality to web graphs
- Optimized sparse matrix computation for billions of pages
- Implemented convergence algorithms with criteria ||r^(t+1) - r^(t)|| < ε

### **BackRub Project (1996-1998)**
**Architecture:**
- **Languages:** Java and Python
- **Hardware:** Sun Ultra computers, Intel Pentiums running Linux
- **Storage:** Sun Ultra II with 28GB primary database disk
- **Scale by August 1996:** 75.2 million indexable URLs, 207GB downloaded content
- **Seed:** Started from Larry Page's Stanford home page

**Technical Components:**
- Web crawler with link extraction and analysis
- Sparse matrix representation for efficient computation
- Power iteration for eigenvector calculation
- Large-scale data processing systems

## **Key Publications**

### **Primary Academic Papers**
1. **"The PageRank citation ranking: Bringing order to the Web"**
   - **Date:** January 29, 1998 (Stanford Technical Report)
   - **Authors:** Page, Lawrence; Brin, Sergey; Motwani, Rajeev; Winograd, Terry

2. **"The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual web search engine"**
   - **Journal:** Computer Networks and ISDN Systems, Volume 30, pages 107-117
   - **Year:** 1998
   - **DOI:** 10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X
   - **Co-authors:** Sergey Brin

## **Patents**

### **Primary Patent**
- **Patent US 6,285,999:** "Method for node ranking in a linked database"
- **Filing Date:** January 9, 1998
- **Granted:** September 4, 2001
- **Innovation:** First patent covering eigenvector-based ranking in linked databases

### **Additional Patents**
- US 6,799,176: Scoring methods in linked databases
- US 7,058,628: Enhanced node ranking methodology  
- US 7,269,587: Advanced document scoring techniques

## **Division of Technical Contributions**

### **Larry Page's Focus:**
- Core PageRank algorithm mathematical framework
- BackRub project leadership and web crawler development
- System architecture and hardware integration
- Citation analysis concept extension to web structure

### **Sergey Brin's Focus:**
- Data mining systems and pattern extraction
- Mathematical optimization and convergence algorithms
- Iterative computation enhancement

## **Work Experience Before Google**

Based on extensive research, Larry Page had **minimal professional work experience** before founding Google. His career timeline shows:

- **1991-1995:** University of Michigan (undergraduate)
- **1995-1998:** Stanford University graduate studies
- **1996-1998:** BackRub research project at Stanford
- **1998:** Co-founded Google Inc.

**Key Insight:** Page transitioned directly from academic research to entrepreneurship, with Google developing from his Stanford graduate project rather than prior industry experience.

## **Academic Recognition**

- **World Economic Forum Global Leader for Tomorrow** (2002)
- **Marconi Prize winner** (2004, with Sergey Brin)
- **Elected to National Academy of Engineering** (2004)
- **Member:** National Advisory Committee, University of Michigan College of Engineering

## **Technical Impact**

Larry Page's inventions revolutionized information retrieval by:
- Transitioning web search from keyword frequency to link-based importance scoring
- Introducing scalable mathematical algorithms for massive web graph analysis
- Creating the foundation for modern search engine architecture
- Establishing principles for ranking in networked data structures

The PageRank algorithm remains one of the most influential inventions in internet technology and information retrieval, directly emerging from Page's academic research at Stanford and forming the technical foundation of Google's early competitive advantage.

In 1983 Apple Computer introduced the first mass-marketed microcomputer with a graphical user interface, the Lisa. 基于我对可用资源的搜索和研究，以下是关于史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克和拉里·佩奇的详细对比分析，重点关注他们的教育背景、技术贡献和作为公司技术联合创始人的相关经历：

## **史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克——技术概况与教育路径**

### **教育背景**
- **早期教育尝试**：科罗拉多大学博尔德分校（仅就读一年后被黑客行为开除）
- **继续深造**：迪安萨学院（继续工程学业）
- **学位完成**：加州大学伯克利分校（电气工程与计算机科学理学学士，1986年/1976级）

### **技术贡献与发明（苹果创立前/期间）**
**苹果I（1976年）**：
- **关键创新**：首批采用价格合理的MOS 6502处理器的计算机之一
- **设计理念**：强调简洁性、可靠性和低成本
- **技术成就**：展示了用最少部件创造优雅解决方案的能力

**革命性的苹果II工程（1977年）**：
- **芯片数量最小化**：让单个芯片执行多种功能
- **视频系统创新**：使用内存交错技术替代复杂的视频控制器
- **色彩生成**：无需专用芯片，通过操作NTSC时序创建彩色图形
- **Disk II控制器（1978年）**：利用软件时序循环取代昂贵的控制器芯片

**苹果创立前相关经历**：
- **自学成才的工程师**：精通电子学和计算机设计的自我教育
- **蓝盒子项目**：与史蒂夫·乔布斯合作开发电话系统设备
- **广泛的电子学实验**：青少年时期进行了大量动手电子学实践

---

## **拉里·佩奇——技术概况与教育路径**

### **教育背景**
- **密歇根大学（1991-1995年）**：计算机工程理学学士，以优异成绩毕业
- **斯坦福大学（1995-1998年）**：计算机科学理学硕士（1998年），创立谷歌时辍学攻读博士学位
- **主要学术导师**：特里·温诺格拉德
- **研究背景**：斯坦福数字图书馆项目

### **技术贡献与发明（谷歌创立前/期间）**
**PageRank算法**：
- **数学基础**：G · r = r（Google矩阵特征向量公式）
- **核心创新**：将学术引用分析方法扩展到网页链接结构
- **实施过程**：自1996年起开始定制的"BackRub"项目，1996年8月实现7520万个索引URL

**谷歌创立前相关经历**：
- **极少的行业经验**——直接从学术研究转向创业
- **BackRub项目**（1996-1998年）在斯坦福成为谷歌的技术基础
- **主要学术出版物**：
  - "PageRank引用排名：为网络带来秩序"（1998年）
  - "大规模超文本网络搜索引擎的构造"（1998年）

**技术创新**：
- 将特征向量中心性概念应用到大规模网络图表
- 实现了数十亿网页的稀疏矩阵计算
- 为网络图表分析创建了可扩展的数学算法

---

## **创新路径比较**

### **史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克的路径：**
- **实践工程师模式**：自我指导学习 → 动手实验 → 产品创新
- **硬件约束** → 创造性解决方案 → 制造卓越
- **非正规教育** → 应用型创新

### **拉里·佩奇的路径：**
- **学术研究路径**：直接将博士研究转化为商业技术
- **正式教育完成**：在顶尖大学拥有扎实的学术基础
- **理论基础**：应用数学原理（特征向量、马尔可夫链）进行网络分析
- **协作研究**：与学术导师（温诺格拉德、莫特瓦尼）和研究伙伴合作

---

## **关键技术对比**

**沃兹尼亚克的优势**：
- 硬件架构设计
- 简洁工程哲学
- 成本效益组件利用
- 实际电子产品实现

**佩奇的优势**：
- 算法设计与数学分析
- 大规模系统架构
- 理论到实际应用的转换
- 协作研究方法

---

## **对各自公司创始阶段的影响**

**对苹果的影响（沃兹尼亚克）**：
- 提供了使Apple I和Apple II获得商业成功所需的核心工程能力
- 创造了使早期个人电脑价格合理、功能可靠的技术解决方案
- 确立了贯穿苹果历史的简洁创新设计理念

**对谷歌的影响（佩奇）**：
- 开发了使谷歌区别于早期搜索引擎的核心算法优势
- 为可扩展的互联网搜索系统创建了数学基础
- 为谷歌的技术驱动文化奠定了理论基础

### **技术贡献与发明（苹果创立前/期间）**
**苹果I（1976年）**：
- **关键创新**：首批采用价格合理的MOS 6502处理器的计算机之一
- **设计理念**：强调简洁性、可靠性和低成本
- **技术成就**：展示了用最少部件创造优雅解决方案的能力

**革命性的苹果II工程（1977年）**：
- **芯片数量最小化**：让单个芯片执行多种功能
- **视频系统创新**：使用内存交错技术替代复杂的视频控制器
- **色彩生成**：无需专用芯片，通过操作NTSC时序创建彩色图形
- **Disk II控制器（1978年）**：利用软件时序循环取代昂贵的控制器芯片

**苹果创立前相关经历**：
- **自学成才的工程师**：精通电子学和计算机设计的自我教育
- **蓝盒子项目**：与史蒂夫·乔布斯合作开发电话系统设备
- **广泛的电子学实验**：青少年时期进行了大量动手电子学实践

---

## **拉里·佩奇——技术概况与教育路径**

### **教育背景**
- **密歇根大学（1991-1995年）**：计算机工程理学学士，以优异成绩毕业
- **斯坦福大学（1995-1998年）**：计算机科学理学硕士（1998年），创立谷歌时辍学攻读博士学位
- **主要学术导师**：特里·温诺格拉德
- **研究背景**：斯坦福数字图书馆项目

### **技术贡献与发明（谷歌创立前/期间）**
**PageRank算法**：
- **数学基础**：G · r = r（Google矩阵特征向量公式）
- **核心创新**：将学术引用分析方法扩展到网页链接结构
- **实施过程**：自1996年起开始定制的"BackRub"项目，1996年8月实现7520万个索引URL

**谷歌创立前相关经历**：
- **极少的行业经验**——直接从学术研究转向创业
- **BackRub项目**（1996-1998年）在斯坦福成为谷歌的技术基础
- **主要学术出版物**：
  - "PageRank引用排名：为网络带来秩序"（1998年）
  - "大规模超文本网络搜索引擎的构造"（1998年）

**技术创新**：
- 将特征向量中心性概念应用到大规模网络图表
- 实现了数十亿网页的稀疏矩阵计算
- 为网络图表分析创建了可扩展的数学算法

---

## **创新路径比较**

### **史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克的路径：**
- **实践工程师模式**：自我指导学习 → 动手实验 → 产品创新
- **硬件约束** → 创造性解决方案 → 制造卓越
- **非正规教育** → 应用型创新

### **拉里·佩奇的路径：**
- **学术研究路径**：直接将博士研究转化为商业技术
- **正式教育完成**：在顶尖大学拥有扎实的学术基础
- **理论基础**：应用数学原理（特征向量、马尔可夫链）进行网络分析
- **协作研究**：与学术导师（温诺格拉德、莫特瓦尼）和研究伙伴合作

---

## **关键技术对比**

**沃兹尼亚克的优势**：
- 硬件架构设计
- 简洁工程哲学
- 成本效益组件利用
- 实际电子产品实现

**佩奇的优势**：
- 算法设计与数学分析
- 大规模系统架构
- 理论到实际应用的转换
- 协作研究方法

---

## **对各自公司创始阶段的影响**

**对苹果的影响（沃兹尼亚克）**：
- 提供了使Apple I和Apple II获得商业成功所需的核心工程能力
- 创造了使早期个人电脑价格合理、功能可靠的技术解决方案
- 确立了贯穿苹果历史的简洁创新设计理念

**对谷歌的影响（佩奇）**：
- 开发了使谷歌区别于早期搜索引擎的核心算法优势
- 为可扩展的互联网搜索系统创建了数学基础
- 为谷歌的技术驱动文化奠定了理论基础

---

<title>History of Google</title>
<fragment>

In the search of a dissertation theme, Larry Page had been considering among other things exploring the mathematical properties of the World Wide Web, understanding its link structure as a huge graph.[8] His supervisor, Terry Winograd, encouraged him to pick this idea (which Larry Page later recalled as "the best advice I ever got"[9]) and Larry Page focused on the problem of finding out which web pages link to a given page, based on the consideration that the number and nature of such backlinks was valuable information about that page (with the role of citations in academic publishing in mind).[8] Larry Page told his ideas to Hassan, who began writing the code to implement Larry Page's ideas.[3]

Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[19] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd later co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998. Héctor García-Molina and Jeff Ullman were also cited as contributors to the project.[20]


PageRank was influenced by a similar page-ranking and site-scoring algorithm earlier used for RankDex, developed by Robin Li in 1996. Larry Page's patent for PageRank filed in 1998 includes a citation to Li's earlier patent. Li later went on to create the Chinese search engine Baidu in 2000.[21][22][23]

<fragment>
Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed PageRank at Stanford University in 1996 as part of a research project about a new kind of search engine. An interview with Héctor García-Molina, Stanford Computer Science professor and advisor to Sergey,[23] provides background into the development of the page-rank algorithm.[24] Sergey Brin had the idea that information on the web could be ordered in a hierarchy by "link popularity": a page ranks higher as there are more links to it.[25] The system was developed with the help of Scott Hassan and Alan Steremberg, both of whom were cited by Page and Brin as being critical to the development of Google.[5] Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd co-authored with Page and Brin the first paper about the project, describing PageRank and the initial prototype of the Google search engine, published in 1998.[5] Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc., the company behind the Google search engine.

<fragment>

Brin began his graduate study in computer science at Stanford University on a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, receiving an M.S. in computer science in 1995.[11] As of 2008[update], he was on leave from his PhD studies at Stanford.[12]



## Search engine development

[edit]

![](image)Left to right, Eric Schmidt, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, 2008
During an orientation for new students at Stanford, he met Larry Page. The two men seemed to disagree on most subjects, but after spending time together they "became intellectual soul-mates and close friends." Brin's focus was on developing data mining systems while Page's was on extending "the concept of inferring the importance of a research paper from its citations in other papers".[13] Together, they authored a paper titled "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine".[14]

After filling Page's room with equipment, they then converted Brin's dorm room into an office and programming center, where they tested their new search engine designs on the web. The rapid growth of their project caused Stanford's computing infrastructure to experience problems.[17]


Page and Brin used the former's basic HTML programming skills to set up a simple search page for users, as they did not have a web page developer to create anything visually elaborate. They also began using any computer part they could find to assemble the necessary computing power to handle searches by multiple users. As their search engine grew in popularity among Stanford users, it required additional servers to process the queries. The earliest evidence of algorithms is found in the Babylonian mathematics of ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq). A Sumerian clay tablet found in Shuruppak near Baghdad and dated to c. 2500 BC described the earliest division algorithm.[11] During the Hammurabi dynasty c. 1800 – c. 1600 BC, Babylonian clay tablets described algorithms for computing formulas.[86] Algorithms were also used in Babylonian astronomy. Babylonian clay tablets describe and employ algorithmic procedures to compute the time and place of significant astronomical events.[87]


Algorithms for arithmetic are also found in ancient Egyptian mathematics, dating back to the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus c. 1550 BC.[11] Algorithms were later used in ancient Hellenistic mathematics. Two examples are the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which was described in the *Introduction to Arithmetic* by Nicomachus,[88][14]: Ch 9.2 and the Euclidean algorithm, which was first described in *Euclid's Elements* (c. 300 BC).[14]: Ch 9.1

**Euclid** (/ˈjuːklɪd/; Template:Lang-grc-gre; fl. 300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[2] Considered the "father of geometry",[3] he is chiefly known for the *Elements* treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved new innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

<document>
<title>History of mathematics</title>
<fragment>
In the 9th century, the mathematician Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī wrote an important book on the Hindu–Arabic numerals and one on methods for solving equations. His book *On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals*, written about 825, along with the work of Al-Kindi, were instrumental in spreading Indian mathematics and Indian numerals to the West. The word *algorithm* is derived from the Latinization of his name, Algoritmi, and the word *algebra* from the title of one of his works, *Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī hīsāb al-ğabr wa’l-muqābala* (*The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing*). 
</fragment>
<fragment>
The speed and data processing abilities of computers also enabled the handling of mathematical problems that were too time-consuming to deal with by pencil and paper calculations, leading to areas such as numerical analysis and symbolic computation. Some of the most important methods and algorithms of the 20th century are: the simplex algorithm, the fast Fourier transform, error-correcting codes, the Kalman filter from control theory and the RSA algorithm of public-key cryptography.


</fragment>
</document>

Based on my search results, I can provide you with comprehensive information about who invented algorithms and who is credited as the "father of algorithms":

## The "Father of Algorithms": Al-Khwarizmi

**Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi** (c. 780-850 AD) is most commonly credited as the "father of algorithms." Here's why:

- **Etymology**: The word "algorithm" is derived from the Latinization of his name, "Algoritmi"
- **Historical context**: He was a 9th-century Persian mathematician who worked in Baghdad
- **Contributions**: His book "On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals" (written about 825 AD) was instrumental in spreading Indian mathematics and numerals to the West
- **Dual honor**: Both "algorithm" and "algebra" come from his work - "algebra" from the title of his book "Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī hīsāb al-ğabr wa'l-muqābala" (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing)

## Ancient Precursors to Algorithms

However, algorithms existed long before Al-Khwarizmi:

### **Babylonian Mathematics (c. 2500-1600 BC)**
- **Earliest evidence**: A Sumerian clay tablet from Shuruppak near Baghdad, dated to c. 2500 BC, described the earliest known division algorithm
- **Hammurabi dynasty (c. 1800-1600 BC)**: Babylonian clay tablets described algorithms for computing formulas
- **Astronomical algorithms**: Used to compute time and place of significant astronomical events

### **Ancient Egyptian Mathematics (c. 1550 BC)**
- **Rhind Mathematical Papyrus**: Contains algorithms for arithmetic, dating back to c. 1550 BC

### **Ancient Greek Mathematics (c. 300 BC)**
- **Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BC)**: Contains the famous **Euclidean algorithm**, which Donald Knuth called "the granddaddy of all algorithms, because it is the oldest nontrivial algorithm that has survived to the present day"
- **Sieve of Eratosthenes**: Another algorithmic method described by Nicomachus
- **Earlier origins**: The Euclidean algorithm was probably not discovered by Euclid himself but likely known to mathematicians like Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 375 BC) or even earlier Pythagoreans

## Summary

While **Al-Khwarizmi** is deservedly called the "father of algorithms" due to the word's etymology and his systematic work with computational methods, the concept of algorithms dates back much further:

- **2500 BC**: Babylonian division algorithms
- **1550 BC**: Egyptian arithmetic algorithms  
- **375 BC+**: Greek algorithms (Euclidean algorithm)
- **825 AD**: Al-Khwarizmi formalizes and spreads algorithmic methods

So while Al-Khwarizmi gave algorithms their name and systematized their study, the honor for the **first algorithms** goes to the ancient Babylonians, with important contributions from Egyptians and Greeks.

- **Dual honor**: Both "algorithm" and "algebra" come from his work - "algebra" from the title of his book "Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī hīsāb al-ğabr wa'l-muqābala" (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing)

## Ancient Precursors to Algorithms

However, algorithms existed long before Al-Khwarizmi:

### **Babylonian Mathematics (c. 2500-1600 BC)**
- **Earliest evidence**: A Sumerian clay tablet from Shuruppak near Baghdad, dated to c. 2500 BC, described the earliest known division algorithm
- **Hammurabi dynasty (c. 1800-1600 BC)**: Babylonian clay tablets described algorithms for computing formulas
- **Astronomical algorithms**: Used to compute time and place of significant astronomical events

### **Ancient Egyptian Mathematics (c. 1550 BC)**
- **Rhind Mathematical Papyrus**: Contains algorithms for arithmetic, dating back to c. 1550 BC

### **Ancient Greek Mathematics (c. 300 BC)**
- **Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BC)**: Contains the famous **Euclidean algorithm**, which Donald Knuth called "the granddaddy of all algorithms, because it is the oldest nontrivial algorithm that has survived to the present day"
- **Sieve of Eratosthenes**: Another algorithmic method described by Nicomachus
- **Earlier origins**: The Euclidean algorithm was probably not discovered by Euclid himself but likely known to mathematicians like Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 375 BC) or even earlier Pythagoreans

## Summary

While **Al-Khwarizmi** is deservedly called the "father of algorithms" due to the word's etymology and his systematic work with computational methods, the concept of algorithms dates back much further:

- **2500 BC**: Babylonian division algorithms
- **1550 BC**: Egyptian arithmetic algorithms  
- **375 BC+**: Greek algorithms (Euclidean algorithm)
- **825 AD**: Al-Khwarizmi formalizes and spreads algorithmic methods

So while Al-Khwarizmi gave algorithms their name and systematized their study, the honor for the **first algorithms** goes to the ancient Babylonians, with important contributions from Egyptians and Greeks.

Another controversy arose over a century later when the U.S. Congress passed a resolution in 2002 recognizing Italian-American Antonio Meucci's contributions *in* the invention of the telephone (not for the invention of the telephone), a declaration that bore no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). <title>Alexander Graham Bell</title>
<fragment>

**Alexander Graham Bell** (/ˈɡreɪ.əm/, born **Alexander Bell**; March 3, 1847 – August 2, 1922)[4] was a Scottish-born[N 1] inventor, scientist and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. He also co-founded the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) in 1885.[7]


Bell's father, grandfather, and brother had all been associated with work on elocution and speech, and both his mother and wife were deaf; profoundly influencing Bell's life's work.[8] His research on hearing and speech further led him to experiment with hearing devices which eventually culminated in Bell being awarded the first U.S. patent for the telephone, on March 7, 1876.[N 2] Bell considered his invention an intrusion on his real work as a scientist and refused to have a telephone in his study.[9][N 3]

<title>Johann Philipp Reis</title>
<fragment>
[edit]

Main article: Invention of the telephone

Besides Reis and Bell, many others claimed to have invented the telephone. The result was the Gray-Bell telephone controversy, one of the United States' longest running patent interference cases, involving Bell, Thomas Alva Edison, Elisha Gray, Emil Berliner, Amos Dolbear, J. W. McDonagh, G. B. Richmond, W. L. Voeker, J. H. Irwin, and Francis Blake Jr. The case started in 1878 and was not finalised until 27 February 1901. Bell and the Bell Telephone Company triumphed in this crucial decision, as well as every one of the over 600 other court decisions related to the invention of the telephone. The Bell Telephone Company never lost a case that had proceeded to a final trial stage.[9]

**Elisha Gray** (August 2, 1835 – January 21, 1901) was an American electrical engineer who co-founded the Western Electric Manufacturing Company. Gray is best known for his development of a telephone prototype in 1876 in Highland Park, Illinois. Some recent authors have argued that Gray should be considered the true inventor of the telephone because Alexander Graham Bell allegedly stole the idea of the liquid transmitter from him.[1] Although Gray had been using liquid transmitters in his telephone experiments for more than two years previously, Bell's telephone patent was upheld in numerous court decisions.

The **Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell controversy** concerns the question of whether Gray and Bell invented the telephone independently. This issue is narrower than the question of who deserves credit for inventing the telephone, for which there are several claimants.


At issue are roles of each inventor's lawyers, the filing of patent documents, and allegations of theft.

<document>
<title>Timeline of the telephone</title>
<fragment>
* 1871: Meucci files a patent caveat (a statement of intention to file a patent application)[3] for a Sound Telegraph, but it does not describe an electromagnetic telephone.
* 1872: Elisha Gray founds the Western Electric Manufacturing Company.
* 1872: Professor Vanderwyde demonstrates Reis's telephone in New York.
* July 1873: Thomas Edison notes varying resistance in carbon grains due to pressure, and builds a rheostat based on the principle but abandons it because of its sensitivity to vibration.
* May 1874: Gray invents an electromagnet device for transmitting musical tones. Some of his receivers use a metallic diaphragm.
* July 1874: Alexander Graham Bell conceives the theoretical concept for the telephone while vacationing at his parents' farm near Brantford, Canada. Alexander Melville Bell records notes of his son's conversation in his personal journal.

<title>Johann Philipp Reis</title>
<fragment>

Another controversy arose over a century later when the U.S. Congress passed a resolution in 2002 recognizing Italian-American Antonio Meucci's contributions *in* the invention of the telephone (not for the invention of the telephone), a declaration that bore no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Canada's Parliament quickly followed with a tit-for-tat declaration, which clarified: "....that Alexander Graham Bell of Brantford, Ont., and Baddeck, N.S., [was] the inventor of the telephone."[10] Prior to his death, Meucci had lost his only concluded Federal lawsuit trial related to the telephone's invention.

<document>
<title>Alexander Graham Bell</title>
<fragment>
As is sometimes common in scientific discoveries, simultaneous developments can occur, as evidenced by a number of inventors who were at work on the telephone.[112] Over a period of 18 years, the Bell Telephone Company faced 587 court challenges to its patents, including five that went to the U.S. Supreme Court,[113] but none was successful in establishing priority over the original Bell patent,[114][115] and the Bell Telephone Company never lost a case that had proceeded to a final trial stage.[114] Bell's laboratory notes and family letters were the key to establishing a long lineage to his experiments.[114] The Bell company lawyers successfully fought off myriad lawsuits generated initially around the challenges by Elisha Gray and Amos Dolbear. In personal correspondence to Bell, both Gray and Dolbear had acknowledged his prior work, which considerably weakened their later claims.[116]

<title>Johann Philipp Reis</title>
<fragment>

Another controversy arose over a century later when the U.S. Congress passed a resolution in 2002 recognizing Italian-American Antonio Meucci's contributions *in* the invention of the telephone (not for the invention of the telephone), a declaration that bore no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Canada's Parliament quickly followed with a tit-for-tat declaration, which clarified: "....that Alexander Graham Bell of Brantford, Ont., and Baddeck, N.S., [was] the inventor of the telephone."[10] Prior to his death, Meucci had lost his only concluded Federal lawsuit trial related to the telephone's invention.

Main article: Invention of the telephone

Besides Reis and Bell, many others claimed to have invented the telephone. The result was the Gray-Bell telephone controversy, one of the United States' longest running patent interference cases, involving Bell, Thomas Alva Edison, Elisha Gray, Emil Berliner, Amos Dolbear, J. W. McDonagh, G. B. Richmond, W. L. Voeker, J. H. Irwin, and Francis Blake Jr. The case started in 1878 and was not finalised until 27 February 1901. Bell and the Bell Telephone Company triumphed in this crucial decision, as well as every one of the over 600 other court decisions related to the invention of the telephone. The Bell Telephone Company never lost a case that had proceeded to a final trial stage.[9]

<title>Elisha Gray</title>
<fragment>

On July 27, 1875, Gray was granted U.S. patent 166,095 for "Electric Telegraph for Transmitting Musical Tones" (acoustic telegraphy). His experiments with transmitting musical tones went further, and on February 15, 1876 Elisha Grey was granted US Patent for electro-harmonic telegraph with piano keyboard.[9][10]


He was elected as a member to the American Philosophical Society in 1878.[11]


On July 31, 1888, Gray patented the telautograph, an analog precursor to the modern fax machine. Gray's patent stated that the telautograph would allow "one to transmit his own handwriting to a distant point over a two-wire circuit." It was the first facsimile machine in which the stylus was controlled by horizontal and vertical bars.[12] The telautograph was first publicly exhibited at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition held in Chicago.

The **Reis telephone** was an invention named after Philipp Reis of a telephone-like device he constructed. Reis's first successful work is dated to October 1861.




## History

[edit]

In 1861, Philipp Reis succeeded in creating a device that captured sound, converted it to electrical impulses which were transmitted via electrical wires to another device that transformed these pulses into recognizable sounds similar to the original acoustical source. Reis coined the term *telephon* to describe his device.


In 1862, Reis demonstrated his telephone to Wilhelm von Legat, Inspector of the Royal Prussian Telegraph Corps who produced an account of it (Legat, 1862), a translation of which was obtained by Thomas Edison in 1875 and which was used in Edison's successful development of the carbon microphone. The Legat account included drawings that are different from that below, suggesting that it is of a later version. Edison acknowledged his debt to Reis thus:




</fragment>
<fragment>

> The first inventor of a telephone was Phillip Reis of Germany only musical not articulating. The first person to publicly exhibit a telephone for transmission of articulate speech was A. G. Bell. The first practical commercial telephone for transmission of articulate speech was invented by myself. Telephones used throughout the world are mine and Bell's. Mine is used for transmitting. Bell's is used for receiving.[1]
> 
> 


## Microphone

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Johann Philipp Reis telephone
Reis's speaker worked by magnetostriction. In his first receiver he wound a coil of wire around an iron knitting needle and rested the needle against the F hole of a violin. As current passed through the needle, the iron *shrank* and a click was produced. The image, below, shows an advanced version where the iron bar is clamped to a cigar-box-shaped resonator. This receiver is not very sensitive. It produces weak sound but has good fidelity. It requires very high current and is a current-sensitive device rather than a voltage-sensitive device.


This instrument could transmit continuous musical tones but produced indistinct speech.[*citation needed*] In 1865, however, British scientist David E. Hughes used the Reis telephone with "good results".[4]

<title>Alexander Graham Bell</title>
<fragment>
As is sometimes common in scientific discoveries, simultaneous developments can occur, as evidenced by a number of inventors who were at work on the telephone.[112] Over a period of 18 years, the Bell Telephone Company faced 587 court challenges to its patents, including five that went to the U.S. Supreme Court,[113] but none was successful in establishing priority over the original Bell patent,[114][115] and the Bell Telephone Company never lost a case that had proceeded to a final trial stage.[114] Bell's laboratory notes and family letters were the key to establishing a long lineage to his experiments.[114] The Bell company lawyers successfully fought off myriad lawsuits generated initially around the challenges by Elisha Gray and Amos Dolbear. In personal correspondence to Bell, both Gray and Dolbear had acknowledged his prior work, which considerably weakened their later claims.[116]

<document>
<title>History of the telephone</title>
<fragment>
Credit for the invention of the electric telephone is frequently disputed, and new controversies over the issue have arisen from time to time. Antonio Meucci, Alexander Graham Bell, and Elisha Gray amongst others, have all been credited with the telephone's invention. The early history of the telephone became and still remains a confusing morass of claims and counterclaims, which were not clarified by the huge number of lawsuits filed in order to resolve the patent claims of the many individuals and commercial competitors. The Bell and Edison patents, however, were commercially decisive, because they dominated telephone technology and were upheld by court decisions in the United States.



* ![Antonio Meucci, 1854, constructed telephone-like devices.](image)

Antonio Meucci, 1854, constructed telephone-like devices.

The modern telephone is the result of the work of many people.[10] Alexander Graham Bell was, however, the first to patent the telephone, as an "apparatus for transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically". Bell has most often been credited as the inventor of the first practical telephone. Johann Philipp Reis coined the term "telephon".[11] Models of it were sent abroad, to London, Dublin, Tiflis, and other places. It became a subject for popular lectures, and an article for scientific cabinets. Edison credited him as the "first inventor of the telephone."[12]
The Italian-American inventor and businessman Antonio Meucci has been recognized by the U.S. House of Representatives for his contributory work on the telephone.[13] Several other controversies also surround the question of priority of invention for the telephone.

<title>Elisha Gray</title>
<fragment>

On July 27, 1875, Gray was granted U.S. patent 166,095 for "Electric Telegraph for Transmitting Musical Tones" (acoustic telegraphy). His experiments with transmitting musical tones went further, and on February 15, 1876 Elisha Grey was granted US Patent for electro-harmonic telegraph with piano keyboard.[9][10]


He was elected as a member to the American Philosophical Society in 1878.[11]


On July 31, 1888, Gray patented the telautograph, an analog precursor to the modern fax machine. Gray's patent stated that the telautograph would allow "one to transmit his own handwriting to a distant point over a two-wire circuit." It was the first facsimile machine in which the stylus was controlled by horizontal and vertical bars.[12] The telautograph was first publicly exhibited at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition held in Chicago.

<title>Johann Philipp Reis</title>
<fragment>

Another controversy arose over a century later when the U.S. Congress passed a resolution in 2002 recognizing Italian-American Antonio Meucci's contributions *in* the invention of the telephone (not for the invention of the telephone), a declaration that bore no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Canada's Parliament quickly followed with a tit-for-tat declaration, which clarified: "....that Alexander Graham Bell of Brantford, Ont., and Baddeck, N.S., [was] the inventor of the telephone."[10] Prior to his death, Meucci had lost his only concluded Federal lawsuit trial related to the telephone's invention.

Besides Reis and Bell, many others claimed to have invented the telephone. The result was the Gray-Bell telephone controversy, one of the United States' longest running patent interference cases, involving Bell, Thomas Alva Edison, Elisha Gray, Emil Berliner, Amos Dolbear, J. W. McDonagh, G. B. Richmond, W. L. Voeker, J. H. Irwin, and Francis Blake Jr. The case started in 1878 and was not finalised until 27 February 1901. Bell and the Bell Telephone Company triumphed in this crucial decision, as well as every one of the over 600 other court decisions related to the invention of the telephone. The Bell Telephone Company never lost a case that had proceeded to a final trial stage.[9]

The Court's decision in the *Telephone Cases* is notable for the size of the opinions delivered; together, they occupy the entire 126th volume of the *United States Reports*.



## Notable cases

[edit]

Among the notable court cases involving the Bell Telephone Company, later renamed to the American Bell Telephone Company, were those related to challenges by Elisha Gray, a principal in Western Electric, as depicted in the Elisha Gray and Alexander Bell telephone controversy.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Additionally the Bell Company became embroiled in a number of challenges from those companies associated with Antonio Meucci, as shown in the Canadian Parliamentary Motion on Alexander Graham Bell, itself a response to the United States HRes. 269 on Antonio Meucci.

## The 2002 Telephone Controversy (House Resolution 269)

**What Actually Happened:**
In 2002, the U.S. House of Representatives passed **House Resolution 269**, which recognized Antonio Meucci's contributions to the invention of the telephone. The resolution stated:

> "Expresses the sense of the House of Representatives that the life and achievements of Antonio Meucci should be recognized, and his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged."

**Key Details from Wikipedia:**
- The resolution recognized Meucci's "contributions *in* the invention of the telephone" (not necessarily as the sole inventor)
- This resolution had "no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)"
- Canada's Parliament responded with a "tit-for-tat declaration" reaffirming Alexander Graham Bell as the inventor

## The Broader Context

**Multiple Claimants to Telephone Invention:**
According to Wikipedia, telephone invention involved several key figures:
1. **Antonio Meucci** - Italian-American who demonstrated telephone-like devices as early as 1854
2. **Johann Philipp Reis** - German inventor who constructed what is considered the first telephone in 1861, and coined the term "telephon"
3. **Alexander Graham Bell** - First to patent the telephone in 1876 as "apparatus for transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically"
4. **Elisha Gray** - Filed a patent application on the same day as Bell, leading to controversial patent disputes

**The Telephone Cases:**
Wikipedia documents extensive litigation called "The Telephone Cases" (126 U.S. 1, 1888), which involved:
- 587 court challenges to Bell's patents
- Multiple claims from various inventors including Edison, Dolbear, McDonough, Richmond, Voelker, Irwin, and Blake Jr.
- Bell and his companies "never lost a single case that was concluded with a final stage judgment"

Another controversy arose over a century later when the U.S. Congress passed a resolution in 2002 recognizing Italian-American Antonio Meucci's contributions *in* the invention of the telephone (not for the invention of the telephone), a declaration that bore no legal or other standing at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). <title>Invention of the telephone</title>
<fragment>
A retired director general of the Telecom Italia central telecommunications research institute (CSELT), Basilio Catania,[8] and the Italian Society of Electrotechnics, "*Federazione Italiana di Elettrotecnica*", have devoted a Museum to Antonio Meucci, constructing a chronology of his invention of the telephone and tracing the history of the two legal trials involving Meucci and Alexander Graham Bell.[9][10][11]


They claim that Meucci was the actual inventor of the telephone, and base their argument on reconstructed evidence. What follows, if not otherwise stated, is a summary of their historic reconstruction.[12]

<fragment>

An American District Telegraph (ADT) laboratory reportedly lost some of Meucci's working models, his wife reportedly disposed of others and Meucci, who sometimes lived on public assistance, chose not to renew his 1871 *teletrofono* patent caveat after 1874.


A resolution was passed by the United States House of Representatives in 2002 that said Meucci did pioneering work on the development of the telephone.[4][5][6][7] The resolution said that "if Meucci had been able to pay the $10 fee to maintain the caveat after 1874, no patent could have been issued to Bell".


The Meucci resolution by the US Congress was promptly followed by a Canada legislative motion by Canada's 37th Parliament, declaring Alexander Graham Bell as the inventor of the telephone. Others in Canada disagreed with the Congressional resolution, some of whom provided criticisms of both its accuracy and intent.

[edit]

The first American demonstration of Meucci's invention took place in Staten Island, New York in 1854.[3] In 1861, a description of it was reportedly published in an Italian-language New York newspaper, although no known copy of that newspaper issue or article has survived to the present day. Meucci claimed to have invented a paired electromagnetic transmitter and receiver, where the motion of a diaphragm modulated a signal in a coil by moving an electromagnet, although this was not mentioned in his 1871 U.S. patent caveat. A further discrepancy observed was that the device described in the 1871 caveat employed only a single conduction wire, with the telephone's transmitter-receivers being insulated from a 'ground return' path.

**Johann Philipp Reis** (Template:IPA-de; 7 January 1834 – 14 January 1874) was a self-taught German scientist and inventor. In 1861, he constructed the first *make-and-break* telephone, today called the Reis telephone.




## Early life and education

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Documents of 1947 in London's Science Museum later showed that after their technical adjustments, engineers from the British firm Standard Telephones and Cables (STC) found Reis' telephone dating from 1863 could transmit and "reproduce speech of good quality, but of low efficiency".


Sir Frank Gill, then chairman of STC, ordered the tests to be kept secret, as STC was then negotiating with AT&T, which had evolved from the Bell Telephone Company, created by Alexander Graham Bell. Professor Bell was generally accepted as having invented the telephone and Gill thought that evidence to the contrary might disrupt the ongoing negotiations.



### Johann-Philipp-Reis Preis (Award)

[edit]

The VDE (the German electrical engineering association), Deutsche Telekom and the cities of Friedrichsdorf and Gelnhausen biannually present the *Johann-Philipp-Reis Preis* (prize) to scientists for "....distinguished scientific achievements in the area of communication technology".



## Telephone invention controversies


</fragment>

Prior to 1947, the Reis device was tested by the British company Standard Telephones and Cables (STC). The results also confirmed it could faintly transmit and receive speech. <title>Invention of the telephone</title>
<fragment>
The Reis telephone was developed from 1857 onwards. Allegedly, the transmitter was difficult to operate, since the relative position of the needle and the contact were critical to the device's operation. Thus, it can be called a "telephone", since it did transmit voice sounds electrically over distance, but was hardly a commercially practical telephone in the modern sense.


In 1874, the Reis device was tested by the British company Standard Telephones and Cables (STC). The results also confirmed it could transmit and receive speech with good quality (fidelity), but relatively low intensity.[*citation needed*]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* In August 1870, Meucci later claimed that he obtained transmission of articulate human voice at a mile distance by using as a conductor a copper plait insulated by cotton. He called his device "*teletrofono*". Drawings and notes by Antonio Meucci dated September 27, 1870, show coils of wire on long-distance telephone lines.[16] The painting made by Nestore Corradi in 1858 mentions the sentence "Electric current from the inductor pipe".


The above information was published in the *Scientific American* Supplement No. 520 of December 19, 1885,[17] based on reconstructions produced in 1885, for which there was no contemporary pre-1875 evidence. Meucci's 1871 caveat did not mention any of the telephone features later credited to him by his lawyer, and which were published in that Scientific American Supplement, a major reason for the loss of the 'Bell v. Globe and Meucci' patent infringement court case, which was decided against Globe and Meucci.[18]



### Johann Philipp Reis

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Reis' new invention was articulated in a lecture before the Physical Society of Frankfurt on 26 October 1861, and a description, written by himself for Jahresbericht a month or two later. It created a good deal of scientific excitement in Germany; models of it were sent abroad, to London, Dublin, Tiflis, and other places. It became a subject for popular lectures, and an article for scientific cabinets.


Thomas Edison tested the Reis equipment and found that "single words, uttered as in reading, speaking and the like, were perceptible indistinctly, notwithstanding here also the inflections of the voice, the modulations of interrogation, wonder, command, etc., attained distinct expression."[19] He used Reis´s work for the successful development of the carbon microphone. - A description was written by himself for Jahresbericht a month or two later

## 2. Technical Details of Operation

### Transmitter Mechanism
- The transmitter worked as a "make-and-break" circuit - contacts that opened and closed
- **Controversy**: While it's regarded today as having varied the resistance of the contacts, Reis's description claimed the contacts opened and closed like switches
- The transmitter was difficult to operate since the relative position of the needle and the contact were critical to the device's operation
- Used a needle that vibrated against a contact point to create the electrical signal

### Receiver Mechanism  
- **Magnetostriction-based receiver**: This was the key innovation
- **First version**: Reis wound a coil of wire around an iron knitting needle and rested the needle against the F hole of a violin
- **Advanced version**: Iron bar clamped to a cigar-box-shaped resonator
- **Operation**: As current passed through the needle/iron bar, the iron **shrank** (due to magnetostriction) and produced a click
- The receiver was **current-sensitive** rather than voltage-sensitive
- Required very high current to operate
- Produced weak sound but had **good fidelity**

### Overall Operation
- The device captured sound, converted it to electrical impulses which were transmitted via electrical wires to another device that transformed these pulses into recognizable sounds similar to the original acoustic source
- Reis coined the term **"telephon"** to describe his device

## 3. Specific Components Used
- **Iron knitting needle** (in early version)
- **Iron bar** (in advanced version)
- **Coil of wire** wound around the iron
- **Violin** (used as resonator in early version - needle rested against F hole)
- **Cigar-box-shaped resonator** (in advanced version)
- **Contact points** for make-and-break operation

## 4. Evidence About Speech Transmission

### Positive Evidence
- **1862**: Demonstrated his telephone to Wilhelm von Legat, Inspector of the Royal Prussian Telegraph Corps who produced an account

- **1865**: British scientist David E. Hughes used the Reis telephone with "good results"

- **1947**: Engineers from British firm Standard Telephones and Cables (STC) found Reis's telephone dating from 1863 could transmit and "**reproduce speech of good quality, but of low efficiency**"

### Negative/Limitations
- The instrument could transmit **continuous musical tones** but produced **indistinct speech**
- Thomas Edison tested the Reis equipment and found that "**single words, uttered as in reading, speaking and the like, were perceptible indistinctly**"
- The receiver was not very sensitive and produced weak sound

## 5. "Reis-Telegraph" Device
The sources don't specifically mention a "Reis-Telegraph" device by that name, but refer to:
- **Reis telephone** (the primary device)
- The device was sometimes called a "**make-and-break** telephone"
- Contemporary accounts sometimes referred to it in telegraphy terms since it used similar transmission principles

## Key Technical Controversies
- **Legal issue**: At the time it was held that a circuit with such a 'make and break' circuit was incapable of transmitting intelligible speech, which was used legally to portray Reis's invention as invalid when Bell made his patent claim
- **Cover-up**: Sir Frank Gill, chairman of STC, ordered the 1947 test results to be kept secret as STC was negotiating with AT&T (which evolved from Bell Telephone Company)

The Reis device was scientifically important and functional, capable of transmitting speech with good fidelity, though it was not commercially practical and required very high current to operate.

- Used a needle that vibrated against a contact point to create the electrical signal

### Receiver Mechanism  
- **Magnetostriction-based receiver**: This was the key innovation
- **First version**: Reis wound a coil of wire around an iron knitting needle and rested the needle against the F hole of a violin
- **Advanced version**: Iron bar clamped to a cigar-box-shaped resonator
- **Operation**: As current passed through the needle/iron bar, the iron **shrank** (due to magnetostriction) and produced a click
- The receiver was **current-sensitive** rather than voltage-sensitive
- Required very high current to operate
- Produced weak sound but had **good fidelity**

### Overall Operation
- The device captured sound, converted it to electrical impulses which were transmitted via electrical wires to another device that transformed these pulses into recognizable sounds similar to the original acoustic source
- Reis coined the term **"telephon"** to describe his device

## 3. Specific Components Used
- **Iron knitting needle** (in early version)
- **Iron bar** (in advanced version)
- **Coil of wire** wound around the iron
- **Violin** (used as resonator in early version - needle rested against F hole)
- **Cigar-box-shaped resonator** (in advanced version)
- **Contact points** for make-and-break operation

## 4. Evidence About Speech Transmission

### Positive Evidence
- **1862**: Demonstrated his telephone to Wilhelm von Legat, Inspector of the Royal Prussian Telegraph Corps who produced an account
- **1863**: The device was widely publicly demonstrated and had been used to transmit speech from 1861
- **1865**: British scientist David E. Hughes used the Reis telephone with "good results"
- **1874**: The Reis device was tested by British company Standard Telephones and Cables (STC) - results confirmed it could transmit and receive speech with **good quality (fidelity)**, but relatively low intensity
- **1947**: Engineers from British firm Standard Telephones and Cables (STC) found Reis's telephone dating from 1863 could transmit and "**reproduce speech of good quality, but of low efficiency**"

### Negative/Limitations
- The instrument could transmit **continuous musical tones** but produced **indistinct speech**
- Thomas Edison tested the Reis equipment and found that "**single words, uttered as in reading, speaking and the like, were perceptible indistinctly**"
- The receiver was not very sensitive and produced weak sound

## 5. "Reis-Telegraph" Device

- The device was sometimes called a "**make-and-break** telephone"
- Contemporary accounts sometimes referred to it in telegraphy terms since it used similar transmission principles

- **Cover-up**: Sir Frank Gill, chairman of STC, ordered the 1947 test results to be kept secret as STC was negotiating with AT&T (which evolved from Bell Telephone Company)

The Reis device was scientifically important and functional, capable of transmitting speech with good fidelity, though it was not commercially practical and required very high current to operate.

**Elisha Gray** (August 2, 1835 – January 21, 1901) was an American electrical engineer who co-founded the Western Electric Manufacturing Company. Gray supporters cite the fact that Bell's first successful experiment in transmitting clear speech over a wire was on March 10, 1876 using the same water transmitter design described in Gray's caveat but not described in Bell's patent.[24] A book by Evenson,[25] concludes that it was Bell's lawyers, not Bell, who misappropriated Gray's water transmitter (variable resistance) invention.



### Important difference between Bell's patent application and Gray's caveat

The following quote forms part of the information that is found in the left margin of Bell's patent application, and is alleged by some to have been stolen from Gray's caveat:




</fragment>

Some writers continue to accuse Bell of stealing the telephone from Gray,[54] Evenson claims that Bell tested Gray's water transmitter design only after Bell's patent was granted and only as a proof of concept scientific experiment[55] to prove to his own satisfaction that intelligible "articulate speech" (Bell's words) could be electrically transmitted.[56]


Some claim that evidence exists in the Library of Congress and the U.S. Patent Office that Bell had used liquid transmitters from the time of his first electrical experiments in England in 1867 (in which he improved on the tuning fork sounder invented by Helmholtz that send musical tones over a wire using a liquid transmitter). <document>
<title>History of the telephone</title>
<fragment>

The Elisha Gray and Alexander Bell telephone controversy considers the question of whether Bell and Gray invented the telephone independently and, if not, whether Bell stole the invention from Gray. This controversy is narrower than the broader question of who deserves credit for inventing the telephone, for which there are several claimants.


The Canadian Parliamentary Motion on Alexander Graham Bell article reviews the controversial June 2002 United States House of Representatives resolution recognizing Meucci's contributions *'in'* the invention of the telephone (not *'for' the invention of the telephone*). The same resolution was not passed in the U.S. Senate, thus labeling the House resolution as "political rhetoric". A subsequent *counter-motion* was unanimously passed in Canada's Parliament 10 days later which declared Bell its inventor. This webpage examines critical aspects of both the parliamentary motion and the congressional resolution.



### Telephone exchange

<document>
<title>Invention of the telephone</title>
<fragment>
Elisha Gray recognized the lack of fidelity of the make-break transmitter of Reis and Bourseul and reasoned by analogy with the lover's telegraph, that if the current could be made to more closely model the movements of the diaphragm, rather than simply opening and closing the circuit, greater fidelity might be achieved. Gray filed a patent caveat with the US patent office on February 14, 1876, for a liquid microphone. The device used a metal needle or rod that was placed – just barely – into a liquid conductor, such as a water/acid mixture. In response to the diaphragm's vibrations, the needle dipped more or less into the liquid, varying the electrical resistance and thus the current passing through the device and on to the receiver. Gray did not convert his caveat into a patent application until after the caveat had expired and hence left the field open to Bell.


</fragment>
<fragment>

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Water microphone</title>
<content>
Electroacoustic device which generates a varying current in acidulated water

A **water microphone** or **water transmitter** is based on Ohm's law that current in a wire varies inversely with the resistance of the circuit. The sound waves from a human voice cause a diaphragm to vibrate which causes a needle or rod to vibrate up and down in water that has been made conductive by a small amount of acid. As the needle or rod vibrates up and down in the water, the resistance of the water fluctuates which causes alternating current in the circuit. For this to work, the resistance of the water must vary substantially over the short distance the needle or rod vibrates. Acidulated water works well because only a small amount of acid is added. If one millimeter of acidulated water has a resistance of 100 ohms, two millimeters would have 200 ohms which would produce enough alternating current to transmit audio signals in thousands of feet of wire. Mercury will not work because the resistance of one millimeter of mercury is less than a tenth of an ohm and vibration of a needle in mercury would produce negligible alternating current.


Elisha Gray reasoned that a metal rod vibrating up and down in acidulated water would alternately lengthen and shorten the small distance between the bottom end of the rod and a metal plate at the bottom of the glass container holding the water. This is the invention described in Gray's caveat.[1] When Alexander Bell's lawyer heard that Gray had described a vibrating rod in a liquid to vary the resistance, he added a claim for variable resistance in a draft of Bell's unfiled patent application and added an additional seven sentences that mentioned mercury as the liquid.[2] The lawyer knew that Bell had experimented with a wire dipped in mercury to provide a flexible electrical switch.[3]


On March 10, 1876, when Bell and Watson tested their first successful water transmitter, Bell used a needle in the water to minimize the inertial mass moved by the diaphragm and relied on variable resistance in the meniscus of the water on the needle. The depth of the needle made little difference.


Other minor variations and improvements were made to the liquid microphone by Majoranna, Chambers, Vanni, Sykes, and Elisha Gray.


Although the water microphone was commercially impractical, the variable resistance feature inspired Thomas Edison to experiment with dry carbon (graphite and amorphous) to provide the variable resistance. The Edison transmitter with later improvements was used for more than 60 years.

[edit]

* Microphone
* Hydrophone

Based on my search through multiple Wikipedia articles, here are the specific factual details you requested about Elisha Gray:

## 1. Exact 1876 Patent Caveat Filing Date
**February 14, 1876** - Gray signed and had his patent caveat notarized on this date. The caveat described a telephone using a liquid transmitter. His lawyer Baldwin then submitted it to the US Patent Office.

## 2. Technical Details of Liquid Transmitter Design
- **Principle**: Based on Ohm's law, using variable resistance in a liquid conductor
- **Construction**: A metal needle or rod placed "just barely" into acidulated water (water/acid mixture) in a glass container with a metal plate at the bottom
- **Mechanism**: Sound waves cause a diaphragm to vibrate, which makes the needle/rod vibrate up and down in the water
- **Physics**: The needle's movement varies the electrical resistance of the water (1mm of acidulated water = ~100 ohms resistance, 2mm = ~200 ohms), creating alternating current
- **Key feature**: The needle moved up and down, lengthening and shortening the distance between the rod's bottom end and the container's metal plate

## 3. Comparison with Bell's Design
**Gray's liquid transmitter** (variable resistance):
- Used conductive liquid (acidulated water)
- Variable resistance through liquid displacement
- Needle/rod vibration in liquid
- According to Supreme Court testimony, the device described in Gray's caveat "would not work"

**Bell's electromagnetic design** (original patent):
- Used electromagnetic principles
- Permanent magnets and iron diaphragms
- Did not originally include liquid transmitter

However, Bell's first successful transmission on March 10, 1876 used a liquid transmitter nearly identical to Gray's design, which led to the controversy.

## 4. February 14, 1876 Timing Controversy
- **Both files same day**: Gray's caveat and Bell's patent application were both filed on February 14, 1876
- **Arrival dispute**: "Which application arrived first is hotly disputed, although Gray believed that his caveat arrived a few hours before Bell's application"
- **Bell's lawyers**: Had been waiting "for months, under instructions not to file it in the USA until it had been filed in Britain first" (due to British patent regulations)
- **Key similarity**: Bell's March 10, 1876 lab notebook entry shows a drawing of a liquid transmitter "very similar" to Gray's caveat design

## Additional Key Dates
- February 11, 1876: Gray made his liquid transmitter drawing
- January 20, 1876: Bell signed and notarized his patent application (held until February 14)
- March 7, 1876: Bell's patent No. 174,465 was granted
- March 10, 1876: Bell's first successful transmission using liquid transmitter

The controversy centers on whether Bell independently conceived of the liquid transmitter or was inspired by Gray's caveat, with some evidence suggesting Bell's lawyers may have obtained an unfair advantage through the timing and potential access to Gray's design.

<document>
<title>The Telephone Cases</title>
<fragment>

Bell's second fundamental patent expired on January 30, 1894, when the gates were then opened to independent telephone companies to compete with the Bell System. In all, the American Bell Telephone Company and its successor, AT&T, litigated 587 court challenges to its patents, including five that went to the US Supreme Court and, aside from two minor contract lawsuits, never lost a single case that was concluded with a final stage judgment.[1][2]




## Size

[edit]

The Court's decision in the *Telephone Cases* is notable for the size of the opinions delivered; together, they occupy the entire 126th volume of the *United States Reports*.



## Notable cases

[edit]

Among the notable court cases involving the Bell Telephone Company, later renamed to the American Bell Telephone Company, were those related to challenges by Elisha Gray, a principal in Western Electric, as depicted in the Elisha Gray and Alexander Bell telephone controversy.

Based on my search of the Wikipedia articles for "The Telephone Cases" and related content, I can provide you with the specific details from the available information:

## 1. Supreme Court Key Findings and Legal Reasoning

From the available content, the Supreme Court's legal reasoning was limited but included:

- **The decision was narrowly divided**: The Court came "within one vote of overturning the Bell patent because of the eloquence of lawyer Lysander Hill for the Peoples Telephone Company."

- **Court composition and voting pattern**:
  - **Majority**: Chief Justice Morrison Waite, joined by Miller, Matthews, and Blatchford
  - **Dissent**: Justice Bradley, joined by Field and Harlan
  - **Abstained**: Justices Gray and Lamar took no part in the consideration

- **Specific decisions on related cases**:
  - The Supreme Court affirmed: *Dolbear v. American Bell Tel. Co.*, *Molecular Tel. Co. v. American Bell Tel. Co.*, and *People's Tel. Co. v. American Bell Tel. Co.*
  - The Supreme Court reversed *American Bell Tel Co. v. Molecular Tel. Co.*

## 2. Court Statistics and Outcomes

The article provides this comprehensive statistic:

**587 total court challenges** were litigated by the American Bell Telephone Company and its successor, AT&T.

**Key success rate**: 
- **5 cases went to the U.S. Supreme Court**
- **Aside from two minor contract lawsuits, Bell never lost a single case that was concluded with a final stage judgment**

This represents an essentially perfect victory rate in concluded patent litigation cases.

## 3. Details About the 587 Court Challenges

The available information about the 587 challenges includes:

- **Timeline**: These challenges spanned from the 1870s through the 1880s and beyond
- **Outcome**: Overwhelming success for the Bell Company
- ** Exceptions**: Only "two minor contract lawsuits" mentioned as losses
- **Duration**: Continued until Bell's second fundamental patent expired on January 30, 1894, when "the gates were then opened to independent telephone companies to compete with the Bell System"

## 4. Notable Context

- **Daniel Drawbaugh testimony**: In lower court proceedings, the Peoples Telephone Company's claimant testified that he didn't remember how he came to his invention, saying: "I don't remember how I came to it. I had been experimenting in that direction. I don't remember of getting at it by accident either. I don't remember of anyone talking to me of it."
- **Investor reaction**: Peoples Telephone Company stock "rose briefly during the early proceedings but dropped after its claimant took the stand"

## Limitations

Unfortunately, the Wikipedia articles don't contain more detailed legal reasoning from the Supreme Court majority opinion, or a breakdown of how many of the 587 specific challenges were ruled in Bell's favor versus other outcomes. The available content focuses more on the high-level statistics and the fact of Bell's overwhelming success rather than the detailed legal arguments or case-by-case breakdown.

For more detailed legal reasoning, you would need to consult the actual Supreme Court opinion (126 U.S. 1) or other specialized legal sources, as the Wikipedia articles appear to focus more on the historical significance and outcomes rather than the detailed legal analysis.

Based on my comprehensive search through Wikipedia articles, here are the specific factual details you requested about early telephone inventors:

## **Antonio Meucci:**

### Exact 1871 patent caveat filing date for telettrofono
- **Year**: 1871 (exact date not specified in Wikipedia content)

### Patent number if any  
- **None specified** - this was a patent caveat, not a full patent

### What the patent claimed
- Employed **"only a single conduction wire, with the telephone's transmitter-receivers being insulated from a 'ground return' path"**
- **Critical limitation**: "the caveat did not contain a clear description of how the asserted invention would actually function"
- **Meucci supporters claim**: "the attorney erased margin notes Meucci had added to the document"

### When he first demonstrated device and to whom
- **Location**: Staten Island, New York
- **Date**: **1854** (first American demonstration)
- Later claimed to have invented "a paired electromagnetic transmitter and receiver, where the motion of a diaphragm modulated a signal in a coil by moving an electromagnet"

### Technical composition - materials and how it worked
- **Design**: Paired electromagnetic transmitter and receiver
- **Working mechanism**: "the motion of a diaphragm modulated a signal in a coil by moving an electromagnet"
- **1871 caveat version**: Used single conduction wire
- **Insulation**: Transmitter-receivers were insulated from a ground return path

### Why and when it lapsed - specific dates
- **Expiration date**: **December 28, 1874** - "On 28 December 1874, Meucci's Telettrofono patent caveat expired"
- **Cost to renew**: $10 renewal fee
- **Financial dispute**: Meucci supporters claim hardship, but critics note he filed for and was granted full patents in 1872, 1873, 1875, and 1876 ($35 each), plus one additional $10 patent caveat, totaling $150 for other patents

### Recognition received
- **2002 U.S. House of Representatives Resolution H.Res.269**
- Museum established by Basilio Catania and Italian Society of Electrotechnics
- Recognition in Italian encyclopedias (Treccani, Microsoft Encarta, Enciclopedia Italiana)

---

## **Johann Philipp Reis:**

### Exact year/date of first telephone prototype around 1861
- **October 1861**: Reis's first successful work dated to October 1861
- **October 26, 1861**: Reis articulated his invention in a lecture before the Physical Society of Frankfurt

### Technical details of how device worked
- **Make-and-break circuit**: Contacts that opened and closed like switches
- Used a vibrating needle against a contact point to create electrical signals
- Captured sound → converted to electrical impulses → transmitted via wires → transformed into recognizable sounds

### Components and mechanism
**Transmitter Components:**
- Needle with contact point for make-and-break operation

**Receiver Components:**
- **Iron knitting needle** (early version) / **Iron bar** (advanced version)
- **Coil of wire** wound around the iron
- **Violin** (early version resonator) / **Cigar-box-shaped resonator** (advanced version)

### Evidence about intelligible speech transmission
**Positive Evidence:**
- **1862**: Demonstrated to Wilhelm von Legat, Inspector of Royal Prussian Telegraph Corps
- **1863**: Widely publicly demonstrated; used to transmit speech
- **1874**: STC tests confirmed it could transmit/receive speech with **good quality (fidelity)**, though low intensity
- **1947**: STC engineers found 1863 model could "**reproduce speech of good quality, but of low efficiency**"

**Limitations:**
- Could transmit **continuous musical tones** but produced **indistinct speech**
- Thomas Edison's test found "**single words... were perceptible indistinctly**"

### Details about Reiss-Telegraph device
- No separate "Reiss-Telegraph" device documented in sources
- Referred to as: **Reis telephone**, **"make-and-break" telephone**, **"telephon"** (Reis's original coined term)

---

## **Elisha Gray:**

### Exact 1876 patent caveat filing date
- **February 14, 1876** - Gray signed and had his patent caveat notarized, then submitted to US Patent Office by his lawyer Baldwin

### Technical details of liquid transmitter design
- **Principle**: Based on Ohm's law, using variable resistance in a liquid conductor
- **Construction**: Metal needle/rod placed "just barely" into acidulated water in glass container with metal plate at bottom
- **Mechanism**: Sound waves cause diaphragm to vibrate, making needle/rod vibrate up and down in water
- **Physics**: Needle's movement varies electrical resistance of water (1mm acidulated water = ~100 ohms, 2mm = ~200 ohms), creating alternating current

### Comparison with Bell's design
**Gray's liquid transmitter:**
- Used conductive liquid (acidulated water)
- Variable resistance through liquid displacement
- According to Supreme Court testimony: "would not work"

**Bell's electromagnetic design:**
- Used electromagnetic principles with permanent magnets and iron diaphragms
- Did not originally include liquid transmitter
- However, Bell's first successful transmission on March 10, 1876 used a liquid transmitter nearly identical to Gray's design

### February 14, 1876 timing controversy
- **Both files same day**: Gray's caveat and Bell's patent application both filed February 14, 1876
- **Arrival dispute**: "Which application arrived first is hotly disputed, although Gray believed that his caveat arrived a few hours before Bell's application"
- **Bell's lawyers**: Had been waiting "for months, under instructions not to file it in the USA until it had been filed in Britain first"
- **Key similarity**: Bell's March 10, 1876 lab notebook entry shows drawing of liquid transmitter "very similar" to Gray's caveat design

---

## **Legal Controversies:**

### Date of Supreme Court Telephone Cases decision
- **March 19, 1888**

### Key findings
- **"The Bell Company patent was valid and that the Molecular case was reversed"**
- Supreme Court decisions:
  - *Dolbear v. American Bell Tel. Co.* - **Affirmed**
  - *Molecular Tel. Co. v. American Bell Tel. Co.* - **Affirmed**

- **5 cases went to U.S. Supreme Court**
